subtopic: MOTION FOR SECOND READING OF CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY BILL.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before recess, I had been referring to the provision of section 24 in the Act of 1914, which provides that, in case of default the Governor in Council may, if authorized by Parliament, and upon such terms and conditions, if any, as Parliament may prescribe, declare the equity of redemption of the Canadian Northern Railway company and of all other persons to be absolutely foreclosed, notwithstanding any rule of law or equity to the contrary. I regard that as a very important provision. It created a new relation between the company and the Crown. Upon the one side the company said in effect: If you will give us the aid for which we are now asking, that is, if you will guarantee our bonds to the extent of $45,000,000, we shall be able to get along without any further assistance. As horn, members are aware, there was very strong opposition on the part of many hon. gentlemen to burdening the country further in connection with the Canadian Northern Railway company. That company had received large grants of public money in the past; it had been aided by guaranteed bonds, and, in addition, the various provinces had been contributing very extensively to the construction of the road. It was, therefore, universally recognized that no money from any private source had been put into the construction of the railway. This Honse
knew as well then as it knows to-day, after the reports of the Government commission that the road had been constructed entirely out of public moneys. In order to remove as far as possible any objection to the bonds of the company to the extent of $45,000,000 being then guaranteed, the Government asked Parliament to provide certain safeguards, amongst which was this provision in section 24 to which I have referred. The company, when it consented to accept that aid was a party to the contract contained in the statute. The company received its aid upon that condition, and it is hound just as much as if a separate agreement had been entered into under which it had stipulated that in case it should make default in the future the Government and Parliament would not he bound to recognize that there was any value whatever m its equity of redemption, bu1 could at once take steps by Order in Council to foreclose. We are here under circumstances very different from those that existed prior to 1914. We are here in the face of a certain condition created by that statute. We are here as trustees of the people, as guardians of the rights of the people, and we should he acting contrary to our .duty if we in any way attempted to alter those rights, or if we refused to recognize the rights and obligations upon the part of the Canadian Northern, and Mackenzie and Mann Limited and the other holders of the stock in the Canadian Northern and the subsidiary companies. I am, therefore, unable to see any excuse whatever for the Government not taking advantage of the powers which Parliament granted to them under the Act of 1914.
At first it was stated by one or two hon. gentlemen opposite, that the course the Government intends pursuing is the same thing as acting under section 24. In iact, however, it is an entirely different thing. If section 24 were acted upon, the Government, on the authority of Parliament, would have the right, without the payment of a single dollar more of the people's money, to become the owners of this entire railway system. But it is proposed by this arrangement to treat this company as a solvent-concern, and to appoint arbitrators for the purpose of valuing the common stock of the company. I very much mistake the meaning of figures and of statements if I do not see in the statement, which hag been submitted to the Government by the Canadian Northern Railway Company and laid before this House by the Government as containing reliable information, a delib-

erate laying, upon the part of Messrs. Mackenzie and Mann, of a foundation for an enormous valuation of the stock of this company.
The Minister of Finance has said that this company require a large amount of money to carry on their work. He has not offered to this House any request in writing from the Canadian Northern nor from Messrs. Mackenzie and Mann. He has not presented a single statement from them showing what they require or that they require any amount. He has stated that it will take some $20,000,000 to meet, in the immediate future, their interest indebtedness and to provide for necessary rolling stock, and that it will require great financial effort in order to wipe off those shortterm obligations which have been incurred against securities, largely in the city of New York. But there is not the scratch of a pen from Messrs. Mackenzie and Mann, Limited, or the Canadian Northern Railway Company corroborating the statement of the Minister of Finance. It is, therefore, open to those gentlemen, when they come before the arbitrators to say: We are not bound by the opinion expressed by the Minister of Finance; we presented to the Government a statement showing our financial position; we showed that we had a surplus of $37,000,000 after making provision for our common stock at its face value; the Minister of Finance presented that statement to the House of Commons as a statement that could be relied upon; surely, therefore, we are and can be bound only by the statement which we have presented to the Government and which the Government has presented to Parliament. They will be able to say to the arbitrators: So far from our requiring any large amount of money, all that we owe in the way of outstanding accounts with construction is $999,566.95, and they can well show that before the arbitrators in black and white among the statements laid by the Minister of Finance before this House. Then if it is said: Oh, thirty million dollars is required immediately to purchase rolling stock and put the road in good condition, before the arbitration, they will say: In the statement we submitted all that is required up to the 30th June, 1918, for rolling stock and for betterments, as we showed in black and white, is the sum of $6,950,000 instead $20,000,000. Will it not be open to them to say:	This stock has been represented by
absolutely valuable assets at $100,000,000 and our statement shows a surplus of $37,000,000 above that, and who will dare to 
say we are bankrupt? Who will dare to say we cannot go on? The opinion of the Minister of Finance will not be evidence. It will be upon the statements of the accountants such as we have before us, that these arbitrators must aot, because they will be sworn to discharge their duty- in accordance with the evidence which will be presented before them. This statement was prepared evidently with the intention of showing that the company is solvent and perfectly able to go ahead. If you take it as true, it shows they are not insolvent, and shows they do not require any financial aid from, the Government. It lays the foundation for them to submit to the arbitrators that they have a most valuable property. With a surplus of $11,000,000 of revenue over and above operating expenses, and with the prospective earnings-which always will be taken into consideration by arbitrators unless they are expressly excluded from their consideration-Mackenzie and Mann, by these statements which they have submitted to this Parliament through the Minister of Finance will be in a position to urge before the arbitrators that they should receive full par value for the stock issued by the company. Will not that be a condition of affairs to which the people of the country will look forward with a great deal of anxiety? As I have said, this road was built with the money of the people of this country. The commission has declared that the common stock has no present value, nor is it of any potential value. Since the year 1914, when this 'bargain was made, as set out in section 24 of this statute, the Government has been compelled to give Mackenzie and Mann an additional sum of $15,000,000. Last year when that amount was given, the Minister of Finance .stated it was given for the purpose of preventing the company from making default. And we are faced to-day with the extraordinary condition that this Government is actually endeavouring to prevent the conditions under which the provisions of section 24 can be invoked. They have, by giving money to Mackenzie and Mann, prevented the default taking place, which would enable the Government, with the authority of Parliament, to take over this entire system without putting any more money into the enterprise. Whether that Act on the part of the Government can be defended or not, I leave it to the House to say. I do not think it can be defended, and I do not think the people of this country will be disposed to tolerate such a con-

dition of affairs. It is proposed now that arbitrators should value this property, in the face of the fact that the Minister of Finance tells us that the Company is bound to become bankrupt if it is not assisted; in the face of the fact that the Prime Minister stated this afternoon in effect that it is perfectly evident that unless further aid is given the company cannot carry on, and a receiver must be appointed. If that condition of affairs exists to-day, all the Government has to do, and all it has to ask Parliament to do, is to invoke the powers contained in section 24, and take over the road, foreclose the equity of redemption absolutely, without the payment of a dollar.
My right hon. friend says that would be contrary to one's sense of justice. If that be so, I would like to know why it was put in the statute. Was it put in to deceive the members of this House? Did the Government not know what it meant when it was put in? Did they not intend it to be acted upon? They said if default should be made Parliament would have the right, without any terms or conditions whatsoever and without providing for a single dollar to be paid, to foreclose the equity of redemption without resorting to a court of law. Will any member of the Government explain why that was put there if it was not intended to be acted upon? Why it was put there if it meant nothing? Surely, Mr. Speaker, it is impossible for any one to suggest that it was not intended by the Government, and was not taken seriously by this House. I have already called attention to the great weight that was placed upon that provision by my hon. friend the Solicitor General, who made a very able and forcible speech in presenting the matter to the House. I well remember how strongly, and with what force and eloquence, he dwelt upon the provisions of section 24. They were new legislation, he said;-ordinarily, the holder of a mortgage would be compelled to resort to a court of law, and go through the proceedings of foreclosure, but he spoke with pride and very grealt gratification of the fact that the Government had been able to evolve a scheme original with itself and containing powers which would be most beneficial to the country in case any default were made. That statement impressed many members of the House. My hon. friend from St. Antoine (Sir Herbert Ames), a very thoughtful gentleman, took the view, as piany gentlemen upon the other side of the House did, that almost too great aid had *already been granted to the Canadian
Northern, and accepted the proposal of the Government with great reluctance. Let us see what that hon. gentleman said in regard to this proposal. His remarks will be found at page 3733 of Hansard:
There is another feature of this matter which, I think, is well worthy of consideration. What is to happen in case of default? We have hitherto been dealing with the situation in case of success; the Government has very carefully looked ahead in regard to what might happen in case of failure.
And, Sir, when the time comes that the Prime Minister says that, notwithstanding the $15,000,000 we granted last year, failure looms right ahead, the Government draws back, and refuses to act upon this wonderful section, the preparation of which must have taxed its ingenuity 'to the utmost, and which appealed to the favourable consideration of members on the other side of the House at all events. The Government draws back and says: We will not allow default to take place.
We have given over $15,000,000 to prevent default, and before the time shall come when the company must make default, we will pass this Act, we will buy out the common stock from the company as a going concern, treat it as perfectly solvent and pay to these gentlemen whatever the arbi-. trators may choose to determine, whose judgment will be final, over whose judgment this Parliament can exercise no supervision, no control, and from which it will have no appeal. The Government will be bound to pay out of the public funds whatever amount these gentlemen may find this stock to be worth, without any appeal to this Parliament or to any court, even to the Supreme Court of Canada. That is acting upon the provisions of this wonderful section with a vengeance. Let me proceed with the remarks of my hon. friend from Montreal, St. Antoine. He said:
The Government has very carefully looked ahead in regard to what might happen in case of failure. Ordinarily it is a very slow process to foreclose a railroad and for the bondholders gradually to take possession of the physical assets thereof. The Government in this case, however, has supplied a method of quick procedure whereby the axe drops instantly and whereby there can be no coming back for further assistance. It is definitely stipulated in this undertaking what shall constitute any event of default; it is so clearly defined that there can be no possible misunderstanding. Should the Canadian Northern railway fail to pay interest on the securities which are to be issued in connection with the guarantee which we are now authorizing, or should they fail to carry out any of the conditions contained in the trust deed as accompanying that guarantee, they would commit an event of default.

Just as my hon. friend from South Renfrew (Mr. Graham) stated this afternoon. Then my hon. friend from Montreal, St. Antoine, proceeds:
Should the Canadian Northern on any of the previously guaranteed securities or hereafter guaranteed securities fail to pay the interest, they would commit an event of default. If any part of the system goes into the hands of a receiver; if any branch of the whole tree shows signs of decay, that is an event of default and in any of these events the Government can drop the axe without delay. I have heard this agreement described somewhat as a case where the culprit has confessed judgment and has been let out on suspended sentence. Some elements of the agreement certainty can be compared with such a case. The trial is over.
Mark the words, Mr. Speaker. All this in the face of the facts that the arbitrators are to value this equity of redemption, that lawyers, witnesses and expert accountants are to be heard, and that Mackenzie and Mann are to be allowed to prove that because of the prospective earnings this common stock has an enormous value even although the company to-day, as the Prime Minister .says, is actually upon the eve of bankruptcy. The hon. member for St Antoine .says:
The trial is over. The applicants for aid admit that without our help they cannot complete the road. We have undertaken to give them a last chance-[DOT]
We have undertaken to give them a last chance.
-and it will never be necessary for them again to come here, nor will it he necessary for this Parliament to listen to another discussion such as is taking place this session. They have been tried; I may almost say they have been found guilty and let out on suspended sentence. If there is an event of default; if they fail to perform the obligations that by this new trust deed are placed upon them, the axe drops and that is all there Is to it.
How my hon. friend the Solicitor 'General (iMr. Meighen) must have laughed in his sleeve at the innocence of the hon. member for Sit. Antoine when he took his word in 1914 as to the effect and intention of this section and when he said that it would be acted upon when the time arrived !

subtopic: MOTION FOR SECOND READING OF CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY BILL.
speechtext: Would the hon. gentleman read the words that he took from my speech in 1914?

subtopic: MOTION FOR SECOND READING OF CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY BILL.
speechtext:
I cannot conceive that the hon. member for St. Antoine misinterpreted the 'Speech of the Solicitor General. At all events, I read the speech of the Soli-tor General. It will appear in Hansard tomorrow .and I think it entirely justified

the hon. member for St. Antoine in believing that in case of default the axe would fall-that the trial was over-that the last chance had been given, and that if default was made automatically Parliament would be asked to agree that the equity of redemption in the Canadian Northern Railway Company and all other persons interested should be foreclosed summarily by Order in Council. Just let me read this _ last sentence over again:
If there is an event of default; if they fail to perform the obligations that by this new trust deed are placed upon them, the axe drops and that is all there is to it.
That is the interpretation that the hon. member foir St. Antoine places upon it, that is the interpretation that any reasonable man would place upon it, or else why put it in the statute book in such clear, unmistakable language? The hon. member for St. Antoine proceeds to say:
There is a summary method, therefore, by which the Government steps in and takes possession of the whole enterprise. The Government can replace the directors by Order in Council; the new hoard of directors will have all the rights that would be given by a board of directors elected by the shareholders, and they can deal with the physical property as they see fit. Then, the Government can declare the mortgage foreclosed and can enter into the benefit of '.lie equities, subject, of course, to the consent of Parliament. If the Government, in such an event, enters into control, it may become the owner of the system by assuming the responsibilities and powers as provided by this proposed legislation. The Government could then arrange the whole financial system involved so as to protect all concerned. The Government can operate; the Government can lease, or the Government can create a new railway company to manage the road and enter into ownership, if so desired. "
Using, in Teg.ard to the organization of a new railway company, almost the very language which I used in the early portion of my remarks. The Solicitor General, from whom I might quote, did not use the very language which was used by the hon. member for St. Antoine. Perhaps not the very language, but members of the Government sat in their places and heard that hon. gentleman give that as the interpretation of the statute and what could be done under it. No one ventured to say that he had not interpreted the meaning of the statute correctly; no one suggested any idea of that kind. When the Government got that legislation through and induced this House to impose that enormous obligation, upon the people of the country they knew that the members oif this House and the people believed that, in case this company could not carry on its business with the guarantee

which was then given, it would have no right to make 'any claim for this equity of redemption in the road and that Parliament should have the right to become the owners of the entire system and then carry it on either as a Government work or through a company which the Government could be given power by Parliament to create, and with respect to which they might appoint the necessary officers and managers.
,In some remarks which the Minister of Finance made when the resolution was before the House, he objected to expropriation because he said that if the system were expropriated the Government might have to pay, under the circumstances which would then arise, -cash for all the outstanding obligations, and he rather intimated that, even although they might be acquired at their present market value, which, in a great many cases, amounting to many, many millions of dollars, is not over fifty per cent of their par value, it would be an advantage to allow the securities to run on for their full term because they had been placed at a comparatively low rate of interest
Well, Sir, under the provisions of section 24, as the Government well knows to-day and as they knew when they presented the section for the approval of this House, that same result would follow. The Government would not be obliged to pay off these securities until their due date; they would simply foreclose the equity of redemption and all outstanding securities would remain just as they were, subject to the payment of the interest upon them and subject to the payment of the principal when the date of maturity arrived. Therefore, there is every advantage, from the public standpoint in carrying out the provisions of section 24, while no disadvantage can be suggested. And as I have said, these are the rights which the people of Canada have to-day. They have the right, through this Parliament, to foreclose the equity of redemption of the Canadian Northern Railway Company and everybody else upon these securities in case of default occurring. This Government is. committing a crime against the people of this country if they further assist this company financially in order to prevent default. It is the duty of the Government to the people of Canada to let the company carry on as best it can. If it can meet its interest, if it can avoid default through its own efforts and those of the financial men interested in the enterprise,
well and good; this Government and Parliament have nothing further to say about it. But if they cannot carry on, if they must make default, then let them make default; and I would say that this Parliament should be ready with its legislation, and this Government should be ready through the authority of this Parliament, to exercise immediately the powers given to them by section 24 to foreclose the equity of redemption, take possession of the property, organize, if they should think it 'better to do so, a new company, appoint the board of directors, and carry on all the operations of the Canadian Northern system. They would be able to carry them on without any delay, without disorganizing the system and without running the risk, as they are doing to-day, of involving the people of this country in an enormous liability, the amount of which no man can foresee, but the amount of which depends on the arbitrary will of three gentlemen who may be appointed to arbitrate the value of the common stock as between the Government and the gentlemen interested in the securities.
I should like to answer the statement of the Prime Minister (Sir Robert Borden) this afternoon that it did not lie in our mouths to object to this system of taking over the stock on a valuation by arbitrators. My right hon. friend quoted from a resolution which I moved in 1914. But surely, Sir, it scarcely lies in the mouth of the Prime Minister to claim that arbitration is the right thing to do in regard to taking over this stock when he himself voted against arbitration in 1914, even with the limitations which my resolution placed upon that mode of procedure. My right hon. friend voted against it and called upon all his supporters to stand with him in voting against arbitration, and they did all manfully and loyally standing up as one man and denounce this method of taking over stock on valuation by arbitration. Let us see what I proposed and what hon. members voted against. I moved
That all the words after "that" be struck out and the following words be inserted in lieu thereof: "That said resolution be not now concurred in but that it be referred back to the Committee of the Whole House with instructions to amend the same in the following particulars :
(a)	To provide for the reduction of the issued capital stock of the Canadian Northern Railway Company to $30,000,000 par value, subject to the right to make provision for an addition thereto of an amount not exceeding $25,000,000 if it should at any time become necessary for the purpose of exchange of the

income charge convertible debenture stock mentioned in paragraph 12 of the said resolution.
(b)	To provide for the transfer of such stock (with the exception of sufficient shares to qualify the directors) to the Receiver General to be held by him in trust for His Majesty.
(c)	For the holding of the said stock by His Majesty for the period of five years.
(d)	To provide that in case no default is made by the company in the payment of interest on the bonds of the company to be guaranteed by His Majesty as provided by said resolution, and in case the conditions of the said resolution and the agreement therein provided for shall be in all other respects carried out during such period of five years, the said stock shall be transferred to Mackenzie, Mann and Company, Limited, or their nominees, unless His Majesty through the Governor in Council should exercise the option hereinafter mentioned.
(e)	To provide that the Governor in Council shall have the option at any time within such period of five years to acquire the absolute ownership of the said stock and of the said Canadian Northern Railway system, and of all the constituent and subsidiary companies mentioned in the said resolution or proposed agreement, subject to existing encumbrances and to said arrangements regarding the conversion of said income charge convertible debenture stock, for a price to be fixed by arbitration, but not to exceed the sum of $30,000,000, being the par value of such stock so to be reduced as above provided.
Now, what did that provide for? It made no provision whatever, and did not contemplate; that the stock should be taken if there was any default. It provided that if the company should be able to carry on for five years successfully, if it made no default, paid its interest, these, at any time before the expiration of these five years, the Government would have the right to take over the stock by arbitration. That would be in the casp of a concern that was able to meet all its obligations, not of a concern that was bankrupt, not of a concern that had to come back in 1916 and get $15,000,000 more; not of a concern of which the Prime Minister says to-day that it is unable to go on, that unless it gets aid it must stop, must make default and go into the hands of a receiver. The proposition which I made contemplated an entirely different condition, It provided only that the Government might act and take over the stock by .arbitration in case the company should prove successful and should be able to demonstrate its ability to be .successful by being able to look after its interest for the full period of five years. In the meantime, as a condition of granting this aid, the stock was to be reduced to $30,000,000, and was to be handed over and held in trust under the control of His Majesty until such time as the company demonstrated its ability to carry on and per-

form its obligations. That resolution was voted down by a party vote. Then, later on, I think when the Bill name up for third reading, my right hon. friend the leader of the Opposition (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) moved the resolution to which also the Prime Minister has referred. But it must be borne in mind that in interpreting that resolution reference must be had to the previous resolution which had been moved by myself and had been voted down by a majority of this House. Under the rules ef the House the same resolution could not be moved a second time, and that is why the language of the second resolution, in amendment to the third reading of the Bill, was changed; it was necessary to do it in order to comply with the rules of the House. But it must be interpreted in the spirit of the resolution which had been moved previously and voted down, and when the word "reasonable" was used by the right hon. leader of the Opposition, it must he regarded as having reference to what is set forth, namely five years, in the resolution which was previously before the House.
There is one other matter I wish to refer to 'briefly, and that is the question of the lands. I said the other day-and my argument has not been answered-that whatever may he said with reference to the railway system, it seems to me utterly unpardonable for the Government to ask .this country to assume the vast obligation involved in these land debentures. We have a statement before the House that the lands remaining unsold consist of 2,000,000 acres in the province of Ontario, about 400,000 acres in the province of Quebec, and something like 1,000,000 acres in the three western provinces. There are also some sales agreements. The Government is asking Parliament to stand behind these land debentures, just as they are asking Parliament to stand behind and give .a par value to all these underlying securities which to-day are not selling upon the markets of the world at over fifty, sixty, or seventy per cent of their face value, and the Government is asking Parliament to do that without giving us any information by experts as to the value of these lands. Taking, first, the 2,000,000 acres in Ontario, I would ask my hon. friend if these are covered by the land debentures? I do not think they are.

subtopic: MOTION FOR SECOND READING OF CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY BILL.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister (Sir Robert Borden) and the Finance Minister (Sir Thomas White) this afternoon must have anticipated the remarks of the member for St. John (Mr. Pugsley) in the first part of his speech. They so completely answered his remarks that it would be folly for me to take up any more time by entering into a discussion of them.
My hon. friend, however, has called attention to a statement with regard to the value of the lands in Northern Ontario, especially those along the line of the Canadian Northern railway. It was my privilege to spend some fifteen days in a tour of inspection of the Canadian Northern railway some two years ago, in company with a number of members from both sides of the House. We passed through hundreds of miles of valuable pulp lands right alongside the Canadian Northern railway in the northern part of Ontario. I was informed by the officials of that road that the bulk .jf these limits were owned by the Canadian Northern Railway company. If the hon. gentleman would take the trouble of going over that splendid railway he would come to a very different conclusion in regard to this matter; he would not talk about $1 an acre when speaking of such valuable lands as these.
We have been listening to a discussion of the legal and financial sides of this question; let us discuss it for a few moments from the business standpoint. This is the largest undertaking excluding matters pertaining to the war, that this Parliament has had to deal with since Confederation, and it is necessary that hon. gentlemen on both sides of the House should give it their most careful attention. It is the greatest public ownership proposal ever presented to the people of Canada, and its success or failure will mean either life or death to public ownership in Canada, so far as the Dominion Government is concerned.
Some few days ago half a dozen hon. gentlemen opposite suggested five or six different methods of dealing with this question. They emphasized especially the fact that we should not allow politics to creep into the administration of this enterprise. I am satisfied, from the statements made by the Finance Minister, the Prime Minister, and the Minister of Railways (Hon. Frank

Cochrane) that no political interference will creep into the management. It certainly would be a most serious state of affairs ii politics should in any way interfere. The member for Edmonton (Mr. Oliver) the other day asserted that politics would interfere in this case as they did in connection with the administration of the Intercolonial railway. I think that
9	p.m. he did not deal fairly with the Minister of Railways. To my mind, no Minister of Railways has ever more carefully guarded his department in that respect. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Cochrane) has been most careful not to allow politics to interfere with the management of the government railways.
Government ownership operation and control are to receive a serious test. Every man, woman and child in Canada is interested in this proposal. This will be the people's railroad; they will own and control it. All our people recognize the importance of transportation. One of the greatest elements in the price of food and manufactured products is transportation. Railway rates are in effect public taxes, and we should see to it that the management of this road, as well as the management of all the other transportation facilities of our country, is carried on in such manner as to secure to the people the greatest possible benefit at the lowest possible cost.
Hon. gentlemen opposite argue that we are not going to receive value for the money to be invested in this enterprise. I wonder if they have taken into consideration the actual cost of this road. If they will add to the actual cost of the enterprise the additional cost of the rolling stock, rails, and everything connected with it, they will find that this proposal is a most advantageous one for the people of Canada. Take, for example, the rolling stock. It is estimated that $56,000,000 has been paid for the rolling stock on the Canadian Northern railway system. They have taken off $11,000,000 for depreciation, leaving $45,000,000 as the present value of the rolling stock. I have made inquiries of men who are thoroughly acquainted with the handling of railway equipment and its value, and they inform me that the Canadian Northern Railway rolling stock is to-day worth well over $60,000,000.
Further, let us compare the investment in road and equipment in respect of the Canadian Northern railway system with that of other railroads in Canada. It is important that the people should know what this road has actually cost ai*d how it compares in certain respects with other railroads in this country. At the close of the year ending June 30,1916, the investment in road and equipment as carried on the books of the companies or of the Government was as follows:
Canadian Pacific railway, $68,233 per mile. Canadian Northern railway, $54,961 per mile.
Grand Trunk, $127,340 per mile.
Grand Trunk Pacific, $98,018 per mile. Transcontinental, $88,332 per mile. Intercolonial, $76,733 per mile.
The actual average cost per mile of the Canadian Northern was nearly one-third less than the average cost per mile of these other railroads. The average cost of all the railroads was $75,524 per mile, while the actual cost of the Canadian Northern amounted to $54,961 per mile.
Another advantage in taking over this road is that the Intercolonial will through it be connected up with the West. Up to the present time the Intercolonial has been up against a very stiff proposition as to its connections at Montreal and Quebec, but under this proposal it will become part of a great transcontinental railway system.
Let us look at the enormous value of the different terminals owned, controlled and operated by the Canadian Northern Railway company at Montreal, Toronto, Winnipeg and Edmonton, and the 300 acres it owns in the heart of the city of Vancouver, and we shall be able to realize what tremendous terminal advantages this company possesses in those great cities.
This is a most opportune time to take over the road, as hon. members will see if they investigate the financial statements which have been submitted. I congratulate the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Railways upon placing in the hands of members of this House such complete statements bearing on the finances and the general management of the road. This railway has borrowed enormous sums of money at 3J and 4 per cent, whereas if we had to go into the market for money to-day we would be compelled to pay over 6 per cent. In addition to that, the securities run for ten, twenty, thirty and forty years, and at the end of those periods I am sure the people of Canada will be in a position to meet the obligations of the road, which will then, I believe, be one of the greatest assets of our Dominion.

There is no question that this railroad has developed Canada as no other great enterprise has done within the last fifteen years. No enterprise has developed the natural resources and the great mining interests and industries of our country to anything like the extent that the Canadian Northern railway has. It was my privilege to spend fifteen days on that railway on a tour of inspection, and it was of great advantage to me to have the opportunity to investigate the enormous resources along its right of way. If one takes into consideration, not only the thousands and thousands of homesteads, but the many manufactories located along its main line and branches in the Northwest, one can readily understand the enormous benefits this road confers on the people of Canada. On the train I travelled a 35 per cent engine drew twelve or fourteen pullman cars from Montreal all the way to Vancouver. I will give to the members of this House a statement in regard to the grades on that road so that the people of Canada may know what a valuable asset they have in this great railway.
'"The Canadian Northern Railway Company's transcontinental line is superior in grades and alignment to any of its competitors, having been built to five-tenths of one per cent westbound grades and to four-tenths of one per cent eastbound grades, with the exception of 28 miles of seven-tenths of one per cent eastbound grade on the western slope of the Rocky mountains, and with the further exceptions of about 327 miles of short momentum or pusher grades which can be reduced later on when necessary. Of this 327 miles of grades in excess of five-tenths of one per cent westbound and four-tenths of one per cent eastbound, there are only six miles of one per cent grade and less than one mile of 1.15 per cent grade. All other temporary grades are less than one per cent. This places the Canadian Northern Railway Company in a very strong position. At the present time it is handling about one-third of the total grain moved in Western Canada, and with the opening up of Vancouver as a grain shipping port, it will have the advantage of being able to handle grain equally as well to the Pacific coast as to Port Arthur. In other words, it can handle from the prairies an equal tonnage with one engine for delivery at Vancouver or at Port Arthur. The Canadian Northern Railway Company has handled a 16-car passenger train through the mountains with one engine.
This merely goes to show the splendid 
grades and curves on that line of railway. There are also enormous possibilities in water-powers along its right of way in Ontario and in British Columbia. Cities, towns and villages, have sprung up along its line. For the last two years it has been able to handle, for several months in the year, over 45 per cent of the grain coming out of that western country, and it has 6,000 miles of branches serving the most productive districts in the western provinces.
The policy now proposed by the Government is progressive and businesslike. By it, the people will own, control and operate 9,648 miles of railway including branches in all the provinces except New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island. Not only i? this railway connected up with the most important cities, but there are many other advantages in connection with it. I have here a small plan showing that if a short branch line were constructed between Fort William and Titania on the Transcontinental by way of Long lake, a distance of sixteen miles, it would shorten the distance on the Canadian Northern between Fort William and Montreal by over 100 'miles. That would be of enormous advantage during the winter months in connection with the back haul of the grain by way of lake Superior Junction down to Montreal and the back haul of the coal for the operation of the road by way of Superior Junction along the Transcontinental east of Titania. The proposed link would make a composite line composed of the Transcontinental from Winnipeg to Titaqia, a proposed line to the Canadian Northern at Long lake and thence by the Canadian Northern to Montreal, a total distance of 1,347.7 miles as against the present routes; Canadian Pacific railway, 1,411.6 miles; Canadian Northern railway, 1,455.7 miles; the Grand Trunk Pacific railway and National Transcontinental railway, 1,425 miles Then it would keep the traffic east and west, instead of north and south.
Let us look at the mileage of some of the government railways in this country, when you connect up the Canadian Northern with this proposition. The Intercolonial, 1,514 miles; the Prince Edward Island Railway, 275 miles; the Transcontinental, now operating, 1,810 miles, making a total mileage of 13,247 miles, when you include the Canadian Northern. The mileage of the Canadian Pacific is only 12,900; that of the Grand Trunk Pacific, 1,964; that of the Grand Trunk, 3,556, and the other roads, such' as the Pere Marquette, the Great Northern, the Michigan Central, and so on, make the balance, until we have in Canada

about 40,000 miles of railway. After this proposition is finally closed the people of Canada'will own, control and operate practically one-third of the railway mileage of the Dominion.
What other advantages are to he derived from taking over this road? To-day we have government-owned telegraph lines to the extent of 11,792 miles, 330 miles of which are cables. Add to that the telegraph system of the Great North Western, taken over by the Canadian Northern, together with the lines along the Canadian Northern, and you have 55,364 miles of single wire, of government-owned telegraph, telephone, and cable lines in this country. This proposition includes the Canadian Northern Telegraph Company's lines, and the telegraph system operated by the Great North Western Telegraph company, having 1,570 offices in Canada. An exclusive traffic agreement, renewable from time to time, exists with the Western Union Telegraph Company, and under it the Great North Western company have connection with the thousands of offices of the Western Union in the United States, and also with the Atlantic and other cable lines owned or controlled by that company. Those of us who in years gone by strongly advocated an Atlantic cable between Canada and the Motherland will find in this a very favourable outlook, because the Great North Western Telegraph system is connected up with the cable system, and for a very small expenditure a government cable could be connected up with the Motherland.
Then let us take into consideration the advantage we shall derive from a government-owned express company in this country. I have been strongly advocating that on the Government lines of railway we should have a government-owned express company. This we will have when the Canadian Northern Express company is connected up with the Intercolonial and the government-owned railways. I hope when this proposition is consummated the Minister of Railways will see that the Canadian Express company, and the American Express company remove their agents and offices from the Government lines of railway, and that the Canadian Northern Express company will extend its business throughout the government railways.
What else do we find in connection with this scheme? There are six Canadian Northern steamships running from Montreal to Port Arthur on the Great Lakes. These steamships are estimated to be worth double the figure at which they appear on the books of the railway company. I have been advocating that vessels on- our inland waters should come under the control of the Railway Commission. We are starting out, under this proposition, with six government-owned boats. They will be an enormous advantage in investigating the needs of the shippers, both east and west., Then we have the government elevators. We have to-day one government-owned elevator at Moosejaw, with a capacity of 3,500,000 bushels ; one at Saskatoon with a capacity of 3,500,000 bushels; one at Calgary vdthacapacity of
2.500.000	bushels; one at Vancouver with a capacity of 1,250,000 bushels; one at Port Arthur with a capacity of 3,250,000 bushels; one at Port Colborne with a capacity of
2,000,000; one at Montreal with a capacity of 4,000,000 and another with a capacity of
2.600.000	bushels; one at Quebec with a capacity of 1,000,000, and one at Halifax, on the Intercolonial railway, with a capacity of 500,000 bushels-making a total of ten government-owned elevators, with a capacity of 24,100,000 bushels. Take the five Canadian Northern elevators that will now be government-owned, with a capacity of ten million bushels, and you have fifteen government-owned elevators with a capacity of
34.100.000	bushels.
To impress upon the House the enormous possibilities- of this road, especially in the West, let me show the number of elevators located along the rights of way of this system, first licensed elevators and warehouses in the province of Alberta on the Canadian Northern, 70 stations, 154 elevators, capacity
4.946.000	bushels; second licensed warehouses and elevators in Saskatchewan, 239 stations, 593 elevators, capacity 17,-
790,000	bushels; third, licensed warehouses and elevators in Manitoba, 136 stations, 237 elevators, capacity 6,474,000 bushels, making a total of 999 elevators with a capacity of 63,310,000 bushels, which will be located along the rights of way of the Government-owned roads. If you take out the government-owned elevators, you still have a capacity of 29,210,000 bushels in the elevators located along the rights of way of this road. The total capacity therefore of the elevators located along the rights of way of this road in the western provinces will be over 60,000,000 bushels.
Surely this is worthy of consideration in the taking over of this enterprise. Then, we must remember that in taking over this rail-



way the Government is not assuming any responsibility that they are not compelled to assume in the public interest. The interest on the securities must be met. Receivership is impossible. The public will surely suffer ii the roads go into liquidation. Our credit would be impaired. Betterment/ are needed. Rolling stock is needed. The company cannot possibly meet the interest charges, and keep up and improve the roadbed and the rolling stock. The Government must either advance money or take over the road. The Finance Minister has placed before the House so much information in regard to the finances of the company that it would serve no purpose for me to enlarge upon what he has said.

MOTION FOR SECOND READING OF CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY BILL.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in seconding the amendment of my hon. friend from South Renfrew (Mr. Graham), to the motion for the second reading of the Bill, I wish to assure you that 1 did not do it with a view of confiscating any value that the Canadian Northern directors or owners may have in the property.
I would be the last one in the world to confiscate anybody's property, no matter in what form it was, without giving him value. I have no hesitation in agreeing with my hon. friend who has just sat down (Mr. Armstrong) in all his premises, practically speaking, that is, that the road has a considerable property value, that it has been an influence in opening up the country, that it has subsidiaries connected with it that are valuable, and that it is a good proposition for the Government to assume control. I absolutely agree that the Government should take over the control in place of extending more loans to the company. I do not know that, as a general rule, I am in favour of government operation of anything, but my hon. friend the Minister of Finance, when he introduced this Bill, in answer to a question by myself, said that this railway would be operated by a corporation or company that would be entirely independent of the Governor in Council, that is ts say, it would be operated by a company answerable only to Parliament. I see nothing in the Bill as introduced that would show that ts be the-case, but the Bill as introduced simply contains a provision to take over the stock now owned by the company. Therefore, I have not any hesitation in taking the word of my hon. friend the Minister of Finance that when he as-

sumes control of the stock he will operate the railway through an independent company, not on the same basis as that on which the Intercolonial is operated at the present time, and again-not that I doubt the ability of the present Minister of Railways to do what it is possible to do under such circumstances-I have to say that the government operation of railways, so far as the history of this country has gone, has not tended to encourage us in taking over more operations of the same kind.
The question now is not as to the value of the physical properties of the road; the question is whether it would be .better to refeT the value of the $60,000,000 worth of stock to arbitration or to foreclose under the statute of 1914, by which we loaned $45,000,000 under our guarantee of bonds to the Canadian Northern. That, I understand, is the question now before the House.
There is one thing in which I do not agree with my hon. friend from East Lamb-ton, and that is that the physical properties of the road are worth what we are paying / for them. So far as I can make out, we are paying about $540,000,000- that is, we are assuming about $540,000,000 of indebtedness-for the physical properties of the road. Sir Henry Drayton and Mr. Acworth, who, together with Mr. Smith, were given authority to investigate the best means of operating the railways of Canada, have arrived at certain conclusions as to the value of this property. The Prime Minister said this afternoon that this commission was not appointed for the purpose of arriving at a valuation of the road. I do not see how the Prime Minister can justify this statement, because, as a matter of fact, they were appointed to find out what would be the best means for the Government to take to operate the railways of Canada, and in doing so, if they were going to recommend government control, they would necessarily have to find out what it should cost the Government to obtain that control; so that I cannot appreciate why the Prime Minister should say that it was not within the jurisdiction of the commission to find the values of these roads. The majority of that commission, Messrs. Drayton and Acworth, find that there had been expended on the Canadian Northern, of actual money, $383,302,451.33. They deducted certain amounts, about $13,000,000 net, for advances to controlled companies to pay indebtedness for interest subsequent to construction and operating deficits capitalized when the system was put together not less than $10,000,000; and interest during 1916 
overcharged to construction, not less than $3,000,000; and placed the amount at $370,302,451. They employed a professor in the TTnited States, Professor Swain, for the purpose of arriving at the physical value of the road. Professbr Swain goes at it in two different ways. He places the value, as has been stated before, at about $400,000,000. That is a replacement value. He deducts a certain amount from that for depreciation. My hon. friend from East Lambton (Mr. Armstrong) eulogized very highly the value of the rolling stock. I think he said it cost $56,000,000 and would be worth $80,000,000. It is well known that last winter the Canadian Northern engines were not capable of doing their work. The hon. member is the first man I ever heard who increased the value of any plant in the form of machinery after it had been in use for some years.

They value their "cash on hand, accounts receivable, material, sup. plies, etc.," at $14,446,152. The items are all put together, and we cannot tell what each separate item amounts to. Accounts receivable, for instance, may be very poor. Material and supplies is simply a matter of stock taking. I would not like to say that these items would be worth altogether $14,000,000 in cash. However, Professor Swain, I understand, left out the lands. My own idea is that Professor Swain meant to say he left out the equity in the lands; that is, the amount over and above the mortgages against the lands, and not that he left out the total value of the lands. As the company themselves value the land at $28,000,000 or $29,000,000, with mortgages against it of $21,000,000, it is very questionable whether there would be much equity left in the land. It all depends, of course, upon when and how they were sold. At a forced sale, for instance, I have no doubt that there would be no equity in the lands at all, judging by how lands depreciate on such an occasion.
My hon. friend the Minister of Finance and the Prime Minister this afternoon said that if we were to acquire the equity in the stock under foreclosure proceedings we would take over the physical property. My hon. friends say that under their proposition, leaving the value of the stock to arbitration, the company would be left in its entity and would operate the road and still be responsible for its liabilities. Now, that	is	the	first time	in	my lifethat	I	ever	heard of	a	company
acquiring the stock of a corporation and not acquiring the property of the corporation. I must confess that I am learning something every day-and I have learned a good deal to-day if it is possible for me, for instance, to take over the entire stock of a company and not acquire the company and not be responsible for all its liabilities. I think the Minister of Finance in discussing this matter the other day told us that we would be liable for all the liabilities of the road. In taking over the stock, no matter how it is taken over, I certainly think we shall assume all the liabilities of the Canadian Northern. Surely then, when we are taking over the liabilities, my hon. friend would not say that we were
not taking over the assets as well. When we take over the stock we acquire the property just as much as if we acquired it under foreclosure proceedings. I may be wrong, I frequently am; but it would take a great deal of effort to prove to me that when we acquire the stock of a company we do not acquire the physical assets and the liabilities of the company also.
As to whether the company is in default or not, the Minister of Finance this afternoon did not claim that they were not in default. He did say that unless the Government took over the property in the way that he proposed, the company would have to come to the Government for advances again next year, and, to use his own words, " for the next two or three or four or five years to come." Since 1914, when the guarantee was made and the Government were authorized under section 24 to take over the road in case of default, the company have applied for assistance again, and if the Government had not loaned them $15,000,000>
in 1916 to help them meet their liabilities,, the road would certainly have defaulted.
My right hon. friend the Prime Minister stated this afternoon that surely nobody in this House would confiscate the property. He used a very harsh word when he talked about confiscation. When we take over the equity in the stock, if there is any, by foreclosure proceedings, we certainly are not confiscating anything that the managers of the Canadian Northern have at the present time. Had it not been for our loan of 1916 they would have defaulted. They could not possibly have carried on until now without somebody taking foreclosure proceedings. Supposing they had borrowed this money from a trust corporation or a bank and given the same security that they gave to the Government, and put the same clauses in an agreement that were contained in the statute of 1914-would anybody say that if the trust company or the bank took over the corporation it was con. fiscating the property in the interests of the trust company or bank? I do not think so; nobody would find any fault with that. Suppose I mortgage my property and cannot pay the interest on the mortgage, nobody would ever dream of saying that the mortgagee confiscated the property because he foreclosed. I had the opportunity of carrying out my agreement and I failed.
A great many people do that under certain circumstances. Nobody finds fault with the mortgagee for foreclosing; neither should the owners of the Canadian Northern do so. I have nothing to say against the en-

terprise of Mackenzie and Mann; indeed, I have much pride in the enterprise they have shown as Canadians in building this road. The building of a great deal of it, however, was a great mistake. For. that matter, a great deal of the railway construe-tion work that has been done throughout Canada has been far in advance of the time. Roads are even now being built that, I think, are horrible mistakes; I have spoken about that in the House on frequent occasions. However, these people proceeded with the work, and they were encouraged in it not only by the Dominion Government but by practically all the Provincial Governments as well. They acquired a great property, but I am sorry to say that they have lost out. If I in,vest some money in a stock margin and the stock goes down, nobody comes to my assistance; I lose out. If I mortgage my property and cannot pay the principal or interest upon the mortgage, I lose the property; nobody says that my property has been confiscated. "Confiscation" is a rather harsh word to use in referring to foreclosure of the stock of this company and the taking over of the railway system. They have had every opportunity; we lent them $15,000,000 more than we promised "to lend them when the statute to which I have referred was passed. Moreover, we have paid some three or four million dollars by way of interest upon the guarantee made in 1914 besides the $15,000,000 loan. It is hardly right, therefore, to say that we have treated them unfairly.
I do not see any reason why the stock should not be taken over under foreclosure proceedings. If under this amendment we should take it over, the Government could appoint a commission or a committee to manage the road just as it proposes to do now. An independent commission could be appointed to deal with the matter-I hope,that any commission that is appointed will be really independent. I do not see why this could not be done.
I am not going to discuss the merits or the demerits of the corporation, or its value any more than to say-and this is why I am supporting the amendment-that it is proposed to give the company more than the road is worth. I do not think we should take into consideration what the company may earn ten, fifteen, or twenty years from now if the country is prosperous. Many things may tend to cause our country to prosper in the future. The whole energy of the people, not particularly the work of the Canadian Northern, the Grand Trunk

Pacific, or any other Canadian railway, tends to increase the prosperity of this road and of every other road in Canada. Why, then, the people should pay in advance for ' what they are going to do themselves is more than I can understand. As a matter of fact, the present owners of the Canadian Northern should be grateful to the Government for taking over the road and releasing them from their liabilities without payment in respect of the prospective value of the stock. The Government appointed a commission to find out what would be the best system to adopt in connection with the operation of the various railways in Canada. That Commission took upon itself to value this particular road. They have valued it in two or three different ways and in each case they have arrived at the conclusion that there is no equity in the stock. Take the other side of it: suppose we did not lend them the $15,000,000 in 1916; they certainly would have had no equity in the stock by this time because some of the mortgagees or bondholders would have foreclosed. " For the life of me, therefore, I cannot see that we should be doing anything unfair in taking over the stock under foreclosure proceedings as provided in the agreement and in the statute of 1914 when we guaranteed their bonds to the extent of $45,000,000.
As.to the general principle of the Government's taking over the road, I cannot see that they could do anything else which would be equitable and in the interests of the country. I am sorry that
10	p.m. they did not go further and take over the Grand Trunk Pacific as well. I think I understood the Minister of Finance, however, when he introduced the resolution upon which the Bill was to be founded, to say that eventually the Grand Trank Pacific would be taken over. The Grand Trunk should be very much pleased to hand over the Grand Trank Pacific, even though they may lose what money they have invested in it. They should also be very glad to make running or feeding arrangements with the Government if they are relieved of the Grand Trank Pacific, because this $7,500,000 that it is proposed to lend them now is already used up in losses in operation and interest on bonds. There is no probability that in other years the road will be in any better position. Although it is a dead horse, therefore, a great deal of money would be saved in the way of duplications and terminals if this road were taken over. Per-

haps we might break even in the whole transaction.
However, that is not the question before the House at the moment; we can discuss that when we come to it. The simple question now before the House is not what this road has done for Canada or what Canada has done for it; the question is, what is the better way of acquiring the stock, by submitting the matter of valuation to an arbitration as is proposed, or by foreclosure proceedings? There is no doubt that no matter who the arbitrators are they will take it for granted that Parliament has presumed that there is a value in the stock; otherwise Parliament would not have referred the matter to them for arbitration. That is one good reason why the matter should not be referred to a board of [DOT] arbitration, and it is a good reason in favour of foreclosure proceedings so far as the equity of the stock is concerned. I am strongly in favour of foreclosure proceedings.

subtopic: MOTION FOR SECOND READING OF CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY BILL.
speechtext:
I
understood it was arranged that a speaker on the other side was to follow my hon. friend for North Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt), but if not, I desire bo make some remarks in this connection. I agree with my hon. friend from North Oxford that the question before the House relates to the taking over of $60,000,000 of Canadian Northern stock which has been declared on good authority to have no value. I have not had the privilege of listening to the arguments brought forward by the Government in behalf of what I may characterize as a most remarkable transaction, but, it does not appear to me that any argument can be evolved in support of taking an unstated amount of money, which .may be $60,000,000 or thereabouts, out of the treasury of Canada, at the present time, under the circumstances in which we find ourselves and handing that over except for value received. I cannot understand how the Government of the day, charged with the financial and other responsibilities that rest upon it, can come before Parliament and the country with a proposition to pay an indefinite amount, which may be $60.000,000 or thereabouts, for something that is on record as having no value, and which, if it has a va]ue,'already belongs by statute to the Dominion of Canada. 'It would be impossible to express in isoiitable terms that disregard for the public interest for the financial situation of the country, that is involved in such a proposal. It is to me unthinkable that such a proposal should
be made. The worst enemy that this Government has in this country, I am sure, never would have accused the Government of being willing to bring such a proposal forward.
It has Ibeen said that the opposition to the Bill before the House involves a suggested confiscation of the property of the *Canadian Northern Railway Company. My hon. friend from North Oxford has already dealt with that question. He has shown, in terms that cannot be controverted, that there is no right and that, therefore, there can be no confiscation. But let us assume if you please, that there is a right and a value in this stock. Surely, in that case, it was the business of the Government to come 'before Parliament with a definite proposal as to how much should be paid by the country for that stock if it were desired to acquire the ownership of this road. On what pretense can the Government come before Parliament and the country with a proposal that, in the terms of this Bill, binds Parliament to pay money of an unknown amount? The Minister of Finance has a high reputation as a business man; he had a successful business career before he gave his talents to the service of his country. But I venture to say that, in all his long and successful business career, he never made such a proposal as a business proposition on behalf of any business interest with which he was connected. I certainly say, with all due re'spect to the Minister of Finance, that he is not, in this transaction, showing due regard to the welfare of Canada and to the interest of its people when he comes before Parliament with an indefinite proposition such as this involving the possibility of the payment of so many millions of dollars. I do not wish to use harsh language id this connection. I am and have always been willing to give the Minister of Finance credit for the highest motives, for using his best endeavours in the interest of his country as he sees that interest, although he and I do not see the interest of the country in the same light; but I cannot give him or the Government credit on this occasion for honesty of purpose in bringing before Parliament this proposal as it has been brought. If that stock be worth money, there are means of coming to a conclusion as to what amount of money it is worth, and it is the business of the Government first to arrive at that estimate and then to present it to Parliament. If it be a just estimate, it will be supported by Parliament and no one will find fault; but if it

be a fact that this Government cannot come to a conclusion as to what is a fair value for that stock, then when the Government comes with a proposition such as this, it is evidence of anything but good intent.
We are staggering under financial burdens which are increasing from day to day because of circumstances not under our control. We must bear those burdens, and if this Government has any duty to perform in the interest of the cause for which these burdens are being borne, its duty is to see that not a dollar goes out of the treasury of Canada except for good value. By this Bill, we are made subject to the possibility of having to pay out of the public treasury a sum aggregating $60,000,000 for the common stock of the Canadian Northern Railway Company, which stock already belongs to us because of the default of the company under the statute. And if it did not so belong to us, the Government still should not come to Parliament except with a definite proposition as to how much we should pay for that stock.
But that is only a small part of the liability that is being assumed by the country under this Bill. Section 3 says:
-the Governor in Council may assist the Canadian Northern Railway Company, or any company included in the Canadian Northern Railway system, in paying and settling any indebtedness of such company, or postponing the payment thereof, on such terms as may he agreed upon, and for such purposes may make advances out of the Consolidated Revenue Fund, may guarantee payment in whole or in part, and may give the obligations, or securities of the Government in connection therewith.
It may be- that the Government has already informed the House as to the extent and nature of the obligations that will be assumed under this section of the Bill. I have not heard any such statement, and I do not think it has been made. If it is wrong to ask the country to become committed to the payment of an unknown amount for stock that is of no value, it is an outrage to commit the country to an absolutely unknown and indefinite amount in payment of obligations incurred or to be incurred, and that responsibility to be imposed upon the country, not by Act of Parliament, but simply by order of the Governor in Council. Canada never saw such legislation before. There never was such a proposal in kind or in amount ever brought before the Parliament of this country. I cannot believe that such an extraordinary and remarkable proposition-involving so many hundreds of millions of dollars- 
can be brought forward with good intentions. It has not the appearance and it has not the character of a measure with good intentions. I claim the right to condemn the Government for their proposal because of its terms, but even more because of the lack of good intent as evidenced by those terms.
There is involved in this the general question of railway policy of our country. I alluded to that policy when the resolutions were before the House, and I will again give my views in regard to it. Possibly my views may not agree with those already expressed by others. If that be so I am sorry, but I think the responsibilities are so great that it is only right I should give the views which I hold and hold very ' strongly. I have stated that judged by the experience of Canada this Government, under the most favourable circumstances, cannot operate the Canadian Northern Railway system either as efficiently or as economically as does the company now operating it. There is no evidence to lead us to believe for an instant that the Government can do so. There is no evidence to lead us to believe that they want to do it, or that it is any part of their intention to do it, or that they could do it, if it was their intention to do it- and I say this with all due respect to the Minister of Railways (Mr. Cochrane). I am not here as a champion of the Canadian Northern Railway Company, either in its inception or in its management, but if the people of Canada have to make a choice between government operation of this railway and its operation by the company, the interests of the Dominion of Canada demand that the present company shall continue to operate it. We have government operation of the Intercolonial and we have government operation of the Transcontinental. There is nothing in the operation of these roads to show either superior economy or superior efficiency over the operation of the Canadian Northern Railway Company. I am not blaming my hon. friend in the matter: It is a condition he has to deal with. There is a condition surrounding the government operation of railways in this country which makes their efficient and economic operation impossible. In taking over and operating 9,000 miles of railroad, we are assuming a responsibility so terrific in its magnitude that I think very few of us understand it or realize it.
There are the three points-the payment of possibly $60,000,000 for stock that is of

no value; the payment of an unknown and uncalculated amount of indebtedness of the company, on the authority of the Governor in Council; and the management of a vast system of transportation, comprising 9,000 miles of railway, by the Government, which has proven itself not as efficient as the company in railway management. Surely these are conditions that should cause us to look much more carefully than we have yet done on this transaction which we are facing so light-heartedly.
It has been said here and elsewhere that Canada has a railway problem on her hands, and the problem is that she has too many railways, and because she has too many railways we are to reduce the number by combining the systems. I absolutely take issue with that view. I maintain that Canada has not too many railways; that ehe needs the railways she has; that she will need more railways in the future, and that she can get better service and better -value from these railways under competitive management than she can in any other way. It is true that the Grand Trunk Pacific and the Canadian Northern were just completed at the outbreak of the war, and the outbreak of the war prevented that further development of [DOT]the country along their lines which would have brought them traffic and would probably have made them- financial successes before now. Still, we did not create the war, and they did not create it; it is a condition which has overtaken us all, and it is childish to, speak of either the country or the railways being discredited .because of conditions having arisen which no wisdom could have foreseen, and which in the nature of things cannot last much longer.
When those conditions have passed away the railways will be needed for the development of the country. The Canadian Northern is supposed to be a failure as a business proposition because it is not able to pay the interest on its securities. I find from the statement placed before the House that it had the following net earnings:
1915	$ 6,600,000
1916	 9,373,000'
1917	 11,500,000
These were net earnings available for the payment of interest on bonds, betterments, etc. I submit that a railway showing such progress in net earnings under present conditions ought not to be written down as a failure. It is true it is not able to meet its obligations; it is true it is in default; it is true we are entitled to foreclose it to-
morrow if we so desire and that we have no right to pay a cent of money for the common stock; but it is also true, as shown by the statement which has been laid before the House, that so far from its being ill-advised and foredoomed to failure, with the assured growth of our country and of our railways it cannot help but be an abounding success in due time. But, of course, it will have to be carried until that time arrives. Speaking for myself individually, and only individually, I would be strongly in favour of dealing with the Canadian Northern exactly as we are dealing with the Grand Trunk Pacific. So long as we are satisfied that the railways are being economically and efficiently managed, and that the money they earn is going where it should go, the country would be justified in carrying these railway companies over the difficulties of the present time by loans, well secured and at interest, as is being done in the case of the Grand Trunk Pacific. No. reason has been placed before the ' House why the same should not be done in the case of the Canadian Northern.
If this action proposed to be taken is taken in the belief that the people are crazy on the subject of the government ownership of railways, and that any sort of a proposition that will put into their hands
9,000	miles oi railway is going to be pleasing to them, I am one to take the view that the people are not fools and that the Government which makes its calculations on the basis that the people do not realize what is in their own interest is making a huge mistake. There is no charm in government ownership unless government ownership means economy and efficiency.
A government ownership that means extravagance and inefficiency is surely not a business proposition which will appeal to the people. When, in addition to that, we eliminate the principle of energetic individual competition in our railway services, and in addition that again, we are paying an unknown and vast amount of money for something for which there is no value, I think I am warranted in saying that this is the most unjustifiable transaction that was ever brought before the Parliament of Canada.	.
