speechtext: The House resumed debate from Tuesday, August 14, on the motion of Sir Thomas White for the second Teading of Bill No. 125, providing for the acquisition by His Majesty of the capital stock of the Canadian Northern Railway Company.

subtopic: DEBATE CONTINUED ON MOTION FOR SECOND READING OF CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY BILL.
DEBATE CONTINUED ON MOTION FOR SECOND READING OF CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY BILL.
speechtext: Three, is it not?

subtopic: DEBATE CONTINUED ON MOTION FOR SECOND READING OF CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY BILL.
speechtext:
Yes, three cars. I ask hon. gentlemen of this House, in what position is a railway desiring to compete with a company like the Canadian Pacific Railway, with cars in proportion of seven to three? I think it goes without saying that something must be done, in order to provide the Canadian Northern with further rolling stock, in order that it may, at least, compete and give proper service to the people of the country, and, after all, it is the people of this country in whose interests we are acting. It was for the benefit of the people of the country, that we gave assistance, and only for their benefit, and if it were not for the benefit of the people of the country, we had no justification in advancing the money. Having loaned the money which we did for the benefit of the people of this country, it is our duty to see that that benefit is preserved to them, even if it costs more than we anticipated.
As to the question of receivership, I do not know that any man in this House has directly said that he is in favour of the company going into receivership. I do not think any man will say that, but the idea seems to be abhorrent to pretty nearly every one I have met. The Drayton-Ac-worth report sums up the question of receivership in this way:
Under a, receivership the holders of the junior securities have to submit to compound their claim, and the fixed charges are reduced to an amount that the net revenue from operation suffices to meet. Ought this drastic course to be adopted here? We think not. We think the security holders of the companies have to some extent a moral claim on the Government. Their schemes of extension have been matters of public knowledge for many years. So far from discouraging them, the governments, both of Dominion and of the Provinces, have by subsidy and by guarantee, by loans and cash advances, encouraged them to go on.
But there is more than this. The bonds and debentures of the Grand Trunk Pacific and Canadian Northern have been placed in the main through London with non-Canadian holders. And these holders in subscribing have unquestionably been influenced by the fact that the companies were backed by the Canadian Government. Technically, of course, the Government has no responsibility beyond that of meeting its own guarantees. But if the two companies went into the hands of receivers, we cannot doubt that investors outside Canada would believe, however erroneously, that the Dominion Government had treated them badly, and that the result would be serious injury to the credit of the Canadian Government, and indeed of all Canadian enterprises. And this result is one that, putting



it on pecuniary grounds alone, the Canadian people should in their own interest spend a good deal of money to avoid. We therefore consider that Canada should assume the responsibility of seeing that the interest on these securities is met.
And then my right hon. friend the leader of the Opposition, speaking in this House, in reply to the Premier, at page 3677 of the Hansard of 1914, said:
My right hon. friend said, and I altogether agree with him, that we cannot allow this enterprise to fail. We have too much money in it-not only the money of the country, hut of the provinces and of the bond-holders themselves.
Later on he says:
We require this railway. My right hon. friend said he would not let it go into liquidation. It must not go into liquidation, tout we should have the control of it. Since we must go into partnership with the Canadian Northern Railway, let us see that we are the master, not the servant.
Under this measure we propose to be the master, not the servant. As I have said, we have assisted to the extent of $151,000,000, and- the provinces to the extent of $107,000,000, in the way of guarantees. We are the last mortgagees; our claim comes last, and we must either come to the rescue of this system or let it go by default and thereby forfeit what interest we have in it. What does the Dr ayton-Ac worth report say in summing up the situation with regard to the Canadian Northern Railway system? This is the opinion of the commissioners?
We sum up the Canadian Northern situation as follows:	The company is not at present
able, and will not for some years to come be able,: to meet its fixed charges. It will, we doubt not, increase its net earnings as the years go by. But the increased net earnings will be fully absorbed for some years to come by the interest on new capital, which must be put in, if the system is to render efficient service. The company has not now, and as far as we can see will not have in the near future, such credit as to enable it* to raise the necessary capital. As we have already shown, the public investment, direct and indirect, in the Canadian Northern system amounts to $298,000,000. We do not recommend further public investment in the system, as at present constituted.
The people of Canada do not want this Government or any other Government to grant further assistance to the Canadian Northern Railway system while the owners are either Mackenzie or Mann or any other private interest. The Finance Minister very neatly summed up the situation in the following words:
The true policy would seem to be that which will ensure not only the best public service but a substantial degree of public ownership

in order that the benefit of the large financial assistance granted from the public exchequer during the critical period of the development of these roads shall enure to the benefit of the public when the enterprises reach a period of fruition. If the public does the financing, the public should enjoy the ultimate reward.
That is a sound summing up of existing conditions, and which are amply provided for in the Bill now before the House.
I now come to the question of the value of the equity. The member for South Renfrew (Mr. Graham) introduced an amendment which, apparently, he thought was something new; something not contained in the Bill before the House. But if he will examine his amendment closely he will find that to all intents and purposes we have acted under section 24 of the Act of 1914, although we have eliminated its dbjection-able features. This section says:
If authorized by the Parliament of Canada, the Governor in Council may on such terms and conditions (if any) as Parliament may prescribe-[DOT] '
The whole section rests upon that sentence.
-at any time while any event or default shall exist and be continuing, by order declare the equity of redemption of the Canadian Northern and of all other persons whomsoever in the mortgaged premises to be foreclosed and thereupon the equity of redemption of the Canadian Northern (and of such other persons) in the mortgaged premises and every part thereof shall be and become absolutely barred and foreclosed, and the same shall thereupon be vested in His Majesty in right of the Dominion of Canada, any statutory enactment, or any rule of law or equity to the contrary notwithstanding.
There seems to be ta great divergence of opinion on the other side of the House in regard to what action we should now take in this matter. For instance, the member for Welland (Mr. German) does not deny that Mackenzie and Mann have some interest in the stock iof this company. He goes so far as to say that he is willing that the judge of the Exchequer Court should determine the value, if any, to be placed upon the equity of Mackenzie and Mann in the $60,000,000 worth of stock. Well, we are with him in that respect. He says that some court should determine the value of that stock. The only difference, therefore, between our opinion and his is whether the matter should he decided by a judge of the Exchequer Court or by a board of arbitration, as proposed in this measure. But a judge is an arbitrator; if the matter were submitted to a judge he would he the sole arbitrator in respect of the value of the equity in the Canadian Northern stock. Per-

son-ally, I would -rather trust to the judgment of three gentlemen than to the judgment of one. Under the method proposed, one arbitrator is to be appointed by the railway -company, one by the Government, and the third by the two arbitrators -so appointed. If the arbitrator -appointed by the Dominion Government comes to the conclusion that the other two -are, to use a vulgar expression, trying tlo " put it over " him, he may, under the provisions of this proposed measure, refuse- to agree to the arbitration and then an appeal may be had to the 'Supreme Court of Canada. If the Government cannot trust such -a matter to the Supreme Court of Canada, why should it be willing to trust to that court cases in which any other persons are interested? It seems -to me that that argument cannot be refuted.	_
Then we come to- the member for Carle-ton (Mr. Carvell). I do not say that these hon. gentlemen have not come honestly to these conclusions, but the fact that they differ emphasizes the difficulty of the problem with which we are dealing. If I interpreted -aright the remarks of the member for Carleton, he took the ground that we should not take this road over; that we should give the Canadian Northern Railway Company another loan; that we should continue the -plan that we have hitherto been following. He believed that in a short time the Canadian Northern would be able to finance successfully its own operations. He expressed himself as not being in favour of public ownership. Here iwe have another difference of opinion.
Then we come to the member for South Renfrew (Mr. Graham). If I interpreted his remarks aright, he is in- favour of foreclosing under section 24 of the Act of 1914, but as to the value of McKenzie and Mann's stock says: Let us have the courage to state definitely what the stock is worth. Well, if we had taken that stand if we had said that the Canadian Northern stock was worth $100,000, $5,000,000 or $10,000,000, the member for South Renfrew would have said: why did you not leave this matter to arbitration? You have come to some sinister understanding with Mackenzie and Mann as to the value of the stock, knowing that a board of arbitration would not find the stock to have that value. I think we took the proper course when we provided that tlm matter of value should be referred to a tribunal for determination.
What does the member for St. John say? Give them nothing at all; foreclose under
286*
the mortgage and deny them -the right to have any value that may be in the stock determined by any tribunal. It seems to me that that would be a sort of star chamber proceeding. We should be saying to them: you are guilty; we condemn you; we give you no opportunity of saying whether the stock is worth one dollar or ten million dollars. We will just take it and there is nothing coming to you. I do not think anybody would support such a proceeding as that.
Then, what does the member for Edmonton (Mr. Oliver) say?
He says: Let the road go on as it is; let it continue to be operated by the present management, and I have no doubt that in time it will be able to finance itself. We cannot follow the advice of all these hon. gentlemen (because of the diversity of their views. We must act on our own views. We are, in effect, acting under section 24, in that we are taking -advantage of those features of -section 24 which are favourable to ourselves, and following the Drayton-Acworth report as to the balance. Is not the effect of what we are doing to-day this? We are asking Parliament to authorize us to become the owners of the stock and the road upon the prescribed condition that the value of the stock or equity, if any, shall be determined by arbitration. That is practically following -the wording of section 24. That is the first thing we are doing. We are, however, eliminating certain features of that section of the Act. If we acted altogether under section 24, we would become the owners of the physical property of the Canadian Northern, and when one becomes the owner of any physical property, one immediately has- to control and operate it. If we acted according to the provisions of section 24 exactly as it stands to-day, the Minister of Railways would have to operate the Canadian Northern railway. I have aheady bad an application from a man- for an appointment as trainmaster on the Canadian Northern, and my hon. friend from St. Antoine (Sir Herbert Ames) has had a similar -application. That shows that if we carried out the provisions of section 24 and became the owners of the physical property of the Canadian Northern, every hon. member would be hounded by applicants for positions on that road, and I for one will not consent to any such -course being adopted. By the course we purpose adopting, we preserve the entity of the Canadian Northern as a corporation. We become -the owners of the stock of the Can-

adian Northern, ,and as owners of that stock we consequently become the owners of the railway, but we leave the operation, control and management in a body still called the Canadian Northern, but operated by directors appointed by this Government. I hope, in their operation, they will be as entirely free from political control and party patronage as is the Board of Railway Commissioners for the Dominion of Canada.
In addition to that, by the course we purpose adopting, we eliminate the possibility of having to renew all those bonds and agreements outstanding against the Canadian Northern. We eliminate anything in the nature of a financial crisis, because the Canadian Northern, so far as its operations are concerned, goes on just as it is to-day, but under our direction and ownership. We follow the Drayton-Acworth report in this respect. If we acted under section 24, we would become the owners of the physical property of the Canadian Northern railway. The Drayton-Acworth report says that this country should not become the owners of the physical property of that road, and in order to avoid that, they recommend a scheme of a Dominion Railway company, the stock of which should he owned by the Dominion of Canada, but the physical property of which should belong to the Dominion Railway Company. In that way they endeavour to divorce the operation of the railway from politics and political control. We follow that recommendation by means of the present Bill, because we simply buy the stock, and in that way become the owners of the road.
I do not know whether we are very much concerned with the question as to whether or not the stock has any value, because the Bill purposes leaving that question to arbitration. As, however, allegations have been made in this House that the stock has no value and that therefore we should not appoint arbitrators and thereby give the company an opportunity to claim any value, I will read what the Drayton-Acworth report .says on the matter. It did not occur to. me that it was within the jurisdiction or the province of the Drayton-Acworth Commission finally to fix and determine the value of the equity of the railway or of the stock of the Canadian Northern Railway. I read from the commission appointing them. They were to inquire into:
2.	The status of each of the three transcontinental railway systems, that is having special reference to the following considerations:-
(a)	The territories served by each system

and the service which it is capable of performing in the general scheme of transportation:
(b)	Physical conditions, equipment and capacity for handling business;
(c)	Methods of operation;
(d)	Branch lines, feeders and connections in Canada;
(e)	Connections in United States;
(f)	Steamship connections on both oceans;
(g)	Capitalization, fixed charges ,!and (net earnings having regard to (i) present conditions, and (ii) probable future development with increase of population.
3.	The reorganization of any of the said railway systems, or the acquisition thereof by the State; and in the latter case, the most ef-ffective system of operation, whether in connection with the Intercolonial railway or otherwise.
4.	Generally speaking, all matters which the members of the Board may consider pertinent or relevant to the general scope of the inquiry.

speechtext: How would the hon. member interpret what is submitted to the commissioners under paragraph (g) of section 2, and under section 4?

speechtext: I would admit that paragraph (g) of section 2 comes nearest to the question of determining the value of the equity, but it says "capitalization."

subtopic: DEBATE CONTINUED ON MOTION FOR SECOND READING OF CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY BILL.
speechtext: How about section 4?

subtopic: DEBATE CONTINUED ON MOTION FOR SECOND READING OF CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY BILL.
speechtext: That is a general clause. If. the Drayton-Acworth Commission were arbitrating for the purpose of determining between the Government and Mackenzie and Mann as to the value of the equity of the latter, surely Messrs. Mackenzie and Mann would have the right to appoint one of the arbitrators on the board to determine the value of the stock. I mean that, as between the Government and Mackenzie and Mann and the Canadian Northern, we surely would not have the right to appoint all three arbitrators, giving Mackenzie and Mann or the Canadian Northern no voice in the appointment of one of them, and to say: Now this absolutely fixes and determines the value of your stock.

subtopic: DEBATE CONTINUED ON MOTION FOR SECOND READING OF CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY BILL.
speechtext: How does my hon. friend account for the fact that so much of the report on the Canadian Northern relates to this question? Does he suppose that the commissioners were not able to judge as to the scope of their commission?

subtopic: DEBATE CONTINUED ON MOTION FOR SECOND READING OF CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY BILL.
speechtext:
I do not suppose that Messrs. Drayton and Aeworth assumed that whatever value they put on the stock of the Canadian Northern would be the final determination of the value. I might just as well appoint three members on this side of the House as a commission to

determine the value at which my hon. friend should sell his farm to me. It was never intended by this House that the Government should have that power. The only thing intended by this commission was to give this House some general information upon which it might base future action, and then it was for the House to act upon it or not as they saw fit. It is true that Messrs. Drayton and Acworth in their report say that they do not think the common stock is of very much value, but nevertheless they say this:
We think that, on the whole, the equity of the case would be met, if the Canadian Northern shareholders were permitted to retain a moderate portion of the $60,000,000 of shares which they now hold.
Then under the heading of "arbitration recommended/* they go on to say:
But under the scheme we propose, the Trustees will operate the Canadian Northern lines as part of a combined system. It will be impossible, therefore, for the Canadian Northern Company, as such, ever to earn a dividend on its separate stock. We suggest that, if it is decided to permit the present shareholders to retain a portion of their holding, the Act of Parliament constituting the Board of Trustees, shall contain a provision for arbitration between the Trustees and the Canadian Northern Company establishing an arbitration board to act forthwith. The Trustees should appoint one arbitrator and the Canadian Northern shareholders the other, and the two arbitrators should agree on the appointment of an umpire; failing agreement, an umpire should be appointed by the Chief Justice of the Exchequer Court; and the decision of the board should be final.
The arbitrators should be empowered to decide two questions:
(1)	What proportion of the Canadian Northern common stock may fairly remain the property of the present holders?
(2)	What proportion of the earnings of the Dominion Railway Company may fairly be regarded as attributable to the Canadian Northern lines?
To illustrate our meaning, we will assume that the arbitrators decide that 5 per cent of the Canadian Northern shares shall remain the property of the existing holders, and further decide that one-half of the total earnings of the Dominion Railway Company will be fairly attributable to the Canadian Northern lines. Then their decision will mean that, out of any dividend declared in future by the Dominion Railway Company, 2i per cent (one-half of 5 per cent) will be payable to the existing Canadian Northern shareholders or their transferees.
What I want to point out is this. The commissioners themselves confess that Mackenzie and Mann had some interest at least in that equity of $600,000,000-1 do not care whether it is $1 or $1,000,000-and they recommended arbitration for determining the value. That is exactly what we are proposing to do. We do no-t want to
commit ourselves as my hon. friend from South Renfrew and his followers did in 1914, by setting a maximum price upon the stock of the Canadian Northern, because to do that suggests that you are willing to pay any amount, up to that maximum, and it might induce the arbitrators to come to the conclusion that the stock is worth more than what it is. So we say that the arbitrators shall determine the value of the stock, whatever it may be.
Then there is this other point-and I am sure my hon. friends will admit the justice of this. It has been proved by the Minister Oif Finance that when the Drayton-Aoworth Commission came to the conclusion that the stock of the Canadian Northern might not be worth anything, or that its liabilities were practically equal to its assets, they omitted to take into consideration some very valuable assets of the company. For instance, they omitted 3,000,000 acres of land the value of which I tlhink was put at $3 an acre; that would give $9,000,000. They also omitted $7,000,000 of deferred payments on lands which have been actually sold.
In my humble opinion that would be the best kind of an asset, because if the lands have been sold no- doubt a very 4 p.m. substantial payment has been made on account, and the balance would therefore be properly secured. The commissioners also omitted $2,400,000 in trust account in respect of lands sold. That -gives something like $18,000,000 of assets thalt the commissioners apparently did not take into consideration when they stated that the stock was not worth anything. I do n-ot want to -suggest for one moment that the Canadian Northern Railway are entitled to any such sum as $18,000,000, because that .mistake was made. I do not -want them to get -one dollar more than the stock is worth, but I am not prepared to stand up here and approve of any -Star Chamber method o.f taking a man's property for the benefit of the Crown and saying that he shall not have the right to prove that it is worth something. What would hon. gentlemen think of a municipal council that went to a man and said: " We want your land for the purpose of a park. We find there are $4,500 encumbrances against it. We do not think your property is worth more than such a figure, and we are not going to give yoti anything for it. You shall have no opportunity of going before a court and .proving thalt your property is worth more than the figure we set." That is the position hon. gentlemen opposite take, because section 24, under which my hon. friend moved his amend-

ment, expressly states that it shall he upon such terms us Parliament m>ay prescribe. Now Parliament may do anything. Parliament may prescribe that they may take my property and not give me a cent. Parliament is .all-powerful. But this Parliament says: "We are going to take your property, but its value shall be determined by arbitration."
The .most remarkable thing about this whole discussion is that in 1914 hon. gentlemen opposite were in favour of this very principle of arbitration. When we were proposing to guarantee the bonds of the company to the amount of $45,000,000, the hon. member for St. John seconded, and the right hon. leader of the Opposition moved, the following resolution:
That the said Bill be not now read a third time, but that it be resolved that under existing circumstances no assistance should be given to the Canadian Northern Railway unless at the same time it is provided that the Government have power within a reasonable time to acquire the ownership and the entire stock of the company at a price to be fixed by arbitration but not to exceed $30,000,000.
When we were proposing to guarantee the bonds hon. gentlemen opposite said: " No, you should not do that. You should do what we propose in that resolution." That is the resolution they voted for in 1914. Now the common stock of the Canadian Northern Railway is worth just as much to-day as it was worth in 1914, if not more, because every dollar of the $45,000,000 has gone into the road, and the net earnings of the railway are increasing from time to time. Yet 'hon. gentlemen opposite in 1914 were willing to give as high as $30,000,000, provided the arbitrators decided upon that amount. Among those who voted for that resolution were Messrs. German, Lemieux, .Macdonald, Maclean (Halifax), McKenzie, Murphy, Nesbitt, Oliver, Pugsley, and Sinclair. The very fact of fixing a maximum price of $30,000,000 for the stock presupposes that you think it might be worth $30,000,000; otherwise you would have no right to fix that maximum price. A day or two after that resolution was moved, we got $40,000,000 of that .same stock for nothing, or as part of the terms of the 45 million loan. Therefore, we got $12,000,000 of a possible value in that stock immediately the Act went through, as the 40 million is two-fifths of the whole stock.

Now, does it not seem that the company having been obliged to come again to the Government for an additional $15,000,000, the Government ought to take an option from the company, on reasonable terms, for a reasonable amount, which option could be exercised or not as Parliament in the future might determine. I would not suggest that any injustice whatever should be done to the company. I should think that it ought to be recognized that these two gentlemen, Sir William Mackenzie and Sir Donald Mann, notwithstanding what may be said by their critics, are deserving of a large measure of praise, a large degree of credit, for the enterprise and foresight they have shown.
In 1914 I moved a resolution, the effect of which would have been that the Government would have the right to take over the equity of Mackenzie and Mann, Limited, which means Sir William Mackenzie and Sir Donald Mann, at a sum not exceeding $30,000,000.
But the time has arrived when with the company coming back again for assistance, for the enormous sum of $15,000,000, the Government should come to an understanding with Sir William Mackenzie and Sir Donald Mann, and have it clearly understood that if, within a reasonable period, say within five years, the Government and Parliament should, in the interests of the people of Canada, take over this road they will affix to it as a condition a reasonable sum at which the equity of these gentlemen should be acquired for the country.
Even as late as last year the hon. gentleman was willing to enter into an agreement with the Canadian Northern to buy the stock of the company, because the equity in the stock, at a reasonable sum provided it should not exceed $30,000,000. Yet to-day he objects to arbitration for any amount. In conclusion, let me say that I think the measure before the House is the only solution of one of the most difficult and complex problems that has presented itself for the
consideration of Parliament in the railway and financial history of Canada. I have looked at the matter in many ways and f cannot see any better solution. As far as I am personally concerned, I would vote against any solution that was not in the interest of Canada at the present time. I claim that the proposal as contained in the Bill should receive our support because:
1.	We become the owners of the road.
2.	We become the masters and not the servants of the Canadian Northern railway.
3.	The arrangement preserves the entity of the company and avoids physical ownership and consequently political partisanship in the operation of the road and the appointment of the servants and agents thereof.
4.	It does not disturb existing securities.
5.	It avoids further loans to private owners.
6.	It prevents receivership and financial panic at a critical period.
7.	Any benefit or increase in the value of the road in future, due to our efforts and assistance will enure to the public benefit and not of Mackenzie and Mann.
8.	It will permit operation ' and control by an independent board of directors free of political control.
9.	It will enable a better public service to be given through proper provision for adequate rolling stock and betterments.
10.	So far as the Canadian Northern Railway is concerned, it is in line with the recommendations of the Drayton-Acworth report in that it avoids receivership, assumes liabilities, avoids further aid under old conditions, and gets the ownership of the road through the ownership of the common stock. All these considerations have been recommended by the Drayton-Acworth report.
11.	If this suggestion is any good, it carries out Sir Wilfrid Laurier's resolution of 1914 which proposed that we should become the owners of the stock, and be the masters of the situation, and which was supported by his followers.
As far as I can see this is the only reasonable solution during these strenuous times and the only one that is fair not only to the people of Canada but to the Canadian Northern Railway as well.

In that year, the policy was, in the main, put before the people in this Parliament. In 1904 the Prime Minister went to the country upon his railway policy and the then leader of the Opposition opposed it. What happened is generally known; that railway policy was .almost unanimously ratified by the people from the Atlantic to the Pacific. What happened in Nova Scotia, from which province the distinguished Prime Minister comes? Every constituency in that province, by overwhelming majorities, favoured the railway policy of the then Administration. At that time the leader of the Opposition, like Noah's dove, could not find a place to rest, politically speaking, in Nova Scotia. Indeed, he was poorer than those foxes and

He had no part or place in his own province, because the people were overwhelmingly in favour of the railway policy of the right hon. gentleman who now leads the Opposition. Four years afterwards the people had an opportunity of passing judgment upon the railway policy of the then Administration, but very little was said about it. I ran the election in 1904 and in 1908. Despite the serious vicissitudes through which the western wheat crop has passed and the unusual heat experienced in the province of Ontario during the past summer, the field crops of Canada show a bountiful yield and with the high prices prevailing for practically all its produces the great basic industry of agriculture continues in a flourishing condition. I wish to direct this to the attention of the member for South Ontario to. this further from the Minister of Finance:

Our increased bank deposits, clearings and circulation, the amount of public and private building evidenced in municipal and business structures, extensions to manufacturing plants and residences in almost every part of the country, all attest that the general prosperity of Canada at the present time is very great.
Our Dominion continues to be the land of hope and promise to the home seeker. During the last year, as before shown, our immigration from Europe and the United States reached an average of nearly a thousand a day, bringing -their capital, their intelligence and their energy to assist in the great task of developing the resources of Canada and building up her nationality. Much has been said in the past with which I am in accord as to the selection of immigration as far as possible with an eye to the quality and character of our future citizenship. Notwithstanding the large stream of immigration, labour conditions are good and extreme poverty, from any reason other than incapacity or direct misfortune, is hardly known.

Under the favourable conditions- which X have described, and with every prospect for their continuance, the future of Canada looks bright indeed. In the enjoyment of peace, plenty and prosperity her energetic, loyal and patriotic people look forward with hope and Expectation to an ever great and greater future.
To my hon. friend from South Ontario (Mr. Smith), I would point out that condition of the anatomy of the finances and business conditions of the country when they were placed in the hands of my worthy friend the Minister of Finance, and I would ask him if that is the condition of a country with its back broken, would it not be well for it always to have a broken back?
I am now -going to depict the other -side of the shield, calling the attention of hon.
' gentlemen opposite to it. In this case I will give the House the evidence of that Tory of Tories, Lieutenant-General Sir Sam Hughes. No one will question his fidelity to the Tory party and his desire to tell the truth about them -and to -put them on the highest pinnacle on which he can possibly place them. But, -speaking in this House (not -speaking elsewhere), on the 9th day of July, 1917, only a short time ago, he was obliged to tell the truth. His speech may be found on pages 3268 and 3269 of Hansard. He is dealing with the financial conditions as they existed three years -after my hon. friends came into power, qfter, I suppose, they had tried to mend the back of the country. This is what he -says: I
I need make no apology here, or elsewhere regarding my loyalty to the business interests of Canada. When the hon. the Finance Minister had Canada on the verge of financial ruin, at the beginning of the war, my loyalty to their cause was then shown by my actions in establishing industries in Canada which resulted in placing her industries of every class on a sound financial basis; hut I have never made any pretence of placing anything on a par with the soldiers in the trenches. They stand first in the heart of every honest Canadian. The Finance Minister's letter in every reference places them secondary.
Considerable interest is evidently manifesting itself on the general aspect of this case.
The rest of this speech .has in it references which are rather of a personal character in a way, attacking the Minister of Finance, and I am not going to read it. The evidence, however, given here at least according to a gentleman who was for a long time a minister, and who is to-day a strong follower of the Conservative party, is that the Minister of Finance has brought the country to the verge of ruin. I have read to the House a glowing picture of the con-
TMr. McKenzie.l
dition of this country in February, 1912, and the quotation which I have just read is from a speech delivered this year but having reference to conditions existing during the year 1914, at all events, up to the time of the breaking out of the war, because the remedy which the ex-Minister of Militia suggests for conditions then existing is to start industries in connection with the war. That was the condition in which the country was found and into which it was brought by hon. gentlemen opposite, -according to the testimony delivered in this House on the responsibility of an exminister and member of the party now in power. I am, therefore, accepting as the truth the statement made by that hon. gentleman. Such extreme conditions as the hon. gentleman has described did not exist in the days when my right hon. friend (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) was in power, and I believe they would not have come into existence had the people thought proper to continue my right hon. leader in office.
I wish to deal as -briefly as -possible with the main question now before- the House, that is: What shall we do in connection with this railway? There is not much doubt now as to what will be done. The Government of the day have their majority. 1 suppose they held a caucus on this question, and that after that they drafted this measure, and this measure is now 'before ns with, I presume, the understanding that n will receive a majority support from the Wends of the Government. Consequently, we have before us in crystallized form in this Bill what the Government purposes doing. I -criticise the Government for the opportunity they are giving to the holders of the stock of the Canadian Northern Railway to give that stock a fictitious value. If it has any value at all, it should have the value -it had on the date the Government received that report from Sir Henry Drav-ton and his associates. What do the Government do? They say in this Bill that the value of the stock is to be as of the date of an agreement to be made after this measure becomes law, after it is fixed and irrevocable that we are to take over this stock, and when the whole world knows that. Is that reasonable? If you are going to expropriate land for a railway, the value fixed by the arbitrators, is not. the value it may have after the railway goes through it; it is the value that it had -before the railway was constructed at all, because, if it has a higher value after the railway goes through it, that is due to the railway

and not to the intrinsic value of the land itself.
They have taken, the most extraordinary course of saying: "We are going to take over this property by Act of Parliament. We must have it. Messrs. Mackenzie -and Mann may be worth nothing, and their property behind this stock may be worth nothing, but we are taking it over and the Dominion of Canada is now behind it."
I ask the Minister of Finance and the business men on the other side of the House if that is good business. I submit that it is not. They have given this stock a fictitious value by placing themselves in the position where they are going to buy it themselves. Everybody knows that this Bill is going to pass, and I suppose now that some of this stock is being sold to establish a value. Everybody will be willing to pay a big price for it, and evidence will be established as to the value of the stock. I say it is poor business the way this thing has been handled.
But I go back to my first proposition, that there was not the slightest occasion for dealing with the company in this way at all. It may be said that I have no business to be talking about this matter, and that I am simply taking up the time of the House, as hon. gentlemen to whom millions mean nothing-evidently $600,000,000 means nothing to them-have made up their minds in the caucus that they are going to vote for this Bill, and that is the end of it. But, Sir, if any measure ever came before Parliament that deserved careful thought and consideration, it is this proposition involving the expenditure of this vast amount of money. Therefore, I make no apology for taking up a little of the time of the House in setting forth my views and quoting from the records. The carrying out of the agreement that was solemnly entered into in 1914 should be the confession of faith of every honest man in this House; it is the basic principle of the action that should be taken here. I submit that under the agreement of 1914 we absolutely own this property, and there is no need of saying another word about it. The Government cannot say that this company is not in default; they are estopped from saying that. The company must be in default under the agreement of 1914 or they would not be here, and I base my argument upon that assumption. The Government would not be presenting these proposals to Parliament if the Company had not made default. Section 21 of the Act
of 1914 for giving assistance to the Canadian Northern Railway system says:
The following shall be events of default within the meaning of this Act, viz,-
(a)	if the Canadian Northern shall make default in payment of the principal or interest of the guaranteed securities or any part thereof, or default in observing or performing any of the provisions of the New Trust Deed, and the security constituted by the New Trust Deed shall thereby become enforceable ;
(b)	if while any of the guaranteed securities are outstanding the Canadian Northern or any Constituent or Subsidiary Company shall make default in the payment of the principal or interest or any part thereof, or any securities heretofore or hereafter created or issued under the existing trust deed or mortgage securing the same, or under any future trust deed securing securities having priority to the guaranteed securities, or default in observing of performing any of the terms of any such existing or future trust deed or mortgage, and the security constituted by any such trust deed or mortgage shall thereby become enforceable;
(c)	if, while any of the guaranteed securities are outstanding, an order be made by any court against any company in the Canadian Northern System for the appointment of a receiver or for possession, or if a receiver be otherwise appointed or possession be otherwise lawfully taken of the whole or part of the undertaking-
In the event of any one of those conditions arising, the Government could step in and take possession of the property. Section 22 says:
Upon the happening of any event of default and at any time or times while the same shall continue, it shall be lawful for the Governor in Council after such notice to the Canadian Northern as the Governor in Council may direct, to declare to be vacant the offices of the directors of the Canadian Northern and of any of the Constituent or Subsidiary Companies "which may he subject to the legislative authority of the Parliament of Canada, and to appoint a board or boards of directors in lieu thereof respectively (any former director being eligible for appointment).
2. The power of appointment herein conferred upon the Governor in Council shall be a continuous power and shall be exercisable from time to time and so often as any event of default may exist and be continuing.
23.	The directors so appointed by the Governor in Council shall hold office during the pleasure of the Governor in Council, and any such director may be removed and another appointed in his place. Vacancies occurring from
^ time to time may be filled by the Governor in Council. The said boards respectively shall have all the powers of a board of directors elected by the shareholders; and acts of the board requiring the authority and approval of the shareholders shall if authorized or approved by the Gorvernor in Council be as valid and effectual as if authorized or approved by the shareholders.
24.	If authorized by the Parliament of Canada, the Governor in Council may on such terms and conditions (if any) as Parliament may prescribe, at any time while any event of default shall exist and be continuing, by order declare the equity of redemption of the Canadian Northern and of all other persons whom-

soever in the mortgaged premises to be foreclosed ,and thereupon the equity of redemption of the Canadian Northern (and of such other persons) in the mortgaged premises and every part thereof shall be and become absolutely barred and foreclosed, and the same shall thereupon be vested in His Majesty in right of the Dominion of Canada, any statutory enactment or any rule of law or equity to the contrary notwithstanding.
Those are the powers which this Parliament took to itself in 1914, and I submit that they are absolute and conclusive. I am not going to read section 25, as it is rather long, but it provides for the appointment of directors-an absolute board without any representation of Mackenzie and Mann, and empowered to do the very thing that has been held up as a bugaboo by the Minister of Finance in this House. Under this Act they have power to avoid those very difficulties. The Minister of Finance frightened us the other day by saying that if we took over the physical as-5 p.m. sets and the whole material property of the road we should have to pay off the securities and should have tp borrow money at six per cent to pay the interest on bonds that may run for a number of years at a very much lower rate of interest. Now, under section 25, the Government is empowered to take over those securities. The Government is authorized to take the place of Mackenzie and Mann in every way, and to continue the securities just as they are now. What is the good of the Minister of Finance or anybody else trying to frighten this House into a bad bargain by saying that we may be obliged to pay off all those securities and borrow money in the markets of the world at a high rate of interest to pay off the low rate of interest on these bonds that may run for many years to come, when, in 1914, some good man on the Government side had the prescience to incorporate in the statute a provision by which we could take over all these bonds and not disturb them in the slightest degree, but go on paying the interest on them just as the company is doing now, or would do if it had the means.
I am sure that I can appeal to the business men of this House and of the country and that they will lall say that they would be glad to take the credit of the Canadian people instead of that of Mackenzie and Mann or of any private individual or concern. That is what will happen under the provisions of section 25. Mackenzie and Mann go out, we take the property and the credit of Canada goes, in their place, behind those bonds. Will anybody say that those who will hold those securities-doubt-
ful securities, many of them-will force them to foreclosure and sale if they have the backing of- the Canadian people behind them? That is what has been held out to us as the bugaboo reason why we should jump at the course of action which this Government is taking. Those are the terms of the agreement that we made in 1914.
I am now going to -give you an explanation of how the bargain was understood by the Government of that time, and I am going to give you the way in which my hon. friend the Solicitor General (Mr. IMeighen) understod the statute. If anybody understood that .statute or ought to have understood it, it was the Solicitor General. He drafted it or helped to draft it. He had the full responsibility of preparing that measure, of getting it through 'Council and of bringing it before this House. When it was before this House he gave an explanation of it which will '->e found .at page 3687 of Hansard, May 13, 1914. I 'seriously invite the attention of hon. gentlemen in this House, and particularly of hon. gentlemen on the other side, to the language of the Solicitor General and I would ask them to say if they can find any loophole for Mackenzie and Mann, or .anybody else, to come here for consideration after they had made default. (He makes it as clear and distinct as the English language can make it that the moment they make default that is the end of it. He says further that everybody is made a party to 'this agreement who has any interest whatever in the company. All persons who hold stock in the .company are, .according to the Solicitor General, made parties to the agreement. The agreement is -binding and conclusive and these men cannot find fault if they do not keep their part of it and we keep ours. This is what the hon. gentleman said:
Under the present Bill-
That- is the Bill which is now the twentieth chapter of the Acts of 1914.
-we have a summary method of taking over the road, a summary method which in effect gives us as security the other sixty per cent of stock.
That is the 60 per cent that we were talking about buying. The Solicitor General tells, us that it is under the mortgage and that we have it. He continues:
We know we have the ordinary right which any mortgagee has, and the right which any guarantor of a mortgage has, the right 'by subrogation of getting into the shoes of the lender and in the event of default exercising the rights of a mortgagee and taking possession of the road as a receiver; we know we have that right, but we have the additional summary remedy of proceeding by mere Act of Parliament to

take over the road as the property of the people of this country and eliminate once and for all, all other parties interested in that railway. And we have not only so arranged it that the interests of the Canadian Northern and all other persons whatsoever in the Canadian Northern system shall be eliminated, and that in the event of default all shall he the property of the Canidian people, but furthermore, the ten million dollars of stock in the townsite and the ten million dollars bonds are put into hotchpotch, although they are the property of Mackenzie and Mann, and although Mackenzie and Mann alone made investment in them, and in the event of our foreclosing and taking over the enterprise we ourselves get the whole benefit of the townsite. That summary method is given us. It is true Parliament has to act. The Government did not think it wise to in any way tie the hands of Parliament in days to come. We provide though that Parliament in days to come, should there be default, shall have in its own hands the power to put in directors of the road, and we clothe the directors so appointed with full power to sell that road to any corporation established by the Parliament of this country for the purpose of taking over the road. Or, if we choose, we can ourselves, by Act of Parliament, legislate that that road is the property of the people of this country and that the interests of all persons whatsoever outside of the people of Canada are eliminated, the idea of that is that we are at this time making the interested parties and all the stockholders, parties to this contract, and we say to them-
I wish to point out that all the parties who are interested are made parties to the statute and that, to use a vulgar expression, they will have no kick coming if they are ruled out.
The idea of that is that we are at this time making the interested parties and all stockholders parties to this contract, and we say to them: We now and here bind you that should the day of default come you shall not appeal to the Parliament of Canada on the ground of your road being confiscated in any way whatever, but you here and now leave the Parliament of this country free from any such question and untrammelled in every way to deal with the property of the Canadian Northern as it may be advised in the interests of the people of this country. That is the summary procedure outlined here for taking over the road.
I want to ask where any loophole is left in this for anybody to look for any -consideration. Mackenzie and Mann had given several mortgages and entered into several obligations before which it was hoped they would redeem. They came at last to 1914 and the -Government said to them: You 'have come often enough, you have come -again, but if we -are going to give you any money now there must not be any talk of foreclosure or any round-about methods of that kind; you must sign a bond, which shall be embodied in a statute, providing that if yo-u make default the Canadian people shall be entitled to take the whole thing over. I can not conceive of
any stronger language that -a learned counsel like the Solicitor General could use to make it clearer or more distinct than he used in that speech. Taking his speech, with the language of the statute, and taking the circumstances of the case, can there be any question that at that lime we had the right to believe that we were getting everything that this company had under the agreement of 1914 and that if they made default they could not complain if we should take over the whole thing?
Mow, we find that there is to be another deal altogether. This stock has value, the Government say. The Solicitor General says in his speech and the Act -says in its language that whether it has value or not it belongs to the people of this country. Whose business is it whether it has value or not? It belongs to us absolutely and conclusively. But now it turns out that this stock is in the -hands of some friends of the Government influential millionaires who have taken it as security for money advanced to Mackenzie and M-ann, I suppose, and now they -say: Whatever else may be forfeited, do not forfeit this stock, because the money for it will go into our pockets. The hon. member for North Grey told us that the $45,000,000 we gave them went into the road. If they get the par value for this stock, how much of it will go into the road? Not one farthing; it will go into the pockets of the millionaires who now hold the -stock. I object to the line of procedure in picking out this stock any more than anything else, and I object to disturbing the agreement which, taken together with the speech of the Hon. Mr. Meighen, -makes it clear beyond controversy that the property belongs absolutely and conclusively to the people of Canada once the company has made default. This effort to find value in this stock, or to direct -the blood currents once more into the reins of this stock and give it life, is simply for the purpose of gratifying and paying off the holders of the stock, whoever they may be.
I am not in favour of public ownership; I am against it. But if we are down to the position when we have to take over the ownership of this road, let us take it clean-cut, let us take everything in connection with it that will be of benefit and service to the people. It has been found by a court, representing, as I said, the wisdom of three nations in railway matters, that the common stock which we are taking over has no value, yet we -are going to over-rule their judgment and say it has got value, and we are making an agreement under which

it will be possible for the owners of this stock to say it has more value than it ever had before. The whole course in trying to give value to this stock is absolutely wrong. It would be in every way better to refer this matter to a judge of the Exchequer Court, a man of vast experience and known skill in dealing with matters of this kind, than to refer it to three arbitrators, who may or may not be experienced in dealing with matters of this kind. In entering upon any arbitration you have, in practice, although not in theory, one-third of the court against you, and if he can persuade the other two members of the court to his way of thinking, ihe is able to obtain a verdict against you. It is much better to leave it in the hands of one experienced, skilled and just man than to a court of three arbitrators. If a man had to undergo a surgical operation, he would place himself in the hands of an eminent and experienced surgeon rather than in the hands of a clinic of three doctors, one of- whom he knew would not desire to do anything to save his life, but would be glad to kill him if he could.

speechtext: Did not the hon. member, in 1914, vote for a resolution moved by Sir Wilfrid Laurier, seconded by the Hon. Mr. Pugsley, advocating the principle of appointing arbitrators to fix the value which should be handed over for this very road?

subtopic: DEBATE CONTINUED ON MOTION FOR SECOND READING OF CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY BILL.
speechtext:
There are cases where a man is not doing justice to himself by saying yes or no to any question. I did vote for that proposition, but in the early part of my speech to-day I explained the position and circumstances, and if the hon. gentleman cares to know my attitude and position he will see my remarks in Hansard and I shall not need to go over the same ground again. In brief, I say that we were willing perhaps to pay an amount at that time not exceeding $30,000,000 for the whole thing.
But the Government at that time, instead of paying something less than $30,000,000, paid $45,000,000, and are willing to pay more now. They are taking chances on having to pay $60,000,000 more. We were willing to pay something ranging under $30,000,000. That is a very much better .bargain than paying $45,000,000, and taking chances of paying $60,000,000 more. I explained that matter before, and I think the hon. gentleman understands my position. I certainly did vote for that resolution, and I have nothing to apologize for, or take

back, because we did not even have the advantage of the conclusive evidence that is now before us in the report of that commission, that that stock is worth nothing. I am sure if in 1914 we had had the report of such eminent men as those three gentlemen who have gone over this matter and reported to us that this stock has no' value, the hon. gentleman from St. John (Mr. Pugsley) would not have moved that resolution, and if he did he would never have got anybody on our side of the House to support it. We had not the evidence then, but we have it now.

speechtext:
The hon. gentleman was
iu favour of the principle of arbitration.
