speechtext:
I really forget. It is
three years ago. Supposing we were in favour of arbitration three years ago, as dealing with something we thought had value, it is a different proposition to-day. Now we have discovered that the subject matter of our deliberation at that time has no value at all. It is a dead horse.

subtopic: DEBATE CONTINUED ON MOTION FOR SECOND READING OF CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY BILL.
speechtext: Does that change the principle of arbitration any?

subtopic: DEBATE CONTINUED ON MOTION FOR SECOND READING OF CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY BILL.
speechtext:
It does not matter what my opinion is. Hon. gentlemen opposite would not follow it if they could help. We have the opinion of a court in this country appointed for the express purpose of doing this kind of work, absolutely unbiased, a third of which is not against us at the start. Even if I did ask for an arbitration, why should hon. gentlemen follow my advice, inasmuch as they voted against it before?
Hon. gentlemen opposite then thought that arbitration was wrong and they voted it down, and now we say there is only one other course open to them, namely, to go to the Exchequer Court. A year ago this spring we discussed a similar question in this House in connection with the values of railways. What did hon. gentlemen opposite do? They passed an Act of this Parliament to ascertain the value of the Quebec 'Central Railway. Did they appoint 'an arbitration? No; they selected the Exchequer Court, the very tribunal which we suggest in this instance. What is the difference between ascertaining the value of stock and railway equipment in Quebec and ascertaining the value of stock and railway equipment in the West? Why not get the benefit of the experience of that very learned court as to the value of this Canadian Northern Railway? I will point out to hon. gentlemen opposite what may be the

reason for their changed course. I have had the honour of reading the reasons for judgment of the judge of the Exchequer Court in the Quebec-Saguenay Railway valuation. I find he did not live up to the expectations of those who expected to make a carcass for the delectation of the prairie birds of the Quebec and Saguenay Railway. He did not fall into their ways of thinking. He was a clean-cut business man, and I would commend any lawyer or any layman in this House to read his decision and see the masterful way in which he dealt with that question. They will find that one item alone which he rejected consisted of a million and a quarter dollars. The Government, represented by a lawyer, said it was all right to let the million and a quarter go through, but the judge of the Exchequer Court said: It is not right; it is all wrong, and I will not allow it.

subtopic: DEBATE CONTINUED ON MOTION FOR SECOND READING OF CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY BILL.
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: DEBATE CONTINUED ON MOTION FOR SECOND READING OF CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY BILL.
speechtext:
A claim for a million and a quarter of money in one transaction was disallowed by the judge. If we want a man in this country to deal with a like subject, do hon. gentlemen not think it is a recommendation for him, that he should take that view in the very same sort of case? It commends itself to me, and I think it would commend itself to any ordinary man. I submit, therefore, that if we must have arbitration, we should take the very best kind of arbitration we can get, refer it to the judge of the Exchequer Court, and let him deal with this matter. I am willing to refer to any unbiased lawyer that agreement of 1914, interpreted in the light of the speeches made in explaining it to the House by the Solicitor-General, and I am convinced that any unbiased judge or lawyer will reach the conclusion that there should never be a word said about any further consideration of values in this business, and that we should take the railway over and do the best we can with it. I -submit there is no reason for any consideration of the value of the stock. If it is to be considered, it is because there is some power behind the throne, holding this stock, which has some sinister influence with this Government, and which is trying to put life and value into a dead horse. We have paid enough for the road, and it should be ours. The commissioners say the property is not worth more than about $400,000,000. We are taking over with it obligations to the extent of $620,000,000, and why
should we pay more? For these reasons I will vote for the amendment of the hon. gentleman (Mr. Graham) and against this Bill, if an opportunity be given me to vote against it.

subtopic: DEBATE CONTINUED ON MOTION FOR SECOND READING OF CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY BILL.
speechtext:
I have listened to the remarks of the hon. gentleman from Cape Breton (Mr. McKenzie), and I do not say that I am in a position, from a legal point of view, to answer his arguments. He said that, as a member of this House, he did not believe in public ownership. I am a believer in public ownership of railways, and I intend to justify that belief, as well as I can, on this occasion. I may foe, to use an old phrase, a lone pine in this House in favour of public ownership, although I do not admit even that. But though I should be, I am not ashamed to declare myself in favour of public ownership. I have been in this House a good many years, and for many years I have favoured that policy, and have advocated legislation to carry it into effect. I have addressed the people all over this country on this subject, and, as an ordinary, everyday journalist, I have discussed the question in print, and I am convinced, not only that public ownership is right and in the public interest, but that the people of all countries are already believers in it, or are rapidly becoming such. The thing that marks this century more than anything else is the progress made by the doctrine of public ownership, which has had more to do with the recovery of public rights and the promotion of public welfare than any other factor. The regeneration of Canada and other countries, after this war, will depend almost absolutely on carrying out this principle.
Public ownership is not a new thing; it prevails all over Europe. In every country in Europe, with the exception of Great Britain, they have had public ownership of railways. Germany, all-powerful in this war, has public ownership of railways and she overran Belgium, and got into France, and her allies got into Turkey, all of which was accomplished because of their organization of railways under state control, first for purposes of defence, and, second, for the development of trade and industries, Germany is all-powerful in this contest, largely 'because she has had public ownership of railways. The railways of France are under state control; the same may be said of Russia and of Italy. Russian trade to-day can reach the Pacific only through a national railway; the mission that went



to Russia from the United 'States went by a national Russian railway that had reached out to the Pacific coast through a territory where no private company would (build. Australian and New Zealand have public ownership of railways; so has India, a dependency of the British Crown. Sixty or seventy years ago England made the mistake of deciding that the steel rails which up to that time had been owned by the public should not be kept as the King's highway. So great a man as 'Gladstone allowed to slip by the opportunity then afforded of nationalizing the railways and of retaining them as the King's highway. Rivers and canals have always been kept as the King's highways, though their administration has been changed to some extent by the 'interposition of private corporations. The doctrine, however, in England was that the King's highway should be public property and that principle prevailed in connection with everything but the railways. After the declaration of war the first thing that England did was to take possession of the eighteen or more private companies engaged in Tailway transportation; to consolidate them; to put them under the control and direction of the State. The moment that was done, a splendid service was afforded, not only in transportation connected with the army, but in the promotion of trade generally. Only yesterday I picked up a copy o.f that great enemy of public ownership, the Railway Age, published in New York, the editor of which came to Canada to speak as an opponent of publjc ownership, but in his paper last week he has an article which shows how England consolidated her railways with the distribution of coal to the great benefit of the whole country. This, then, is what happened in England since the war began; with a view to the welfare of the Empire and to the winning of the war, the railways, of England were mobilized and put in a position to render the greatest possible service to the state. The war has been on for three years, and no complaint has been made in England against this nationalization of the railways. But something else happened in England: they .mobilized the coal mines also. These works are now controlled absolutely by the state, for two purposes: the winning of the war, and the promotion of trade and industries. In order to get the best service at a minimum cost, it is provided that coal may be ordered through a national board, and that national board designates the mine from which the coal 
shall come and the nailway over which it must be transported. The result is a maximum of co-operation and co-ordination between the coal mines and the railways. The handling of the coal is, as a consequence, much more economically accomplished. If you live in the north of England your coal must be obtained from the nearest mine and must be transported over the railroad that runs nearest the mine. In this way you get the cheapest, the shortest,, the quickest, and, therefore, the best service. In other words, these public utilities have been pooled in the public interest and for the welfare of the state; they are not being used for the benefit of shareholders who fry to get as much as they possibly can out of the enterprises in which they are interested.

subtopic: DEBATE CONTINUED ON MOTION FOR SECOND READING OF CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY BILL.
speechtext: Is it not true that those people who oppose public ownership must necessarily oppose public control?

subtopic: DEBATE CONTINUED ON MOTION FOR SECOND READING OF CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY BILL.
speechtext: I would think so.

subtopic: DEBATE CONTINUED ON MOTION FOR SECOND READING OF CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY BILL.
speechtext: Is it not true 'that in the matter of public ownership a great deal depends upon the manner in which public affairs are .administered in the jcountry concerned? Does it necessarily follow that in Canada the administration of public utilities would be as honest or as efficient as it is in England?

subtopic: DEBATE CONTINUED ON MOTION FOR SECOND READING OF CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY BILL.
speechtext: As a Canadian, I say yes. I am not afraid to trust the Canadian Parliament; I am not afraid to trust my fellow-men in 'the constituency of South YoTk, in regard to this matter.

subtopic: DEBATE CONTINUED ON MOTION FOR SECOND READING OF CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY BILL.
speechtext: Has the experience in connection with the Intercolonial railway brought the hon. gentleman to that conclusion?

subtopic: DEBATE CONTINUED ON MOTION FOR SECOND READING OF CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY BILL.
speechtext:
No. I am not
afraid of public ownership in respect to the Intercolonial, nor do I apologize for the application of the' principle to that public utility. Public ownership of the Intercolonial has been a good thing. True, it can be made better-and that it has not been better in the past hon. gentlemen on both sides may be more or less responsible for. What can be done in other countries can be done in Canada, and what is good for any other country is good for Canada. Public ownership has vindicated itself the world over. If any hon, gentlemen will show where public ownership has failed, or give reasons of its having failed, he may be able to make out a case against the adoption of that policy. But 1 believe in public own-

ership, though I may be almost alone in that belief; perhaps not many representatives of the people believe in public ownership.

subtopic: DEBATE CONTINUED ON MOTION FOR SECOND READING OF CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY BILL.
speechtext:
The great chief of
the Conservative party, Sir John A. Macdonald, was opposed to public ownership.

subtopic: DEBATE CONTINUED ON MOTION FOR SECOND READING OF CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY BILL.
speechtext: No, he was not; I know as much about Sir John A. Macdonald's views as my hon. friend does.

subtopic: DEBATE CONTINUED ON MOTION FOR SECOND READING OF CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY BILL.
speechtext:
Hv, is on record as
being opposed to it.

subtopic: DEBATE CONTINUED ON MOTION FOR SECOND READING OF CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY BILL.
speechtext:
Granted that he was; he lived fifty years ago; we are in the twentieth century. We are living; Sir John A. Macdonald is dead. We have to deal with this matter not from the viewpoint of what Sir John Macdonald thought fifty years ago, 'but from the viewpoint of the real value of public ownership to-day. Twisting and turning may have been practiced in the past-indeed, I saw a good deal of twisting and turning here to-day that rather surprised me. But I still say that the experience of nations the world over is favourable to public ownership.
I now come to the United States, which is going to be a great factor in the settlement of this war. Immediately upon war being declared by the United States, the railways of the country were mobilized, and the people who, as shareholders and bondholders, have their money in those railways to-day, would like to see that mobilization go forward still further. The United States will, I believe, embark on a policy of public ownership of railways, especially after they see that Canada has decided that public ownership is to obtain in this country. The United States have adopted a policy of public ownership of railways in Alaska, because they are constructing there a national railway to make connection with our railways in British Columbia. They have come to the conclusion that there the principle of public ownership ought to be adopted. They are mobilizing and nationalizing their railways to-day in order to handle their troops, to ship their munitions, to send supplies to their army, which is in France now, and which will be there for a long time to come. They are doing that because it is good public policy, and they are, in that respect, simply following the example of the rest of the world.
I desire to state two or three reasons why I believe in public ownership of railways. I believe in it, not because other nations have adopted that policy, but because of
287J
the advantages and economies that it brings about. Where you have a number of privately-owned roads, you have much unnecessary duplication of .stations, terminals, sidings, and so on, and that means a great deal of unnecessary expense. With public ownership-and we are on the way to it now in Canada-all this unnecessary duplication ceases. In Montreal, the Canadian Northern Company has most expensive terminals, a tunnel, a station, sidings. If there was public ownership, there would be no need of that.

subtopic: DEBATE CONTINUED ON MOTION FOR SECOND READING OF CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY BILL.
speechtext: There are three railway stations in Montreal.

subtopic: DEBATE CONTINUED ON MOTION FOR SECOND READING OF CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY BILL.
speechtext: My hon. friend's statement makes my argument three times as strong as I made it. You have all this waste and unnecessary expense, and you do not get the service; you do not get coordination, and co-operation. By public ownership you get co-ordination of the system, you do away with unnecessary duplication; you get co-operation; you have fewer terminals and sidings, and every siding is available for every citizen of the country. I know siding after siding , on which you can put a freight car only, by the pressure of the Board of Railway Commissioners, but with public ownership, every man will be able to use every siding and every terminal. He will form part of the ownership; the railway will be his, and he will not have to ask the permission of any railway magnate or company to use a siding. The railway will be for the service of the country.

subtopic: DEBATE CONTINUED ON MOTION FOR SECOND READING OF CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY BILL.
speechtext: In Australia there is public ownership of railways. Does the hon. gentleman think the condition of things in Australia, where there is a multiplicity of gauges, where the same car cannot he used on different railways, is better than the system in Canada where there is one gauge?

subtopic: DEBATE CONTINUED ON MOTION FOR SECOND READING OF CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY BILL.
speechtext: That, of course, is a great mistake.

subtopic: DEBATE CONTINUED ON MOTION FOR SECOND READING OF CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY BILL.
speechtext: Still, the hon. gentleman says that public ownership brings about co-ordination.

subtopic: DEBATE CONTINUED ON MOTION FOR SECOND READING OF CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY BILL.
speechtext:
Yes, it does. I remember when the Grand Trunk and the Great Western had different gauges, and they had a third rail on those railways. We have an instance of that in Toronto where the street railway has what is called a bastard gauge. But when you have public ownership of railways, you can standardize everything in connection with them;
4534

you can bring about great economies, and you can give a better service.
In America and in England, railways have been constructed by private companies, ostensibly for the purpose of giving good service, but the real object in most cases has been to make profits for the shareholders. The difference between public ownership and private ownership is that the former seeks to give service and the latter to make profits for the owners, and service and profit do not go together; they have never gone together in this country. No railway in this country has been constructed wholly with the idea of giving service; the men who operate it devote all their energies to meeting the fixed charges and earning profits for the shareholders. That is their duty. They always think of profit first and service second. With public ownership good service is the main thing to be considered, and the orders to those who administer the road should be to see how good a service they can give to the public without regard to the profits. Of course, the fixed charges in connection with the road must be provided for. Public, ownership will put an end to this idea of running a railway to make magnates. We have had some of them in this country and they have had them in the United States, Ithe Vanderbilts., the Goulds and the Hills. The late Mr. J. J. Hill gave an excellent .service in. the northwestern states and in some portions of Canada, but he had in mind one thing more than anything else, and that was to make J. J. Hill a great railway magnate and to leave his sons great railway magnates, and the service they gave to the people was a secondary consideration.
We are not going to make any more railway magnates in this country; we are going to build the railroads by the people, for the people, and with the people's money, on the principle of giving service and not making money for any one, or making great families and consolidating wealth and putting it into the hands of the few. It will not be permitted in future to any body of men or any company or any board of directors to discriminate, as they have done in the past, against individuals or localities. The view that the welfare of the nation is of more importance than the wealth of individuals is in the direction of public ownership. That view is spreading throughout the minds of the people of this country, and go where you will in Canada, you will see that the people are in favour of public ownership. That is especially true of the

West. The farmers of the West, at their conventions, and in particular, at a convention of a political party that met at Winnipeg the other day, voiced the views of the people of the West, declaring in favour of public ownership. I say, therefore, that the verdict of the people of this country is in favour of public ownership, because that is based on the principle of service and not of profit-on the principle of the "welfare of all and not of the wealth of a few. They have before them the fact that public ownership has vindicated itself in Europe. Great Britain resorted to public ownership when she found herself at war. The United States resorted to it in the development of Alaska and in the mobilization of railways and in connection with the war. Japan, China, Australia, New Zealand- the whole world to-day, with the exception of England and the United States, is in favour of public ownership, and these two countries are also accepting it in a measure. We, too, are accepting it', and I thank God I am living in this year 1917 when 9,000 ot
10,000	miles of railway actually pass out of private ownership into the hands of the people, and will be ultimately joined up in creating a great national system of railways owned by the people and devoted to the development and welfare of the nation, and not to the profits of individuals.
I just wish to say a word on the question of discrimination, which public ownership overcomes. Instance after instance can be found in the history of the United States where roads have discriminated against an individual or an interest-the farming interest, for instance-or even against a state. Certain places have been ruined because railway magnates of private-owned roads have discriminated against a certain town or locality, or against a certain interest. Public ownership, on the other hand, is based on the principle of no discrimination; equality of treatment for all. You cannot find a private-owned road that is not open to the charge that they have unjustly discriminated. We have created a railway commission in this country, as they have in the United States, to prevent this discrimination and unfair treatment. The other point in this connection which I wish to emphasize is this: My father often told me, when talking over political questions, that the great mistake the peoiple made in England many years ago in connection with railways and other matters was in thinking that the least government was the best. Now the teaching of this country and of this day, with the advance of civilization

in all its complexity, is that the duty of doing something and protecting the public interest rest more and more upon the State. Therefore, with the complexities of civilization as we know it to-day, and with the questions that are now before us as to the reorganization of our country, there is nothing ahead of us but public ownership of railways in order to fully protect the welfare and the interests of the nation.
