subtopic: DEBATE CONTINUED ON MOTION FOR SECOND READING OF CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY BILL.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the next point I want to make in favour of the public ownership of railways is that it will help to solve the problem of the motive power with which our railways are to be run. There is a great scarcity of coal in various portion of Canada. In my own province of Ontario we have no coal, and there is no coal in Quebec. There is a large store of coal in the Maritime Provinces, but you have to go pretty far west before you come to any large deposits of coal. Therefore, we are largely dependent on distant coal beds, situated in a foreign country, for the coal supply for our railways. The public ownership of railways removes one great difficulty in connection with transportation in this country, namely that if we have not the coal, we have the greatest water powers in the world, and the modern thing in railroading to-day is to get your motive power for transportation from the streams. We have rivers that will produce enough hydro-electric energy to give us an unlimited supply of motive power to operate all our railways and make us independent of the coal companies in foreign countries who ship coal to us. These water powers, if properly controlled, will provide us with motive power which will probably give Canada the finest transportation system in the world. They are largely owned and controlled by the provinces and the Dominion. It is not too late for this Parliament, by its own action and co-operation with the provinces, to declare that every water power in this country must be conserved, kept, owned and controlled by the State. If we are foolish enough to allow < ur water powers and rivers to pass info the control of private corporations, as the coal beds in the United States have passed into the hands of corporations, then the question of coal becomes of supreme importance to the
people of Canada and to those who have charge of transportation.
There are water powers enough in Canada to draw every train and every car we shall ever have. If we nationalize the railways, which I favouT, and if we nationalize our water powers, as we ought to, and use them for the solution of the transportation problem, Canada will have the best railway system in the world. So far, we have made great headway in nationalizing our water powers. In Ontario to-day the work is largely done. We have the Hydro-Electric Commission, publicly owned and controlled by the municipalities of Ontario in conjunction with the Provincial Government, and. we are steadily moving in the direction of the nationalization of all these water powers and the development of power for manufacturing industries as well as for transportation. What is being done in Ontario can be done in every part of the country. What we have done with the Niagara river-can be done in connection with the St, Lawrence. There is enough power on the Niagara river, and enough power can be generated on the St. Lawrence, to drive every car and every train, to run every factory and every industry, and to light all the factories and all the cities and towns and houses in the country.
Right at Cornwall, at the Long Sault, there is an immense quantity of power, and it nearly passed out of the hands of the people of Canada. It was proposed in this very Parliament, since I have been a member of it, to alienate that great water power at Cornwall and to turn it over to a company partly American and partly Canadian in its organization, which would have monopolized the power and sold it to the people and to the railways at the highest price. The railways to-day have to pay the coal owners in the United States a high price for the coal which is used as motive power to run the railways. The two Governments controlling the two sides of the river, could develop the water power on the St. Lawrence, as our Government is developing it on the Niagara, and with these two rivers alone we would have control of the motive power in Ontarid and Quebec, and run every train on the Grand Trunk, the Canadian Pacific and Canadian Northern.
Then, back in the province of Quebec, they have immense, unlimited, water power which can be developed. By reason of the improved system of transmission, notrouble is experienced in sending power to.

a distance of 400 or 500 miles without any great percentage of loss, and that power can be used for driving trains.
The only way to develop this water-power to the greatest public advantage is by State ownership of railways and of water-powers. In that way alone can we provide for the farmer the cheapest and best possible transportation for his products. That idea is spreading in my own province of Ontario where, largely through the development of water-powers on the Niagara river, we are moving our street cars in Toronto, Hamilton, Brantford and London by power transmitted over long distances. The Canadian Pacific has a great scheme for the development of local traffic in Ontario if it oan get the power. Some of the railroads have not the capital necessary to develop power in this direction. The Canadian Pacific may have it, hut the Grand Trunk has not the money necessary to develop water-powers in Ontario and on the St. Lawrence to operate its trains. Once such a system is installed we shall for all time be secure as to our motive power for the operation of our railroads. There is enough waterpower in Northern Ontario, in the drainage basin that goes to Hudson bay, coupled with the power that could be developed in Southern Ontario and on the St. Lawrence and in the valleys of Quebec, to drive every train that carries grain from Winnipeg to the seaboard. Upon the great rivers in the West power can be developed, with a proper system of storage, to make our western railroads absolutely independent of coal fuel. Thus the whole country will be independent of American coal and the owners of mines in Canada.
'To show how this idea of State ownership of railways.and of power supply is spreading, let me quote an item I clipped the other day referring to the proposed national railroad to be built for the development of Alaska. One of the first -things the United States Government did was to acquire coal beds in that country. They realized that in order to have a first-class, cheap system of transportation for Alaska they must not only build a national railroad, but must buy coal beds. The item reads:
The commission will develop the property without delay. Sumner 6. Smith, inspector for the Federal Bureau of Mines, will be in immediate charge of operations, and Geo. W. Evans, district mine engineer of the Bureau of Mines, will act as consulting engineer. Mr. Evans is now in Seattle, arranging for the purchase and shipment of the necessary machinery and equipment.
The purpose of the commission in purchasing the mine is to secure an adequate supply of coal for the construction and operation of

the Government railroad. This object was attainable only through the operation of the mine on a larger scale and by the installation of proper facilities. A washer for cleaning the product will be erected, and other modern equipment added to the plant, to insure the necessary tonnage and the economical handling of the output.
The commission will also take steps at once to open a mine at another point.
The American nation thus finds it necessary, in building a great national road, to acquire a supply of motive power.

subtopic: DEBATE CONTINUED ON MOTION FOR SECOND READING OF CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY BILL.
speechtext: Are they going to pay the Canadian' bondholders of that road, who built it?

subtopic: DEBATE CONTINUED ON MOTION FOR SECOND READING OF CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY BILL.
speechtext: I am unable to answer that question. I know that the United States Government are building that road themselves.

subtopic: DEBATE CONTINUED ON MOTION FOR SECOND READING OF CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY BILL.
speechtext: Freezing out the Canadian bondholders.

subtopic: DEBATE CONTINUED ON MOTION FOR SECOND READING OF CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY BILL.
speechtext:
I am not speaking about the Canadian bondholders, but about the transportation problem. The United States are to-day building this great railroad, and they -are getting control of coal that will supply the motive power.
When the Bill now before this House passes, the people of Canada will own sixteen thousand or seventeen thousand miles of railroad. And if we -are faced with the problem of motive power, as we are to-day in Quebec and Ontario, in order to satisfactorily solve that problem we must not only own the railroads, but also control the motive power and the rivers that supply it. If we do that we shall have the best and cheapest transportation system of any country in the world. Our people see it now in Ontario, where we have a splendid system of radials, and we have already arranged for public ownership of water-powers and the control of the rivers. We are going to develop that power and transmit it throughout the province, and the same system should be extended to the whole Dominion. Privately-owned companies should not be permitted to control these water-powers, and those who believe in public ownership should endeavour now to- secure the development of these water-powers for the public good so that we shall be absolutely independent for all time in respect to motive power to operate our railroads.
That is why there is a good deal of opposition to public ownership to-day-they see it coming. There is often a danger that there will be a coal famine through shortage o-f railway equipment, but there is no

way that I see of getting cheaper rates on railways other than 'by public ownership of the railways to begin with, public ownership of the waterways thereafter, and by mobolizing both 'together the people of Canada will have better and cheaper transportation than they ever had. Compared with other countries, it will give them the best transportation in the world.
I will give another reason why public ownership commends itself to me. A modern word in economics is " valorization," and you can, perhaps, valorize railway rates. That statement may surprise members of this House, but it does not surprise many thinking men. The great question in Canada should be what is best for 'the farmers. We yet do not know the possible resources of that great Peace River district. All that great western country is engaged, and will be engaged for many years, in the production of grain for the use of our own people, and for export, and one of the standing objections to settlement in the farthest west is that the freight rates are higher, that they have to pay more in Alberta to get a bushel of wheat to the seaboard than they have to pay in Manitoba, and still more than they have to pay in Ontario. The day is coming in the new order of economics, I hope, when the freight rates on a bushel of wheat to the seaboard will be valorized; that is, that in order to give equality to the producers it ought to cost no more to ship a bushel of wheat from Alberta to Pacific or the Atlantic seaboard than it costs to ship that same bushel of wheat, say, from Ontario. That is rather a far-fetched idea, and many people would not believe in it, but if you can show the people of the West that by public ownership of railways you can valorize the freight rate on a bushel of wheat so that it will be the same all over the country, then you have a great argument for public ownership. I know that this argument will be met with a great deal of objection, but the valorization of freight rates must come some day, and the country that adopts it first will give the best and fairest transportation to its people.

subtopic: DEBATE CONTINUED ON MOTION FOR SECOND READING OF CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY BILL.
speechtext:
Would you apply the
same argument to electric power?

subtopic: DEBATE CONTINUED ON MOTION FOR SECOND READING OF CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY BILL.
speechtext:
I do not know
why you should not. The great argument against the Hydro Electric Commission in Ontario was that while the people owned that power those who lived further away from it had to use it-
Mr. HANiNA: And pay bigger rates for it.

subtopic: DEBATE CONTINUED ON MOTION FOR SECOND READING OF CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY BILL.
speechtext:
I see no way of valorizing freight rates except by public ownership, so that the man who lives a long distance from the centres of population would at least have the advantage that he would not be under the disability of excessive freight rates, as compared with other localities nearer to the consuming centres. But whether we can valorize freight rates or not, I say that public ownership will cove the best possible Tates, and absolutely fair rates without any discrimination. You cannot attain that in any other way than by public ownership of the railways. We have made some headway in Ontario in public ownership of energy distributed for water-power. If you have public ownership of railways, you will have public ownership of express business, of telegraph business, and, perhaps, some day of the telephone system. That will do more than anything else to uplift the people all over this country. If you have public ownership of railways, telephone, telegraph, express and parcel post, the post office, and the money order system in connection with it, you can extend them all in the smallest village of Canada, and night and day, every day in the year, the people of that smallest community will have access, in one public office, where you can arrange your business, make inquiries about railways, send telegrams, arrange for parcel post and get express service. You will have all these great public utilities which ought to be for the service of the public and not for the profit of private companies, concentrated in every community, be it large or small. By this acquisition of the Canadian Northern System we get a telegraph system to-day, and that, I hope, will soon be turned over to the post office of this country, and will be expanded and extended. It will be the beginning of the naturalization of our telegraph system as they have it ip every other country in Europe. Even Great Britain, although she has not nationalized rai'ways, by reason of her experience of nationalization of telegraph and telephone, will come to a nationalization of her railways, if, for no other reason.
Public ownership of railroads will be absolutely necessary in those countries that have not it when the problem of reconstruction after the war-a problem that is even now before us-comes up for determination. The problem is now being considered in Europe: how are the countries affected by the war to be reconstructed?

To them it is an immense problem, and it will be equally vital in this country. If we mobilize our wealth-a great many gentlemen in. this House have committed themselves to the principle of the mobilization of wealth, of industries, of everything that goes to make our nation strong and great -then we have to nationalize the railroads too. The best possible reconstruction cannot be secured in this country or in the United States unless the railroads are taken over. The world has to be rebuilt and reorganized after this great war, and to my mind nothing will contribute so much to speedy reconstruction and readjustment as public ownership of railroads.

subtopic: DEBATE CONTINUED ON MOTION FOR SECOND READING OF CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY BILL.
speechtext: Will the hon. gentleman apply his argument to the shipment of industrial manufactures from Ontario to the West, having in mind the lower cost of shipment from Winnipeg?

subtopic: DEBATE CONTINUED ON MOTION FOR SECOND READING OF CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY BILL.
speechtext:
That has to be worked out. I am not going into the details; I am setting forth the general principle that, in my opinion, should be adopted. It ought to be worked out so that the western farmer shall not pay a higher freight rate upon his plough than the Ontario farmer does. It may be alleged that that is visionary; I do not think that it is.
I see the truth of it; I think that a great many people see it.
It has been charged against me that I am ahead of my time in some of the principles that I advocate. But I have not advocated anything this afternoon that is in advance of the times, or anything, with the single exception of the valorization of freight rates, that has not already been adopted and successfully worked out in other countries.
What shall we get if we take over the Canadian Northern Railway system? We have over 2,000 miles in the Intercolonial and over 2,000 miles in the Transcontinental. We shall get about 9,000 miles in the Canadian Northern. We shall be starting public ownership, therefore, with about 14,000 miles of railway. At the beginning you cannot line them all up under one organization. We are to keep-so I gather from the Bill-the present company organization of the Canadian Northern. But it is going to be owned by the people, and in a very short time it will he co-ordinated with the Intercolonial and the Transcontinental. The Intercolonial railway will run its cars into Toronto. Sidings will be available there for the purpose of loading and receiving freight moved between Ontario and the IMr. W. F. Maclean. 1
country served by the Intercolonial. The Intercolonial will get a new stimulus from this connection with Ontario and the West; freight will, as a matter of course, go over the Intercolonial. The Transcontinental will be worked into the system, and, with the Canadian Northern, we shall have a great system of 15,000 or 16,000 miles. Great economies can be effected. The Canadian Northern will be helped, because all the freight 'that goes to Toronto can go over the Canadian Northern, a government-owned road. Through this co-ordination and co-opera'tion there will be great reduction in expenses. Of course, that will not come iat the start, because of circumstances which I cannot explain here to-night.
We ought to have acquired the Grand Trunk under this measure. Now that we have the Canadian Northern, the Transcontinental, and the Intercolonial, we ought, to take over the Grand Trunk. The Government have given reasons why they have not taken it over; they say that the financial commitments would be too great, having regard to present conditions.' But I would be prepared to-day to support any measure for the acquiring of the Grand Trunk Railway system, because, when you get the Grand Trunk you get the real benefit of national ownership. Between Toronto and Montreal the Canadian Pacific runs three or four express trains a day. The Grand Trunk runs the same number. The Canadian Northern has two running to Ottawa; they purpose to go on to Montreal. If we had public ownership, with the coordination and co-operation that Would result, we could reduce the number of these trains running between Montreal and Toronto, get a better service and save a lot of money. That could be done ad over the country. Almost immediately there can be consolidation between the Grand Trunk in the West and the Canadian Northern. Out of Toronto every week three trains now go to the West over the Transcontinental line and three over the Canadian Northern. As soon as these two systems are linked up it will be possible to have a daily service over the better line. If you ask me what would be the national line from Halifax to Vancouver, I would say: Take the Intercolonial at Halifax, the Canadian Northern at Montreal, the Canadian Northern to Sudbury, the Canadian Northern to a place called Long Lake, near lake Nipigon, which is 25 miles from the Transcontinental; then take the Transcontinental to Winnipeg, and

the Canadian Northern from Winnipeg to Vancouver. That would give a line superior to any line operating to-day. If, some day, we get the Canadian Pacific Railway-it may come-the suggestions which I have made could be adopted in respect to it and its connections w'ith the other lines.
As I pointed out this afternoon, by public ownership and control of the railways and mines in England, the shortest and most economical service has been secured. Public ownership will give you less haulage; it will give you the best grades for the moving of freight. There are all kinds of grades in different parts of this country that obstruct freight. Where I live, near Toronto, I am on a one per cent grade-a grade that is an obstruction to traffic for all time. That grade is called the Scarboro grade on the Grand Trunk, and the Wexford grade on the Canadian Pacific. The Canadian Northern have a grade between the two, a half per cent grade. We should get rid of all these expensive one per cent grades that are found all over the country. One of the merits of the Canadian Northern Railway system is the splendid grades that they have in many parts of the country. It has excellent grades between Toronto and Sudbury and thence to the West. It has very good grades in the West, but with public ownership those grades could be standardized and used in such a way as to give the best possible service. In sections where those good grades are to be found, an engine can haul a larger number of cars, and with public ownership you get the best grades and no money is wasted on unneces-sary^ competition. Public ownership will ensure cheap motive power, and in every way public ownership does more than anything else I know of towards the solution of the transportation problems of this country.
Many people are opposed to public ownership. Two hon. members who spoke today said that they did not believe in it. Missionaries from the United States have come into my own city to tell the people that public ownership is a curse, that political corruption will bedevil it, and that it can never be worked out successfully. When men, who believe in democracy and who come from a democratic country say that they are afraid to trust the people in the operation of a railway, and that corruption will creep in, my answer is that I will look into that question very carefully. When there is corruption in a country-and there *has been a good deal of corruption in one
way or another in Canada-it comes mainly from public utility corporations which exert their influences in the political affairs of the country. When you remove that private ownership and have public ownership, you go a long way towards remedying the situation. As a Canadian, I have every confidence in my fellow-citizens; I do not say that they are corrupt; I am in favour of removing the source of corruption, and I believe the Canadian people are capable of owning the railroads and of handing them over to non-partisan boards to, operate. When you take politics out of the administration of those roads you will get good service. We have public ownership in Ontario in connection with the distribution of power, and there is not a better example of public ownership than the Ontario Hydro-Electric Commission in its methods of administration. There is no corruption in the operation of that commission, and the people of Ontario are satisfied with its administration. If the people of Ontario are capable of handling that public service, why cannot the people of Canada carry on public ownership successfully? I have every faith in my fellow-countrymen; I believe they are competent to see that the railroads of this country are administered without corruption, and that political influence is kept out of their administration. Public ownership of railways has been carried on in different countries throughout the world. Australia, New Zealand, France, Russia and Japan have public ownership, and surely what they can do, we can do; what is good for them is good for us. I, therefore, disagree with those who say that, with public ownership, you run the danger of getting poor administration and political corruption. The post office of this country is well managed, although the criticism is made that there is some political interference in its administration. I am willing to vote at any time in favour of politics and political influence being done away with in connection with appointments in the post office. I am in favour of all appointments being made after competitive examination; and after a man has been appointed to a position in the post office, he should be permitted to rise on his merits, without any politician interfering in the matter. That system is being carried on in England and in the United States, and it is being carried on here in Canada. I do not like to hear a public man in Canada-to whatever party he may

belong-say on a public platform that the people are corrupt; that they cannot manage their own affairs, and that politics will creep into the administration of great public services such as our railways. I take no stock in such an argument. I believe that the members of this Parliament, when this railway and the railways we now have are consolidated, will evolve a method by which we shall have a businesslike and sound administration through a commission appointed by Parliament or by a responsible Government, and that the necessary legislation for protecting the public interest will be passed. If the doctrine that the people are corrupt and that we cannot get rid of political influence is true, then why does it not follow that you cannot get justice in this country from the courts? If under our present parliamentary institution you can pick out good judges who will administer law impartially, you can surely get good men who will operate the railroads in the same manner. I regret that the nation to-day has not in its service men like Lord Shaughnessy, Sir William Mackenzie, Mr. Hanna, or Sir George Bury. If the people gave any one of these men charge of a government railway, does any one mean to say that he would not operate it just as well as he operates the railway of which he has charge at the present time? These are splendid men; they are trained now to serve their shareholders, and they would be just as willing to serve +>e nation. When we have public ownership we shall have the pick of the best men o,f the country to run our railways. In a very short time we shall get the nucleus of a high-minded board of men who will be glad to devote their lives to the administration of the publicly-owned railways. We can secure them. All we want to do is to say that there shall be no interference with them. And we are gradually eliminating political interference in *connection with the administration of certain public affairs. There is no political influence in -connection with the -administration of justice, and there is none in connection with the administration of the Hydro-Electric Commission, -and they are giving good results. The people are capable of carrying on public ownership successfully, and they are -able to judge as to the men who shall have control of publicly-owned services. This great -system of 16,000 miles of railway that we shall have will gradually be put under one commission, -and we -shall soon have the Grand Trunk and later on the -Canadian Pacific. When 
we get those railways, we shall -have a great public service linked up with -it and co-ordinated and consecrated to service and not to profit. That is my argument-that all these public utilities should ibe consecrated to service and not to profit.
Can you ever, -as things are now. get a privately-owned company to extend its lines, unless it receives a bonus and a profit on construction? When there is public ownership, the telegraph lines, the telephones, the express business, -and the railway lines will toe extended as they are required, and fair treatment will toe meted out. District after district in the -Canadian West cannot get a railroad service to-day for one reason or another. A truly impartial board intrusted with the -administration of our railways would see to it that railway lines were constructed where they were required, and that there was no unnecessary duplication. Is it not a shame to see the duplication that exists between Montreal and Toronto, railways paralleling each other for mile after mile? The same thing is to be seen in the West. That duplication, is unnecessary.
Is it not a shame that the Grand Trunk Pacific should run so close to the Canadian Northern -and the Canadian Pacific? Yet that is what we have got under private ownership. The greatest waste that was ever permitted in this country by unnecessary duplication of lines, of bridges, of officials, and all the other paraphernalia that goes with private ownership, will be got rid of under public ownership, when all the roads are brought under one organization. That may not come in a year or two, but we are making a start and the people of this country see that the thing can be done. This question is being discussed in political gatherings wherever the people see the advantage of political organization. Out in the West the grain growers and the farmers see the importance of political organization, and the importance of acquiring, through political organizations, control of all these public utilities, -and to-day they are demanding that there shall be public ownership of the railways. They are sick and tired of this unnecessary duplication of lines, sick and tired of not -being able to get railways where they ought to get them. They know that public ownership will prevent this unnecessary waste and get the railways where they are wanted. It is true that public ownership will not come in a day, but it is making headway, and the longest step in the direction of public ownership that has ever been taken in this country is the introduction of the measure

we are discussing here to-day. It may have its defects; holes could no doubt be bored into the arguments that all the lawyers in the House have made on both sides of ibis question. But I am not at all influenced by these appeals. I am only concerned with this: that no more than a fair price should be paid for what is taken over.
I have listened to the argument that it would be rather an expensive proposition.
I >am not going to argue to the contrary, but I say that in Sir William Meredith, the arbitrator who is to represent the Dominion, we have a man who has given the best portion of his life to public ownership in Ontario, and it is largely to his assistance and to that of the politicians associated with him that we owe the Hydro Electric movement in Ontario to-day, which some people seem to be so sore on, but of which so many of us in the province of Ontario are justly proud. I remember when public ownership first came up in the province of Ontario. I was a little identified with it myself. I remember the first resolution that was passed in favour of public ownership of the water-powers and the development of power at Niagara falls. I was one of two or three who drafted the short resolution in that direction, which we managed to get one of the private members to move at the tail-end of the session? The Conservatives happened to take 9 p.m. it up, and the resolution was put through the House as a party measure, but not one member got up and made a speech in favour of it; the resolution just slipped through. That was the beginning; of the public ownership movement in Ontario. From that day to this the people of that province have daily become more strongly in favour of public ownership. They see that by public ownership of power, for light, heat and energy, by public ownership of radial roads, and now of steam roads, they can make Ontario the greatest manufacturing province in all Canada. The nationalization of the railways, together with the other benefits that go with it-the consolidation of the express business with the telegraph, parcel post, and perhaps the money order business connected with the post office-will facilitate the development of industry and of transportation, and make this country great. You can make the provinces in the West great if you give the farmer the lowest possible freight rate, instead of following the practice of privately-owned roads of making the traffic pay the highest rate it can bear,-
and this is the only rule that has guided the owners of privately-owned roads up to to-day. Public ownership will get rid of all that, and will build up our great public services both here and in the West. It will improve farming in the West and manufacturing in the East, and improve the life of the people all over the country. Public ownership is coming, and the proposals now before the House, while they may have their defects, are on the whole a move in the right direction. They are, in fact, the greatest move that has yet been made in the direction of public ownership.
I hope we shall soon follow up our taking over of the Canadian Northern by taking over the Grand Trunk, which is the necessary complement of the Canadian Northern in the West. We want feeders in the East for the Canadian Northern in the West, just as much as we want feeders in the West to bring freight down to the Atlantic seaboard. We have not got the Grand Trunk yet, but I hope we shall have it next year.
I hope the proposals for giving relief to the Grand Trunk in its present emergency will ensure our getting control of the road in the public interest. Somebody may say:	If you are in favour of public
ownership, why don't you acquire the Canadian Pacific and take over the whole system? Some newspapers have made quite an argument out of that, contending that if we got the Canadian Pacific the problem would be much easier of solution. So it would. The Canadian Pacific revenue to-day is such that if that road were consolidated with the Canadian Northern, the Grand Trunk Pacific, and the Transcontinental, it could take care of all the fixed charges and operating expenses, give a far better service to the people, and still have a large surplus for improvements and betterments. But we cannot do that just yet; it may be harder to get the Canadian Pacific than any other road. But the Canadian Northern has come into our hadds, and we shall soon get control of the Grand Trunk, and I shall never be satisfied until we do get it. We shall have a fair chance of getting the Canadian Pacific on better terms when we have a well-established system of our own. I believe the shareholders of the Canadian Pacific would be glad to be guaranteed 7 per cent on their stock if the country took over the road. When the Canadian Pacific was here as a suppliant some years ago, on four or five different occasions asking for authorization to increase its stock, I opposed it on every occasion and was laughed at in this House.

I said that if the Canadian Pacific wanted more money it should get it by the issue of 4 per cent bonds, and it could have got the money, for it is paying 10 per cent on that stock now. I said that the greatest danger in authorizing the company to increase its stock issue was that when we came to take over the road we should have $300,000,000 of capital stock to take over, on which they would want 10 per cent. I w.as laughed at for making that statement, but now it has come true. If we want to get the Canadian Pacific to-day and consolidate it with the other railways, using the earnings of them all-and the earnings of them all will maintain the roads if they are consolidated-we shall have to take over this great amount of stock. We are getting wise to that, and hereafter we shall exercise greater control and supervision over stock issues which railroads may make. If there is any difficulty to-day in acquiring the Canadian Pacific, which is an excellent road and would help to carry all the others, it is because we have been improvident in the past in allowing it to make the stock issues it has made. But in spite of that, we shall some day be able to take over the road and then we shall have what the people o;f this country want-a publicly-owned system.
I notice that the people of the Maritime Provinces do not wish to give up their publicly-owned road, for that, road, the Intercolonial, has been of great service to them.
I listened with a great deal of interest the other day to the argument that that road should not come under the jurisdiction of the Railway Commission. Now, if public ownership is good for the Maritime Provinces it is good enough for Ontario and the West, and we have seen that for a long while. We have helped in paying the interest on the construction of the Intercolonial, but have never objected to doing that; we are glad the road has been kept independent and the autonomy preserved. It is now to be linked up with the Transcontinental and the Canadian Northern, and in this way we are making a beginning with a great transcontinental service owned by the people of this country .and passing from Victoria, on the West, through the different provinces right down to the Atlantic seaboard.
The only portion of the country, I am sorry to say, that has not the benefit of public ownership is that part of Ontario that lies west of Toronto. The Canadian Northern, at present, only goes to Toronto 
and runs from there northwesterly to Winnipeg. We have not public ownership of railways in Ontario. That is the reason why the .present proposition, without the inclusion of the Grand Trunk Pacific, is rather a hard thing for us to justify in Ontario. But we accept it in the hope that in a short time we shall have the Grand Trunk Pacific taken into this national system. When we have that, we shall have every city and towm, almost, of any account from ocean to ocean on a publicly owned railway, and we hope that these railways will be so administered for the welfare of the people that the Canadian Pacific will be wise enough, in the interest of its shareholders, to come in and join us. We shall have no trouble in getting men to administer this publicly owned railway. We can get the pick of the railway men of this country. Whoever has the administration of this new departure in connection with the Canadian Northern is bound to take the best men, and there are some good men on the Canadian Northern. Take them over and give them a free hand. Put them under a board of directors and they will give real service.
Without referring at all to political criticism, I want to recognize what the Minister of Finance (Sir Thomas White) and the Minister of Railways (Mr. Cochrane) have been doing in the direction of public ownership. The mind of the people has been moving in the, direction of public ownership. You can see it. It is on the way; it is coming. We are getting 10,000 miles of road and this, joined up with the others that I have mentioned, will give us
15,000	miles. I came into this House an advocate of public ownership. I never thought I should live to .see the day when it would become a reality. I have been laughed at and jeered at in the last few years when I proposed public ownership in this House, and in my own city of Toronto as well, but notwithstanding the laughs and jeers, the idea is taking firm hold of the minds of the people. They see what it can do and they are backing it up in the province of Ontario to-day. Every man in the Government of Ontario who is administering these publicly-owned services is a believer in public ownership. We have not got it here yet in Ottawa. The man who believes in public ownership is thought to be an enthusiast or a madman who should be in the asylum. The late Sir James Whitney made a great reputation for himself by his advocacy of public ownership

in connection "with the Hydro-Electric power scheme. But he was at times afraid of it, and he thought that probably some of his colleagues were going too far. We remember the attitude of Sir John A. Macdonald in connection with the National Policy. He thought it was something that we should not go too fast with and he was always checking up those who advocated it. But, nevertheless, it swept the country. The principle of a National Policy in connection *with the tariff swept the country then, and the question of a National Policy in connection with industry and with the nationalization of our railways is sweeping the country to-day. The people of Ontario believe in it and the people of Quebeo have their own Intercolonial railway and they do not want to surrender it. I have seen assaults made on that road in this House since I have been a member of it, and plots of all kinds to turn it over-at one time to the Canadian Pacific, at another time to the Grand Trunk, and at another time to some other company. But, they have not been able to carry out those schemes. The whole trend of thought in this country is in the direction of public ownership, and it is going ahead.
There are impediments and obstructions, in the way. Some people say that they do not believe in it; that it has been a failure; that our people cannot work it out; that there will be political corruption. And yet the mind of the people of Canada is consolidating, forming, mobilizing, if I may use a modern expression, in the direction of public ownership. It is coming; it is here to-day; it is before us in this measure. With public ownership under the HydroElectric Commission you get good service, there is no loss, there are no unnecessary bonds tbat have to be protected and no dividends to pay on unnecessary issues. You find that in Ontario to-day -under the public ownership of hydro-electric energy. What can be done there can be done in connection with the railways.
For these reasons I have no hesitation in -saying that the measure, with any weaknesses it may have, is in the very best direction and I think the people would approve of it. As to the commission that is to fix the value, it is open to discussion as to how this should be done. Probably there ought to be a limitation of the finding, but I believe that the Government is in the way of obtaining a commission which will arrive at a fair valuation for the stock. It may not be worth a great deal. Various
o-pinions have been expressed by members of this House a-s to what that value ought to be, and the parties have more or less committed themselves to it. -Certainly these people -have some kind of an equity in the proposition and a reasonable amount might be fixed by the- board of arbitration. I think there is no doubt that with a commission composed of men like -Sir William Meredith a fair price will be fixed. Then, we shall have the beginning of a great national system of railways, taking in 15,000 miles of road, and which will soon include the Grand Trunk and in a few years may include the Canadian Pacific. If we can get that we will have -the best transcontinental railway that any country has. It will be publicly owned and administered. There will be no waste due to unnecessary duplication, and no unnecessary overhead charges. And at the proper time, probably after the war, a system of refunding of the whole outstanding liabilities can be worked out. Any way, we are making headway, and we are making i-t in the right direction. I compliment the Government on taking over the road, irrespective of whether there -may be -some question in connection with settling the value. It is a step in -the right direction, it is for public ownership, for public service, for the welfare of the people; it is not for making wealth ot profits for private individuals; it is to put the railway magnate out of existence, and it is putting before the youth of this country the splendid idea that the best thing they can do is to make a reputation in the administration of some public -service and to work for the public welfare. That is a new thing to aspire to. Hitherto men like Sir William Mackenzie, Sir Donald Mann and Sir William van Horne, unfortunately, have given their best energies to -the service of corporations. We still have the same kind of men in this country.

subtopic: DEBATE CONTINUED ON MOTION FOR SECOND READING OF CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY BILL.
speechtext: Is it not true that the great argument in favour of public ownership of the Canadian Northern is the fact that private ownership has proved a complete failure?

subtopic: DEBATE CONTINUED ON MOTION FOR SECOND READING OF CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY BILL.
speechtext:
That may, be.
Private ownership may have built .a lot of unnecessary lines, may have oaused any -amount of duplication; they may have come to grief owing to that fact. Public ownership would not have come to grief in the -same way. Any way, the bulk of the arguments are in favour of public ownership, and I stand here to-night, for myself,

for my province, for the people I represent, for the thinking men of this country and for the farmers, to say that they are in favour of public ownership of the railroads of this. country, and the sooner it comes the better it will be for the nation, for the people, .and for the welfare of all.
Mr. E. iM.. MACDONALD (Pictou): Mr. Speaker, I do. not .intend to follow my hon. friend along the lines on which he has just spoken so. ably .and at such length. I assume that he is to be congratulated and that he should be pardoned for having claimed for himself the honour and distinction of having had his views adopted by the Government. I would not pretend to enter upon all of the lines o;f discussion which my hon. friend has taken up, hut I may point out that there is a delightful absence all through his discussion of any such material and important matter as the question of what all these things are going to cost. My hon. friend has entirely eliminated, both from the consideration of the proposition before the House and everything he has mentioned in the course of his speech, any such thing as money. Money is a very important thing, it is a very essential thing. And now, when the credit of this country is at the lowest ebb it has ever been, with demands for commitments greater than at any time previously, we have submitted to us a proposition iby which the Government undertake to commit themselves and the country to .a liability which is totally unnecessary. This proposition involves the payment of at least $100,000,000 on the lines laid down by the Minister of Finance. I say that at this moment the one serious thing for the Canadian people to consider is whether or not this Government is doing right in paying out $100,000,000-or rather committing themselves to the payment of that amount-'when they do not have to pay a single cent, and when all that my hon. friend (Mr. Maclean) claimed as ideal and proper could be obtained for the country by this Government simply taking .advantage of their own bargain made three years ago and incorporated in a statute.
The Minister of Finance, when he presented his resolution, instead of intituling it "An Act to provide for the acquisition by His Majesty of the capital stock of the Canadian Northern Railway Company" should have intituled it "An Act to reform the statute passed in 1914 with reference to the Canadian Northern Railway Company and to amend section 24 of that Act so as to destroy its full effect and operation."
That is exactly the effect of this Bill. fMr. W. F. Maclean.!
I should like to ask the minister, either at the conclusion of this debate or when the Bill goes into committee, to inform the House who the real owners and pledgees of the stock of the Canadian Northern Railway are. My hon. friend has that information but has not yet given it to the House. In other words, this House and the country do not know with whom this arbitration is to be carried on. We have been discussing it as if Messrs. Mackenzie and Mann, whose names are well known throughout the country, are the people who are to .get this money. I do not know if that is so. No one knows whether it is so. The other parties to the arbitration have not been disclosed to the House or to the country. I ask the minister to let us know whether Mackenzie and Mann own the five-sixths of this stock, and if they are the parties with whom this agreement is made. If not, who are the parties, and with whom has this stock been pledged, and for how much has it been pledged? It would be absurd, ridiculous, for Parliament to consider seriously the passing of a measure involving the purchase of a large quantity of stock which we do not have to purchase, involving the pledging of the credit of the country to an amount in the vicinity of $100,000,000, for the purpose of getting stock from certain people whose names are known to the Government but are not given to the House. My hon. friend should also, tell us who are the owners of the one-sixth of the stock in regard to whom special provisions are made in the latter part of the Bill. This information is essential if the House is to pass upon this measure with any degree of intelligence.
My hon. friend from South York (Mr. Maclean) in his enthusiasm for government ownership, evidently has not taken the trouble to read this Bill, because if he did so he would not find a single provision how this road is to be operated after it is obtained-not a line. All we have here is authority given td the Government to purchase a certain quantity of stock from some person or persons unknown, without a line of declaration of policy as to how that railway is to be operated. The Bill might well be called "An Act to reform Chapter 20 of the statutes of 1914, .and to amend the agreement and stipulations in that Act which provide for the people of Canada getting the Canadian Northern Railway and all its belongings without their costing the Canadian people a cent"-and I propose to prove that beyond the shadow of a doubt. There is but one issue before this House in regard to this measure, that is whether the

amendment of the hon. member for South Renfrew (Mr. Graham) is one which rightly states the previous law and the facts in this case. If it does, there is no justification for this measure, for the creation of a board of arbitrators or for the provisions under which the country is to be committed to a large payment of money. Are the statements in the amendment of my hon. friend true? Every one has assumed in this discussion that the Canadian Northern Railway is in default in its payments. What does that mean? In 1914, after a previous grant had been made to the Canadian Northern Railway the year before of fifteen millions, my hon. friend came to this House with a proposition that there should be loaned to the Canadian Northern the sum of $45,000,000. And there was submitted to the House for ratification an agreement which was made and entered into between the Canadian Northern Railway and Messrs. Mackenzie and Mann who were described as the contractors, and the Government of Canada. It was represented that when the country provided for its guarantee of $45,000,000, the whole railway question, so far as the Canadian Northern Railway was concerned, would be solved, and we would not be called upon for any more money.
We all remember how, when that proposal was made, the hon. member for Calgary (Mr. R. B. Bennett) attacked the proposition in the most aggresive and energetic way. My hon. friend from Kingston (Mr. Nickle), discussing the question at that time, declared that every dollar of the so-called stock of the Canadian Northern was watered stock and that the whole was not worth a cent. The ^energe tic opposition o,f these gentlemen did not avail with the Government, and they proceeded to ratify that proposition and put through the arrangement. What was the attitude of hon. gentlemen on this side? I had the honour of moving, on behalf of the opposition, the six months' hoist to the whole measure. Later on, in the discussion upon the question, my hon. friend from Middlesex (Mr. Ross) moved what was a reasonable proposition-that before Canada should commit herself to any such arrangement as proposed, there should be a complete and full investigation into the affairs of the Canadian Northern. That was voted down by 'hon. gentlemen on the other side. Supplementary to that, the hon. member for St. John (Mr. Pugsley) proposed to amend the proposition, so that, in addition to taking over the portion of the stock which
the Government were taking at that time, which was only 40 per cent of that stock, the whole stock should be taken over, and become the property of the Dominion, the matter to be determined by arbitration. That was voted down. What answer did my hon. friends opposite make in regard to that proposition of the hon. member for St. John? Every one of them went on record, the Prime Minister and all the others, to the effect that the provisions of the statute contained in sections 22, 23 and 24 were so apt, so definite and certain that, if the Canadian Northern ever were in default, automatically, under the provisions of section 24, the title to all the assets and property of the Canadian Northern could simply by this Parliament passing legislation declaring that it was done, become the property of the Canadian people without it costing them a single cent. If that statement is true, then this legislation is entirely unnecessary. Section 22 provides as follows:
Upon the happening- of any event of default, and at any time or times while the same shall continue, it shall be lawful for the Governor in Council after such notice to the Canadian Northern as the Governor in Council may direct, to declare to be vacant the offices of the directors of the Canadian Northern.
My hon. friend (Sir Thomas White) told us, when he moved this resolution, that a very important advantage in getting this stock was that we would be able -to turn out the present directors and get new ones. But he forgot to inform the House on one Very important point-and were it not for the hon. gentleman from South Renfrew (Mr. Graham) dealing with this question, and pointing out what the law was in 1914, the House and the country might have forgotten that the Government of Canada has greater power under the statute of 1914 than it will have under this proposed measure. In the event of default this Government can at once declare to be vacant the offices of the directors of the Canadian Northern and of any of the constituent or subsidiary companies. That power existed beyond all question. Why was it not exercised in the interests of the Canadian people? I ask the hon. Minister of Finance, or any other hon. gentleman on that side of the House, to tell me why it was not exercised last year when they gave the Canadian Northern $15,000,000 more? Why was it not exercised this year, when my hon. friend has to go to New York and pay the highest rate for money, and sell his securities at the lowest rate at which securities have been sold?

Why should my hon. friend ignore that provision, and ask the Canadian people and this Parliament to provide for the payment of money when they need not do so? Section 23 provides:
The directors so appointed by the Governor in Council shall hold office during the pleasure of the Governor in Council, and any such director may be removed and another appointed in his place. Vacancies occurring from time to time may be tilled by the Governor in Council.
My hon.. friend from South York could have sung his paeans of joy just as well without cost to the country, if the powers conferred upon us by chapter 20 of 1914 were exercised. But further let me call attention to section 24, which has been read to the House. The marginal note, epitomizing what the effect of the section was, reads as follows:
Equity of redemption foreclosed on default and vested in His Majesty.
The section provides that, on default, the equity of redemption in the Canadian Northern Railway is automatically foreclosed by order of this Parliament and becomes vested in His Majesty. That is the law. I venture to say that no hon. gentleman in this House who has any regard for his status as a lawyer will venture to declare that, under the provisions of section 24, ample power of the most radical kind was not conferred on the Government by which automatically, and simply by resolution of Parliament, the whole property of the Canadian Northern would .become vested in the Canadian people, withoui costing them a single cent. That that >vas the meaning of the law hon. gentlemen have shown by some of the statements made by various hon. gentlemen at that time. In the light of the rather casuistic argument made by the Prime Minister (Sir Robert Borden), I want to refer particularly to what he said that clause meant in 1914. I quote from page 3674 of Hansard:
It is also provided by clause 24 that, if authorized by the Parliament of Canada, the Governor in Council may, in case of default, declare that the interest of Mackenzie and Mann in the Canadian Northern Railway system is absolutely barred and foreclosed, and that all the properties and assets thereof,' subject to any outstanding obligation, shall thereupon vest in the Crown, in the right of the people of Canada,
Either that meant what the right hon. gentleman said it meant, and what every hon. gentleman who reads it knows it meant, or it did not. If it meant what the Premier said at that time, then the Minister of Fin-fMr. Macdonald.]
ance knows, as does every hon. gentleman that this legislation, is totally and absolutely unnecessary, and it is intended to divprt from the treasury of Canada at least
5100,000,000 which ought to be there in this time of stress and war. My hon. friend from Calgary ventured to 'question the effect of that, and in, an able speech which he delivered at that time this is what hg said about it:	.
They talk about the slow machinery of the courts, but look at this:	''That if authorized
by the Parliament of Canada," you have to come back to Parliament to foreclose. To foreclose what? About $60,000,000 of stock outstanding in the hands of Mackenzie and Mann. Our $40,000,000 is there too, and the $25,000,000 of convertible securities which may not be converted, are there also. We are going to foreclose our interest, but we have to come back to Parliament to do it. Mr. Speaker, those loyal devoted Canadians who believe that democracy's mission is not fulfilled, and that popular government is upon trial, know what that means-a long protracted lobby as to how much we are going to pay to get rid of Mackenzie and Mann.
Now, what was going to happen? We have not had the lobby with members of Parliament, hut there has been some influence working from the owners of that stock, whom the people of Canada do not know, upon this Government, as the result of which they have been induced to forego the effect of section 24 of this Act, and to bring down this measure, taking from the treasury of Canada $100,000,000 which ought to be left there.
What did the Minister of Finance say in reply to the member fir Calgary when he raised that very question? The minister pointed out the ridiculousness of dealing with the stock of the company. I need not delay the House by setting forth the long argument made by my hon. friend to show that the stock was no good. He said that we were getting a better thing-the assets -something that really belonged to the company. He went on to say
If I have a mortgage on a company's undertaking I do not care very much for the stock' as security except that it is advisable to have the stock in order that I can take possession of the company, put in my own receiver, and operate the company with my own board of directors. That is the only advantage. The stock does not give any higher security, but it makes the realization of the security a little more convenient. What security have we? I have seen a good deal of financing in my time, and I know something of law although my hon. friend from Pictou (Mr. Macdonald) does not think so, and I want to say this: I have never seen as effectual a means of entering into possession of a property upon which a mortgage is held as has been devised by the Solicitor General In connection with this transaction.

speechtext:
I am instituting a comparison. I am pointing out that my hon. friend was wrong when he put these two gentlemen on a parity. Every man who has had any practice in the Exchequer Court knows that thesenior judge of the Exchequer Court, during his years of experience, has passed upon the value of property of various kinds, railway property included, in connection with cases that have come before him for determination. The rules that obtain in determining the methods of appraising values are the rules that have been laid down by the Exchequer Court. An hon. gentleman mentions the fact that the matter of the Quebec and Saguenay was referred to Judge Cassels. However, I do not want to stray too far from my argument. With all due deference to Sir William Meredith, those of us who have come from other provinces can speak rather freely in regard to him. In view of the statement made by a minister of the Crown in regard to judges sitting upon commissions, we should not forget that Sir William Meredith has been engaged in all kinds of commissions. Moreover, he seems to be the favoured associate of the Ontario Government, as well as of this Administration. Nor do we forget that during the sitting of a certain commission last year, Sir William Meredith took one course with regard to compensation and the other judge took another. Although my hon. friend puts Sir William Meredith on a parity with Judge Cassels, in the estimation of the Bar of this country they are not on a parity.



The one is a man whose daily occupation has been that of determining the fair valuation of property of all kinds; the other is not.. If any criticism is to be made in regard to the employment of judges upon commissions, that criticism can be directed with the greatest possible force against the gentleman whom my hon. friend puts forward as being, par excellence, the one who should deal with this matter.
In answering the member for Calgary, my hon. friend (Sir Thomas White) said:
Upon default, the Order in Council at once becomes a rule of court, and is absolutely beyond question so far as its authority is concerned. We can displace the board of directors of any or all of the companies by directors of our own choice, who are given power to carry on the road as provided in the resolutions, and it is open to the Government through Parliament to deal with that road by way of sale or otherwise, as may be expedient and in the public interests.
My hon. friend declared that there was nothing in the suggestion of the member for Calgary that there might be some question about that mode of foreclosure. He expressed his admiration for the Solicitor General, who had introduced a clause that would have such a wonderful effect. Such a provision was better, he said, than if the Government had the whole of the stock of the company. Nothing further needed to be done to complete the transaction, except that Parliament should act upon the intimation of the Government whenever default occurred.
The Solicitor General (Mr. Meighen), who was quoted by my hon. friend fro-m North Cape Breton (Mr. McKenzie) this afternoon, spoke along practically the same lines. We have, therefore, the Prime Minister, the Minister of Finance and the Solicitor General, all declaring that beyond the shadow of a doubt section 24 of the statutes of 1914 was so definite and positive in its character that all that was needed to be done in case of default was to pass an Act and automatically everything in connection with the Canadian Northern passed into the hands of the people of Canada, without any arbitration at all. My hon. friend's speech upon that point was so emphatic that my hon. friend from West Peterborough (Mr. Burnham) was carried away completely. He spoke after the Minister of Finance, and for the edification of the House, I will read the remarks he made. He said:
I venture to say that if Mackenzie and Mann and the Canadian Northern come back here next year seeking anything further, if they are not given the foreclosure-
This wonderful weapon of the Minister of Finance.

-but are given any further assistance, there will be not a riot but a revolution in this country.
