speechtext:
That is in regard to the sale or otherwise. It was open to Parliament to hand the road over to some other railway. The discretion of Parliament was not fettered in any way; Parliament could impose any terms or conditions in regard to the whole thing. The minister cannot escape from the position he took at that time, when he emphatically declared to the House that, when Parliament spoke, everything was wiped out. That is the position of the Prime Minister, of the Solicitor General, of all hon. gentlemen opposite who discussed the legal phase of the question.
There is another phase of this matter. There appears in the Schedule of the Act an agreement entered into between Mackenzie, Mann and Company, Limited, Sir William Mackenzie and Sir Donald Mann and His

Majesty the King, under which certain covenants were made by Sir William Mackenzie and Sir Donald Mann as contractors. This is one of the covenants:
That the contractors will not at any time make or seek to enforce any claim for contractors' profits, commissions or otherwise against the Canadian Northern, or against any of the constituent or subsidiary, companies upon or in respect of any express or implied contract, understanding, agreement, or stipulation of any kind, heretofore or hereafter made, whereby or whereunder they, or any one or more of them, may now or hereafter be entitled to receive from the Canadian Northern, or from any of the constituent or subsidiary companies any construction profits, in respect of work heretofore undertaken, or as consideration for transfers of properties, rights or franchises, already transferred, or to be transferred under sub-clauses (a) and (b) of this clause, or for commission or remuneration for services in financing, or for any other services heretofore rendered, and all such claims are hereby by them and each of them absolutely renounced and released.
The importance of that release on the part of Messrs. Mackenzie and Mann, made jointly and severally, must be remembered at this time in the light of the fact that so far the Government have not told us who are the owners or pledgees of this stock. When the Government have given that information 'to the House, and stated whether those gentlemen are the owners who, in 1914, absolutely released all their claims of any kind whatever-in addition to which the abolition of their equity of redemption by this Parliament is provided for by section 24 of the statute of 1914- then we can discuss, as we shall at greater length in committee, what the full significance of section 24 is.

subtopic: DEBATE CONTINUED ON MOTION FOR SECOND READING OF CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY BILL.
speechtext: It is perfectly obvious, I think, from the statute that, in view of what was said in 1914, Mackenzie and Mann and Mackenzie, Mann and Company, Limited, were the owners of this stock, and anybody who takes it, whether by pledge or contract, must have taken it subject to those covenants, and, therefore, they are in no better case than are Mackenzie and Mann.

subtopic: DEBATE CONTINUED ON MOTION FOR SECOND READING OF CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY BILL.
speechtext:
I was simply deferring any comment in regard to that until we were able to obtain from the Government definite information as to who are the owners of the stock. At that time Mackenzie and Mann were the owners of the stock. They disposed of forty per cent of the stock to the Government. They made the bargain for the transfer of it. If the stock is not now in their hands, the parties who hold
288J
the stock now are subject to the same conditions as those to which Mackenzie and Mann are subject and have no more rights than they had. Hon. gentlemen opposite fail to appreciate the full significance of the point I make in regard to- this matter, and the result and effect of the legislation of 1914, which, in plain words, is this-that when the (Canadian Northern Railway, being in default, as it is conceded they are in default, come to Parliament, Parliament can pass a statute declaring that the equity of redemption in all the property franchises and rights of the Canadian Northern Railway Company and of all their subsidary companies is absolutely debarred and forever foreclosed and become forfeit to the Crown. There is no manner of doubt about that. The Minister of Finance declared in 1914 that the Government had a better remedy than they would have if they owned the whole of the stock.
In the light of that, what do the Government do to-day? They say to Parliament: Although that is a fact, yet because the words " upon such terms and conditions, if any ' aTe in the statute, although we said in 1914 that they did not *mean anything, and that they did not affect the right of Parliament to bar the equity of redemption, yet the door is left open. And the door being left open, the lobby of which my hon. friend from Calgary (Mr. R. B. Bennett) has spoken, has taken place- not with hon. members in this House, but with the Government. Mackenzie and Mann have succeeded in getting the Government to introduce this legislation under which the country is committed to an arbitration with the owners and pledgees of the stock, the effect of which arbitration, according to the statement by the Minister of Finance as to the lines upon which it should be conducted, will, in my judgment, cost this country a hundred million dollars. I say, therefore, that this legislation is absolutely unnecessary. It is a crime, under existing conditions, during the war, when taxation is being levied on sources that have never been touched before, to ask this Parliament to create new conditions* amending the solemn compact entered into in 1914 and declared to be the last and final contract, opening the door to arbitration, wide in its extent and ramifications, which will commit this country to the payment of such a huge amount.
What apology is made for it? The Prime Minister took the very curious ground that the Drayton-Acworth report was not to be

considered, because, he said, they had no authority to make an investigation as to the value of the property. I was dumbfounded to hear him make that statement. Even supposing the Order in Council appointing these gentlemen did nor contain that authority, there is not a man in this House but knows that the commission could not make an investigation on which they might base a report that would be of any value to this House and country unless they procured some data in regard to the value of the property involved. That was the very essence of the whole inquiry. The reference expressly states that the commission were to make full inquiry as to the status of each of the three transcontinental railway systems. Now could any commission make an inquiry into the status of the Canadian Northern Kailway Company that would be worthy of the slightest possible consideration by this Parliament without ascertaining whether or not the assets of the company had a value equal to the lia-biliities? How else could you determine the status of the company? In addition to that, the commissioners were directed to have special reference to "capitalization, fixed charges and net earnings . . . and generally speaking, all matters which the members of the board may consider pertinent or relevant to the general scope of the inquiry." That was the power conferred upon the commission by the Order in Council, and I think the Prime Minister was drawing greatly upon our credulity when he ventured to ask this House to believe that we should not attach full weight to the statements of the Drayton-Acworth report in regard to value, as they were not authorized to inquire into that matter. I was astounded also at the attitude of the Minister of Finance who never mentioned this matter in speaking to the resolution or on the first reading of the Bill, but told us on the second reading that on looking over Professor Swain's report, he discovered that Messrs. Drayton and Acworth bad emitted in their report some items in regard to assets and liabilities. With all deference, I would say that the House and the country ought to hear from the commissioners, Messrs. Drayton, Acworth and Smith as to whether or not the items that were omitted would seriously affect the value of property. [DOT] I think we are entitled to know whether they agree with the view that their report is incorrect and misleading in that respect, and whether this House and the country should not therefore have 
regard tO'" their recommendations as to the value of the property.
The commission discussed seriatim the various bases that might be considered. They say:
A purchaser would not consider either original cost or reproduction cost as of much importance. The price he would pay would he based on earning power, present and potential. On this basis he would consider how far the Canadian Northern is at present short of covering its fixed charges, how long it will take to reach equilibrium, how much new capital will have to be spent, how soon a dividend may be expected and at what rate. Calculating on this basis, in the light of the figures set out abovf. it is evident that no purchaser would offer foi the property a sum amounting to the total of its liabilities.
In other words, the commissioners, disregarding altogether the question of the physical value, say that no purchaser of the railway would pay except upon the basis of the road's earning power, present or potential. They say further:
We conclude, therefore, that the shareholders of the company have no equity either on the ground of cash put in, or on the ground of physical reproduction cost, or on the ground of the saleable value of their property as a going concern. If, then, the people of Canada have already found, or assumed responsibility for, the bulk of the capital; if they must needs find what further capital is required; and if they must make up for some years to come considerable deficits in net earnings, it seems logically to follow that the people of Canada should assume control of the property.
The ground upon which these gentlemen suggest arbitration was not that there was any potential value in the road. They said: These people who were originally connected with the Canadian Northern have done a lot of work and you might take into consideration the question of giving them something ex misericordia. As far as paying the stockholders for the value of the road, the commissioners say that there was no value to be paid for.
Now where do we stand? We have the statute of 1914. We have the declarations of the Prime Minister, the Minister of Finance, and the Solicitor General, that that statute provided for this Government taking over the equity of redemption in the property automatically-there would be no question of confiscation. As the hon. member for St. Antoine said in discussing the efficacy of this provision, "the axe would drop." Now why does not the "axe" "drop"? We have in addition to that, the report of Messrs. Drayton and Acworth, who declared there is nothing to arbitrate about, apart entirely from the question as U, the right of Parliament to deal with

this matter under the equity of redemption. Notwithstanding that, my hon. friend provides for the constitution of this tribunal. And he quoted from Professor Swain's report which dealt academically with questions of value, and said that
10 p.m. these were elements which it would be proper for the arbitrators to take into consideration in determining the value. Further on he said:
They will not be bound to the same extent, under the language of this legislation, by the hard and fast rules of evidence, but can proceed expeditiously to the determination of the question of what is the fair value of the stock of .the Canadian Northern .Railway Company.
It is simply another case of a commission on a commission. The history of this Government in dealing with all matters of public responsibility is simply being repeated. Instead of taking the initiative, instead of the Government dealing with the problems that come before them with force' and courage, a commission is appointed, and if it makes a report that does not suit them, they appoint another commission to investigate the commission. And so, in spite of the statute, in spite of their statements, and in spite of the Drayton-Acworth report, we are to have a new commission which is not to be bound by rules of evidence, and which can decide as it pleases. There is to be an appeal to the Supreme Court of Canada from the Board of Arbitration on questions both of law and of fact. I would submit this question: How is the Supreme Court of Canada to be permitted to set aside the findings of a board of arbitrators who are not to be bound by the laws of evidence in coming to conclusions? How is the Supreme Court of Canada to determine whether or not the findings of the arbitrators in the first instance is one that can be sustained? The arbitrators would be able to say in regard to the admissibility of evidence here, and its exclusion there, "We were not bound by the rules of evidence and could listen to anything we wanted to." Of what use is an appeal made under those conditions?	-
Our situation is this: This Government, notwithstanding our financial position, notwithstanding all the commitments of this country in connection with the war, coolly comes to this Parliament and to the Canadian people and proposes to open the door, which was closed by themselves. The Minister of Finance initiates this proceeding and, to some people whom we do not know, says: I will give you an arbitration which will not be bound by the rules of evidence. And he puts this burden on the
Canadian people in the face of the condi-dition3 I have shown. I believe that when the people of Canada know the full effect of this measure-and I trust they will learn it-they will realize that the proposition of my hon. friend from South Renfrew (Mr. Graham) is one worthy of their support. We, on this side of the House, would be recreant to our duty to the people if we did not insist upon its being presented to this Parliament. Every hon. gentleman who has the best interests of Canada at heart will support that proposition when the vote comes.
Mr. FRANCIS N. McCREA (Sherbrooke): Mr. Speaker, the question that is now engaging the attention of the House appears to me to be one of very great importance. It is a question that requires more information than we have to enable us to deal with it properly. A question involving some $620,000,000 appears to be treated by the Government about as I, when a boy at school would trade jack knives with a companion. They do not seem to think it is serious enough to give the people the necessary information. Local and federal governments combined, representing the people of Canada, have contributed to the construction of this road, and what the obligations are that we are now supposed to assume in addition to the money already advanced is something that it would be interesting to know. It appears to me that it would require a very complete and thorough accounting to show what we have already expended, what we are expected to expend further, and what we are going to get for it. if my information is right, we are not getting all the terminals and everything else connected with the Canadian Northern. The model city, the tunnel through Montreal mountain and the terminals on Dorchester street, I understand are not included.

subtopic: DEBATE CONTINUED ON MOTION FOR SECOND READING OF CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY BILL.
speechtext: The terminals are included.

subtopic: DEBATE CONTINUED ON MOTION FOR SECOND READING OF CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY BILL.
speechtext:
Two years ago the Canadian Northern ran a special train from Quebec to Vancouver and invited all the members, senators and others to join in the excursion for the purpose of examining the road and the country. I considered it my duty to myself and to the country to take that trip, not for my own pleasure, but for the information I might get out of it. I am bound to say, the 'Canadian Northern is a well built road with extremely easy grades and good curves. But I am also bound to say that whoever are responsible for two transcontinental railways being

built, east of Port Arthur and west of Edmonton, were very much lacking in judgment. It is not to their credit. Whilst the road was well constructed, and with very easy grades, for the life of me I cannot see where the traffic is coming from to maintain three transcontinental railways in this country for some time to come. I think that the promoters of this road, Mackenzie and Mann, were too bright and too intelligent to have constructed a road paralleling two other roads in the hope that it was going to be a paying proposition. If the effort of Mackenzie and Mann had "been confined to the prairie country, and if one transcontinental railway had been built in addition to the Canadian Pacific, I think there would have been business for two. But I do not think there is business for three. However, the three roads are built and the question is now: what is to be done with them? The Canadian Northern Railway company came to this Parliament on three different occasions since 1911. On the first occasion they got $7,000,000, the next time $15,000,000, and the next time $45,000,000. The understanding was when they got the last assistance, or guarantee, of bonds to the extent of $45,000,000, that that would be sufficient and that they would never come back. They were to be satisfied for the rest of their lives and were to carry on the road. I was talking with some representatives of Mackenzie and Mann and they still say that they are prepared to carry on the road, and that this Government are doing them a great injustice in taking it over. I do not know whether they are sincere when the say that. I doubt it myself.
We have reached .a point where the Canadian Northern Railway Company cannot finance the road themselves and where they must have more money. It is proposed that instead of taking over the system under legislation passed in 1914. there shall be% submitted to arbitration the question of the value of stock that has no value and never cost anything. It is water, and water is pretty cheap. I do not believe the system is right. The/people believe that the country has put all the money into the road that it is worth. We have the report of gentlemen who were appointed to inquire into the matter that the road is not worth the amount of money that the country has spent on it. It has been stated on both sides of the House that all the money voted by the Governments of Canada has not gone into the construction of the road, but has, in many cases, been diverted. The gentlemen who constructed the Canadian North-

ern own a fishing outfit on the Pacific coast, coal mines, copper mines, and other things. Where did the money come from that went into these things outside the railway?
I am not here to accuse those gentlemen of dishonesty. I have great admiration for any men who have the energy and ability that Messrs. Mackenzie and Mann have shown in the construction of this road and other things. But I am not terribly taken with all .their methods of doing this business. I think that when any man or corporation or company goes to the Government of this country, either local or federal, and seeks .aid, if that aid is granted the Government should see to it, and the applicants should be in honour bound to see to it, that every dollar voted is put into the road and not diverted to other uses.
The question before us is what the road will cost the country and what the country is getting for its money. There is not a man on the other side of the House who will not say that the country has spent as much money as it is worth. The wise and proper way to deal with it is to allow it to go into the hands of a receiver, and then, if there is any value in the stock, let the men who hold the stock get their value after the Government have got part of their money back. Outside of the stock there is about $100,000,000 of outstanding liabilities which .this country wall be expected to become'responsible for when they take this road over. I ask any fair-minded man if it is reasonable for this Government to legislate for the people of Canada to become responsible for debts owed by this road, when the promoters of the road have already got more money from the Government than the road is worth. If a banker had loaned to a man or a combination of men all the money the banker was justified in letting them have, and if the banker then found that the assets of that man or company were not worth the money already advanced, would the bank undertake to pay the stockholders for their common stock, practically all water, and, furthermore, would they undertake to pay the oustanding liabilities of the borrower? No banker would act in that way. Yet, that is just what the Government are doing. Although they have advanced all the money that this road is worth or ever cost, they are prepared to arbitrate the value of its stock, which, it is a pretty well-known fact, has never cost anything.
It if said by the Government that if we were to allow the road to go into the hands

vit a receiver it would be detrimental to the credit of Canada. I do not know why that should affect the taxpayers of Canada so much. This would not be the first road on this continent to go into ttie hands of a receiver. There is scarcely one of them that has not gone into the hands of a receiver at some time, and if the present owners of this one, the promoters, are unable to carry it on and cannot find financial means to carry it on,
1 do not see why, especially at this particular time when the people are being taxed and doubly taxed to carry on the war and to meet other expenses, they should be asked to contribute further to the carrying on of a railroad that cannot pay its_ own way. The financial statement prepared by Messrs. Mackenzie and Mann, whether it is correct or not, shows that their earnings are more than sufficient to pay their running expenses, but they claim that there is not enough to purchase the necessary rolling stock and equipment and at the same time do the necessary repairs. Let me tell the minister that if he had millions of dollars to spend for rolling stock, he could not get it just now anywhere, and at this time of storm and stress, when the Government has difficulty in raising the necessary money to meet its obligations, I do not see any logical or sound reason why we should be asked to take over a road and to arbitrate the value of its stock. It is admitted by this report that the stock has no value. The very fact of the Government consenting to arbitrate for that stock is an admission that it has a value. They invite a value in the face of a report made by competent men who say there is no value. The Government say: We shall arbitrate and fin'd out. The moment you admit that you will arbitrate, you admit there is a value.
As to public ownership. I do not quite agree with the hon. memner for South York (Mr. Maclean), and J think the experience of this country will go to show that it is useless to tell what foreign countries are doing. The experience of this country shows that government ownership of railways is not very desirable. The Government own a road that should be a good road and a paying one, and it would pay a good rate of profit if it were handled on business principles. If the Minister of Railways had the right to handle the road unmolested and not interfered with, and if he handled it on business principles, it would be a paying investment and he would have much less trouble. But when members of Parliament can tell him whom
he should employ and whom he should discharge, when appointments are made through members of this House who want to get jobs for their friends, it is impossible to secure economical operation. If the Minister of Railways were asked he would say that he had more trouble from political interference than ne has with the legitimate operation of his roads-and I do not imagine that the taking over of the Canadian Northern Railway will detract from his troubles in that respect. If such roads as the Government control could be placed under a commission, not of politicians, but of gentlemen appointed for their ability, who would be held responsible for the good management of the road, it would be possible to make that road pay, and to operate it as it should be operated-but there will have to be a very material change from anything that has taken place in the past.
But I do not understand how this Government are going to get away from the legislation passed in 1914, which appears to be plain and explicit. The terms specify just what is to be done in case of default, which has now taken place. I cannot see any reason for the legislation in the interest of the people of Canada, and that is what we are supposed to be here for-the Government is not supposed to be legislating for personal ends or for their friends. I want to say there is not a man in this House or in Canada who can sit down and calmly read over this legislation passed in 1914 and get away from the fact that we have no right to arbitrate or anything else, but only to take over this road according to the terms of the agreement if default has been made. I notice the minister questions one of the articles in connection with taking over this road. Though he made it very plain in 1914, not only in the Act, but in the explanation to the House, now he appears to put an interpretation on it entirely different from hm previous statement. I should like to know whether the minister was trying to deceive the people of this country in 1914, or whether he is trying to deceive them now. It must be either one or the other. I am absolutely opposed to government ownership of anything bandied as the present railway system of Canada is handled, and I am also absolutely opposed either to arbitration, or to reference to the exchequer Counrt to put any value on this stock. It has no -value, and if the people who hold consider the stock has any value let them pay off the Government and they will own the road and the stock both.
.COMMONS
It is not up to the Government of Canada, who have advanced the cash and taken proper security, to throw aside their security and take care of the people who are not secured. There appears to be about *100,000,000 of outstanding liability, but the creditors of this road did not have any guarantee from the Government of this country that they would be protected; neither did the stockholders. They have taken the common stock as collate! al, I presume. The Government did not guarantee that the stock was worth a cent.
The people who hold that stock took it, probably, because they could not get anything else, and, if they can get the Government to take over the road and become responsible for all the debts, undoubtedly they have made a good trade. But what kind of trade has the country made? A very bad bargain, and the Government of the day will be responsible for it. I trust that the good sense of the Government will induce them to reconsider what they are doing. If the Canadian Northern have reached the limit, where they cannot finance their own business, let them turn the road into the hands of a receiver, and let him take care of it. If the outstanding debts and stock are worth anything, all right, but if not, the taxpayer of Canada should not be called upon to contribute any further to a matter of this kind. We have enough to take care of without that.

speechtext:
After the very able speech which has been delivered by my hon. friend from Sherbrooke (Mr. McCrea), and the cogent arguments which have been advanced by the hon. gentleman from Pictou (Mr. Macdonald), I do not know that I should delay the House any longer. Yet, Mr. Speaker, as one representing a constituency, composed of a large majority of farmers, who will be called upon to pay further taxes in order to meet the added liabilities which this transaction brings on the people of Canada, I feel that I cannot let this legislation pass without protesting against it. First of all, I think I should characterize this transaction as a most extraordinary if not indefensible one, and I cannot do other [DOT] wise than blame my hon. friend the Minister of Finance (Sir Thomas White) for having introduced this legislation at the close of a long session, and at the end of a long Parliament. This legislation will involve the country in millions, in fact in hundreds of millions, and it is thereby impairing the credit of the country, when the

credit of the country is so essential to enable it to face the present crisis. I am surprised that the Minister of Finance should countenance such a piece of legislation in the midst of the greatest war which humanity has ever seen or will ever see, when Canada is involved in that war, and when all the resources of the country are needed to meet the exigencies of the war. The least we might have expected from the hon. gentleman, if he was in such a rush was that he would wait until the election had taken place, when new legislators had been elected with a fresh mandate, taking into consideration the fact that this House is far from being complete, as at least one-fourth of its membership re not here, and in the next Parliament there will be fourteen new seats in this House. Of course, we have had many instances where the Government, in the course of its administration, has paid little respect to the people of Canada. In the present instance, I do not hesitate to say that Parliament is being treated with contempt by the Government. First of all, we have presented to us the biggest transaction since the Canadian Pacific and the Grand Trunk Pacific contracts, that has ever been brought before the House, involving the credit of the country to the extent of six hundred millions of dollars.
Yet, Sir, in answer to the inquiry whether they would lay on the table of the House the correspondence exchanged between the Government and the parties who are to profit by this transaction, the right hon. leader of this House (Sir Robert Borden) and the Minister of Finance answered, with a bland smile: "There is no such correspondence." Who in this House or in the country will believe- that no correspondence has been exchanged in regard to this matter between the Government and the Canadian Northern Railway Company? You can fool some of the people all of the time; you can fool all of the people some of the time, but you can't fool all of the people all the time. There is a limit to the credulity of the people. The first documents to be laid on the Table should have been the correspondence exchanged between Mackenzie and Mann-or, if you please, the Canadian Northern Railway Company-and the Government.
Not later than yesterday-this legislation not having been fully examined, passed upon, or disposed of-my hon. friend (Sir Thomas White) announced to Parliament and to the country that he had already appointed the arbitrator who was to act on
r

behalf of the Government I have the honour of knowing Sir William Meredith, the Chief Justice of the province of Ontario.
I have nothing to say against the character, the integrity or the ability of that eminent jurist. But it was stated this afternoon by the member^or North Cape Breton (Mr. McKenzie) that one-third of the board of arbitrators was committed to value being given to the $60,000,000 worth of stock. The member for North Cape Breton should have eaid that more than one-third was so committed. The Canadian Northern Bailway Company will appoint one arbitrator; surely that arbitrator will be for the Canadian Northern Railway Company. The Government has already appointed Sir William Meredith and instructed him through the Minister of Finance that there is value in that stock, which, however, according to the report of Messrs. Drayton and Acworth, is valueless. Therefore, two-thirds of the commission is already committed to the declaring of a value in respect of stock so referred to in the Drayton-Aoworth report.
On each occasion upon which the Canadian Northern Railway Company came to Parliament for subsidies, financial aid, or Government guarantee, we were told that they were coming to Parliament for the last time. But many times they have been here for the last time; now they are again before us. I followed with some interest the remarks made by the member for South Renfrew (Mr. Graham) yesterday. He is somewhat of an expert in railway matters, having presided for several years over the Department of Railways. According to his statement, the Canadian Northern has a credit balance of $8,000,000. Mackenzie and Mann, or the Canadian Northern Railway Company, therefore, do not require aid from the Government at this time. I believe that the member for South Renfrew was right in his remarks; I do not believe that the real claimants or the petitioners in the present instance are Mackenzie and Mann. As was stated by the member for South Renfrew-and the circumstantial evidence, in my judgment, proves it conclusively-the proposal which is being considered by the House, and which will be passed to-morrow, has been cleverly devised by bondholders, pledgees and financiers who wish to make secure their investments in an enterprise which, perhaps on account of the circumstances connected with the war, might not be altogether safe. Is it the function of Parliament to come to the
rescue of financiers, bondholders and pledgees who have staked their all on a private enterprise? Is that the duty of the hour? I appeal to my hon. friends who claim to be the only loyalists in this country, is there not something more pressing than this legislation? Every morning I read in the press about meetings that are being held from one end of the country to the other, especially in those highly imperialistic centres, Toronto, Winnipeg, Vancouver, and elsewhere, where the Round Table is so predominant. 'I read about win-the-war meetings, at which resolutions are being vociferously passed demanding of the Government that a win-the-war cabinet be formed and that a union Government be established in order to carry us through the present dire emergency. I notice that when those meetings are held in Toronto they are generally presided over by the pledgees, financiers and bondholders of the Canadian Northern Railway Company. They are the Warwicks of the present Government; they are the makers and maybe the unmakers of this Administration, and this explains, perhaps, why the Prime Minister, the Minister of Finance, and their' majority behind them, are so anxious to obey their dictates.
When I see men playing with patriotism, with Imperialism, as the financiers and backers of the Canadian Northern Railway Company are doing, I am reminded of that little episode in the French revolution. When the famous Madame Roland was approaching the scaffold she saw the statue of Liberty, and she exclaimed as she was passing by: " O, Liberty, how many crimes are committed in thy name!" I say, Mr. Speaker: O, Great War of 1917, O, Imperialism, O, Patriotism, how many crimes are committed in thy name in Canada ! Whilst the financiers, the 'bondholders and the pledgees of the Canadian Northern Railway Company are agitating the country from the Atlantic to the Pacific, in order, -as they say, to win the war, whilst they are thus diverting the attention of the public from the real facts of the case, I regret to say that the press of Canada is unfaithful to its great traditions. I stated the other day, when this resolution was introduced into the 'House,' that the press of Canada appeared to be chloroformed on this question. I repeat that statement., The press of Canada is being chloroformed on this question; it does not rise in its might to protest against the greatest piece of villainy that was ever perpetrated by a Canadian Government.

I accept the correction of my hon. friend, but if I had time to delve into the language used in the memorable speech delivered by my hon. friend in this House a few years ago against the Canadian Northern Railway Company, I should possibly find an expression even more severe than the one I have just used. Did not my hon. friend say, in 1914, that Parliament was legislating in order to make richer the wealthiest man in Canada, Sir William Mackenzie? 1 remember how my hon. friend branded him on that occasion, and his speech, whioh, in some respects, is a classic, inspired me at that time, and if I spoke and voted as I did in 1914, I give my hon. friend credit for convincing me, I ''will not say of the villainy, but of the audacity of the Government thus to give to men who had already received millions of dollars from the various governments an additional subsidy of 45 millions. The press of the country is silent on this transaction. I listened some days ago to the speech delivered by the ex-Minister of Militia (Sir Sam Hughes), and he hinted that the Minister of Finance had sweetened the press for a certain purpose. That was denied, it is true, by the Minister of Finance. We have the word of denial, but we have also the accusation as between two compeers who sat in the same council. I have so far found only one paper which has dared to express its opinion on the present transaction. It is an old paper, and I do not hesitate to state this evening that in my judgment it is the most sound of all papers.
I refer to the Montreal Weekly Witness, edited by Mr. J. R. Dougall, a man who, for the last fifty years, has closely followed political events in Canada. Speaking of the Canadian Northern and referring to the Minister of Finance,, he says:
Sir Thomas White has announced that he is going to buy for the country the Canadian Northern Railway, and make dt a government railway, but keep it separate from the other government railways. We would like to have a great deal more information than we have about this railway and its history, so as to be able to judge of the fairness of the bargain which Sir Thomas White proposes. There are
fMr. Lemieux.]
signs that it needs very careful consideration, and * that Sir Thomas White himself has not gfiven it the kind of consideration that the country would like to give it if the information was accessible. In the purchase of the railway Sir Thomas White is acting as financial agent for the people of Canada, and only a day or two after he has committed the people to the purchase of a railway worth a few hundred million, he stands up and admits in the House of Commons, without a blush, that he does not know whether the Model City Company is a part of the Canadian Northern Railway or whether it is not. Now the Model City near Montreal is representative of a very great deal in this transaction. There are subsidiary properties everywhere. In fact the enterprise is a vast network of subsidiary properties. This particular property became so valuable that*it sold for a price equal to many times the cost of the tunnel under Mount Royal, owing to the magnificent entrance made possible by it to the heart of the city. Here is a company worth millions of dollars and our financial agent does not know whether it is included in the deal which he has completed or not. We might ask for instance whether Sir Thomas White knows whether the Tunnel Company is part of the purchase or whether we must pay toll to it also forever. If any individual had such a financial agent working for him, would that financial agent not. lose his position the moment he acknowledged such singular inadvertence. If Sir Thomas White does not know whether the Model City property belongs to the Canadian Northern Railway or not we have no reason to suppose he knows whether a hundred and one other subsidiary companies of the system, which are really the cream of the whole business, belong to the company bought out or not. It looks very much like as if he might be allowing Messrs. Mackenzie and Mann to get away with all the cream and leave the country with an appalling-

merely since yesterday, but for many years past. It has engrossed the attention of the Parliament of Canada ever since I came here.
There are people who believe that we have overreached ourselves, that we have built too many railways. But I am one of those who believe with my hon. friend the ex-Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Graham), that the transportation necessities of this country require as many and perhaps more railways than we already have. At all events, the Government thought it wise last year to appoint a commission composed of the best men in Canada, the United States and Great Britain. They selected three experts, Sir Henry Drayton, Mr. Smith and Mr. Acworth. For weeks and months, accompanied by engineers, they travelled from one end of the country to the other. They delved into the books of the various railway systems and they were helped in that task by auditors of ability. They made a report as a result of their long and painstaking investigation. Now, this report is discarded. The Government knows that report created an impression on public opinion and that Sir Henry Drayton and Mr. Acworth have some weight with the thinking people of this country. For a few months we w8re told that the Government might perhaps accept the recommendations of the majority report. Then there was silence in the press and mystery in the Government councils. After this session had been called, and when the people had nearly forgotten the Drayton-Acworth report, the Government all of a sudden boldly discards it and now propose to take a step in another direction.
It is strange, Mr. Speaker, how the Government takes little stock in its own commissioners. Some years ago it appointed a judge in Winnipeg on the recommendation of the hon. Minister of Public Works (Mr. Rogers). The appointee had had a long and brilliant career at the Bar and was a man of legal acumen. This judge was appointed by the Manitoba Government to preside over an investigation concerning some of the activities of the ex-ministers in Winnipeg. He made his report and immediately the Government, knowing full well that the conclusions of that report were damaging, if not mortal, to one of the Cabinet ministers, appoints another commission to revise the report of Mr. Justice Galt. Later on a gentleman appointed by the Prime Minister in the Department of Justice, Mr. O'Connor, K.C.,
TMr. Lemieux.]
of Halifax, is entrusted with another mission. He is asked to report on the cold storage system of Canada. Innocently, I must say, but honestly-you will notice, Mr. Speaker, that innocence is always honest-he reports the most damaging conclusions against some of the financiers, some of the trusted friends of the Administration. The Government hastens to appoint another commission to revise the damaging report of its nominee.
As I stated a moment ago, it appointed a commission to report on the railway situation of Canada. The report has been published, and it is one which carries weight. But the Government suddenly finds that the report will not come to the rescue of those who, in 1911, formed a league to defeat the late Government and install in office the gentlemen who are now at the head of affairs. I should compare the Government to Saturn devouring his own children. Nearly every report ordered by the Government has been discarded, thrown into the waste basket; and with regard to the railway situation we are now to expect fuller information from another commission. I remember that in the old Parliament, when the Grand Trunk Pacific project was being considered by the House, the slogan invented by the late Mr. Blair against the late Mr. Cox was: "Cox cannot wait." That slogan created considerable merriment. The Tories repeated it from one end of the country to the other. Yet the late Mr. Cox, then a member of the Senate, offered on many occasions, and his offer was not accepted, to adduce proof of the untruthfulness of the slogan. But, Mr. Speaker, if it was true then that Cox could not wait, it seems ten times truer that certain buccaneers cannot wait to-day in the year of our Lord 1917. In these days of stress, when even the national credit of Canada is imperilled by the dire necessities of war, they must secure at the expense of the treasury the investments which they have made in a private enterprise. This war, with all its sorrows, has made in Canada a crop of millionaires. That explains to a certain degree the unrest of the country. The O'Connor'report has lifted a veil from certain profits which in my judgment are of a nature to sow the seeds of rebellion in any country. You will remember that the French Revolution started at the bakeries in Paris. There were in those days some Flavelles who kept the corn which came from the fields of France

and who allowed that corn to come in only in small quantities and by night into Paris in order to maintain high prices.
The poor people understood that there were men mean enough to speculate on the hunger of the consumers. They invaded the streets of Paris, they broke loose, and that was the beginning of the revolution. If you read the recent history of the Russian revolution, you will find that it started at the bakeries of Petrograd and Moscow. The millionaires and profiteers of this war in Canada are also, I make bold to say, sowing the seeds of revolution. The Government in this present transaction propose to arbitrate the valuation of a stock which has been declared valueless. Shall I read again, for the information of the House, the conclusions arrived at by the commissioners:
A third basis of estimate is the value of the property for sale as a going concern. A purchaser would not consider either original cost or reproduction cost as of much importance. The price he would pay would be based on earning power, present and potential. On this basis he would consider how far the Canadian Northern is at present short of covering its fixed charges, how long it will take to reach equilibrium, how much new capital will have to be spent, how soon a dividend may be expected and at what rate. Calculating on this basis, in the light of the figures set out above, it is evident that no purchaser would offer for the property a sum amounting to the total of its liabilities.
We conclude, therefore, that the shareholders of the company have no equity either on the ground of cash put in, or on the ground of physical reproduction cost, or on the ground of the saleable value of their property as a going concern.
If then the people of Canada have already found or assumed responsibility for the bulk of the capital; if they must needs find what further capital is required; and if they must make up for some years to come considerable deficits in net earnings, it seems logically to follow that the people of Canada should assume control of the property. We return later to the Canadian Northern Company in order to set out our recommendations as to its ownership and management in the future and as to the returns to be offered to the existing shareholders.
Can there be any question as to the conclusions of the commissioners? They declare here that the Canadian Northern Railway have no equity whatever and, in their recommendations, they state further:
We do not recommend that further public aid be given to the Canadian Northern as at present constituted.
The Canadian Northern common stock represents no cash investment, and has no present value, either on the basis of the cost of reproduction of the property, or on the basis of its earning power.
So, basing myself on the report of the majority of the commission, I say that the
Canadian Northern Railway has no claim to have any value put on its stock or to have an arbitration to fix a value. The Minister of Finance has already discredited completely that report. He has ignored its contents. Indeed he has given to Sir William Meredith his brief, because in the speech which he delivered only yesterday he showed Sir William Meredith how value could be given to the common stock. First of all he does what the Minister of Public Works did with the Galt report, he begins by abusing the men he has appointed. He says:
Upon this finding some hon. gentlemen opposite have argued that there should be no submission to arbitration because of the calculations of the commissioners as to the value of the assets, the amount -of the liabilities of the company and their opinion of its value as a going concern. But, I would point out to the House that there are certain important omissions in the Drayton-Acworth report.
Here is a report which has been prepared after long elaboration and searching investigation and my hon. friend, finding that this report goes against his friends, proclaims that very important omissions have been made. It is a pretty strong hint given to Sir William Meredith that he must find out those omissions, and he adds:
In other words, none of these things are conclusive; they are only elements in the question of what is the fair value in connection with a system such as this, which would, I think, be proper for arbitrators to take into consideration in valuing the assets and liabilities-not as determining factors but as elements in the determination of what is a fair value.
There will also be the question of the earnings of the Canadian Northern Railway Company, present earnings and prospective earnings.
Mr. Speaker, with such a brief given to Sir William Meredith, I say that two-thirds of the commission are already committed in favour of the Canadian Northern Company.

speechtext:
I will refer my friend to the legislation passed by this House in 1914, which he eloquently, and myself modestly, opposed. In 1914, when the bargain was made with Mackenzie and Mann or the Canadian Northern Railway, Parliament agreed to aid it to the extent of $45,-

000,000 On what conditions? A cavenant was made between the people of Canada, as represented by the Government, and the Canadian Northern Railway system. I want the Government to live up to that covenant, and I want the Canadian Northern to be made to live up to it. It was agreed that $45,000,000 of common stock should be handed to the Government. It was further agreed that the Government was to have% the right to take over the road in event of default. It was set out by section 21 what would be a case of default by the Canadian Northern system. And if there was default, a certain summary procedure was to be taken and the agreement was thereby to be carried out. What does section 21 of the statute say? It reads as follows.
The following shall be events of default within the meaning of this Act, viz.:
(a) If the Canadian Northern shall make default in payment of the principal or interest of the guaranteed securities or any part thereof, or default in observing or performing any of the provisions of the new Trust Deed and the security constituted by the new Trust .Deed shall thereby become enforceable.
I shall not proceed further. I will take the admission that I find in the speech delivered the other day by the hon. Minister of Finance (Sir Thomas White). He is my witness. He declared, when he introduced the resolution, that the company is not financially able to meet its liabilities. He said:
The result is that the company is short of cash for the purpose of paying interest upon its underlying securities.
And further on he repeats:
It is therefore unable to pay its underlying interest charges.
A little further on he says:
In addition to this, the company has had to do a great deal of short date financing. There is outstanding, secured, for the most part, by Dominion or provincial guaranteed bonds or debentures, short term loans floated in New York or London. The amount of that ordinary, short term liability is about $100,000,000, extending over a period of two years or more.
It is not possible for the company, by the issue of permanent securities, to fund that debt. Therefore, it is obliged from time to time to renew these short-term securities, and to carry on as best it may from year to year. The company have, in the past, come to the Government and asked us, as they did last year, to make them a loan of a sufficient amount to take care of the underlying interest charges and to meet the maturing instalments of principal upon rolling stock.
Sir, my best witness that the Canadian Northern Railway is to the wall at the present time, and unable to meet its liabilities,

is the hon. Minister of Finance (Sir Thomas White). Therefore I say, according to section 21 of the Act passed in 1914, the company is in default, and if the company is in default foreclosure follows, by section 24. The marginal note of that section reads as follows:
Equity of redemption foreclosed on default and vested in His Majesty.
And section 24 itself reads:
If authorized by the Parliament of Canada, the Governor in Council may, on such terms and conditions (if any) as Parliament may prescribe, at any time while any event of default shall exist and be continuing, by order declare the equity of redemption of the Canadian Northern and of all other persons whomsoever in the mortgaged premises to be foreclosed, and thereupon the equity of redemption of the Canadian Northern (and of such other persons) in the mortgaged premises and every part thereof shall be and become absolutely barred and foreclosed, and the same shall thereupon be vested in His Majesty in right of the Dominion of Canada, any statutory enactment or any rule of law or equity to the contrary notwithstanding.
Is it'possible to find a sanction so clear, so precise and so much to the point as the one which is enacted by section 24? I repeat again, if there were a free press in Canada to-day the people would revolt, because the people would know what plot is being hatched at the present moment. Hon. gentlemen in this House have been quibbling, when discussing whether the company is in default or not. First, I have the definition given by the statute. Then I have the corroboration given by the very words uttered by the Finance Minister. But, Mr. Speaker, we have the description of the nature of the sanction enacted by section 24, in the speech delivered in 1914 by my hon. friend the member for St. Antoine (Sir Herbert Ames). That hon. gentleman enjoys the respect of this House and of the community. I do not share his views on-all political matters; I find him rather narrow in many things. But let us be frank; the hon. member from St. Antoine (Sir Herbert Ames) enjoys the respect and the confidence of the business community. He himself, is a business man. He is one of the captains of industry in the city of Montreal. When the Government are in a quandary, when they are in a bad corner, as in 1914, when they were being assailed by my hon. friend from Calgary (Mr. Bennett) and by my hon. friend from Kingston (Mr. Niekle), they go to the member for St. Antoine, and he generally finds the plausible explanation to save them. In 1914, after

the speeches delivered by the two hon. members to whom I have alluded, the Government appealed to the member for St. Antoine to placate public opinion in Canada, because the business men were rather struck by the audacity of the Government when they came forward with a legislation by which the Canadian Northern Railway Company was again receiving such a large amount of public money. The hon. member for St. Antoine undertook to explain how easy it would be to get control of the Canadian Northern Railway system, and to brush away all pretenses they might have, if, perchance they should attempt to exact some value for their stock. Let me quote the language of my hon. friend from St. Antoine. I think it is very important that we should hear it. He said:
What is to happen in case of default?
We were discussing then section 24. He continues:
We have hitherto been dealing with the situation in case of success. The Government has very carefully looked ahead in regard to what might happen in case of failure.
Failure was not prophesied, but failure haunted the minds of many, and, therefore, the member for St. Antoine said:
The Government has very carefully looked ahead to what might happen in case of failure.
Ordinarily, it is a very slow process to foreclose a railroad and foi' the bondholders gradually to take possession of the physical assets thereof. The Government in this case, however, has supplied a method of quick procedure whereby the axe drops instantly and whereby there can be no coming back for further assistance. It is definitely stipulated in this undertaking what shall constitute any event of default. It is so clearly defined that there can be no possible misunderstanding. Should the Canadian Northern Railway fail to pay interest on the securities which are to be issued in connection with the guarantee which we are now authorizing, or should they fail to carry out any of the conditions contained in the trust deed as accompanying that guarantee, they would commit an event of default. Should the Canadian Northern, on any of the previously guaranteed securities or hereafter guaranteed securities fail to pay the interest, they would commit an event of default. [DOT]
Then, comparing the action that could be taken under this .section to the axe that chopped off the head of Charles I, the member for St. Antoine declared that in case of default the axe would fall upon the necks of 'Mackenzie and Mann. I do not see the member for St. Antoine in the House; I suppose we shall not see him during the course of this debate. I hope he will not appear to register his vote in favour of this proposal.	y
Our clear duty is to foreclose forthwith; to act under .section 24 of the statute of 1914. We have .a right to take .possession of that property which the Government of Canada created with moneys out of the public treasury. The Canadian Northern Railway Company have mortgaged their property; they cannot meet the interest charges; under section 24 the Canadian people have the right to exercise foreclosure.
We should take over the road; the Government should appoint a commission to administer it. I see the Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Cochrane) in his seat. Speaking for myself personally, I should not be averse to the hon. gentleman's taking charge of the administration of the Canadian Northern as he has taken charge of the administration of the Intercolonial railway. Some people have found fault with him, but on the whole, .although he has a blunt way of speaking, his dealings with the people of the country have been generally fair, and, as I say, I would not be opposed to entrusting to him the administration of the 'Canadian Northern. At any rate, that would be a lesser evil than that which is proposed under this measure.
You can describe this transaction in one sentence:	Canada will be burdened with
the liabilities of Mackenzie and Mann, and Mackenzie and Mann will continue to run the road. Enough assistance has been given to that system; enough millions have been handed to it. I say -in .all sincerity and earnestness that the .financial condition of the country should make the Minister of Finance, the watch-dog of the treasury, pause and think. We are staggering under the burdens of the war. I am surprised that some hon. gentlemen opposite .smile when I make that assertion. Is.it not a fact that this country is staggering under the burdens of the war? 'Is it not a fact this burden is felt by every man, woman and child of this generation, and that many other generations will feel it? Yet hon. gentlemen smile when I speak of the burden under which we .are staggering. It is a national crime at this moment to increase the financial burden of Canada. The Minister of Finance knows that the increase of that financial burden amounts in round figures to $600,000,000. In the course of his Budget speech the minister said:
While our national saving during the war has been gratifyingly large, it is not so great as it should have been and to-day no better advice can be offered to the public than to exercise the strictest thrift and economy.
What example is the Minister of Finance giving to the people? He preaches one

doctrine and practises another. He preaches thrift and economy to the people who are overburdened by the war, and yet he spends lavishly. The Government of which he forms a part has appointed a Food Controller who, very wisely preaches economy and thrift. The Government should set the example. Speaking of the financial conditions of Canada and of our war expenditure, my hon. friend said:
Coming next to the question of our direct war expenditure, we find that with our increasing military effort it also is continually increasing. Since the beginning of hostilities our total war outlay, including estimated and unadjusted liability to Great Britain for the maintenance of our troops at the front and inclusive of withheld pay, totals, so far as we can calculate, about $600,000,000. As the result of this large war expenditure, the net national debt of Canada, which was $336,000,000 before the outbreak of war, has risen to over $900,000,000.
And if I were to ask my hon. friend this evening what the total war debt of Canada is at this date, I am sure he would have to *admit that it has passed the billion-dollar mark. Speaking further, he said:
During the recess we successfully floated the third Canadian War Loan, an issue of $150,000,000 five per cent, twenty year bonds at 96	It is my present intention to arrange then for an issue of notes or treasury bills and if conditions are favourable offer another war loan in the early fall.
Since the outbreak of the war we have floated in Canada domestic loans aggregating $350,000,000 and have in addition furnished $150,000,000 through our chartered banks to the Imperial Treasury to meet its commitments for munitions and supplies purchased in Canada.
Sir, we have a war debt of over $1,000,000,000, to meet which for the present we have issued war loans. For the first time-and I wish I could say for the only time in the financial history of Canada-we find the Minister of Finance, hat in hand, going to Washington to ask the American authorities to give him a slice of the Liberty Loan. Canada is paying a usurious rate of six per cent, with our bonds selling at 98. Is not my hon. friend afraid of the financial status of our country? Is he not staggered at the position we occupy to-day on this continent? When the republics of the South can borrow at par; when the Government of the United States is lending money to the warring nations of Europe, which are already restless and who have proportionately much greater loans to carry than Canada; when those loans are being issued at low rates, is the Minister of Finance not afraid of the financial position of our country? Is he not at times affrighted when he thinks of the financial obligations of

the future? I will not say that such transactions as those which are being considered by the House at the present time spell bankruptcy, but they bring us very near to the verge of bankruptcy. When the Minister of Finance contemplates adding to our war debt liabilities which he could well ignore to the amount of $600,000,000, he is living in a fool's paradise. Our war debt is huge. Our expenditures are increasing every day; our taxation bills are becoming more and more exacting; yet the ordinary expenditures are still on the increase. The Minister of Finance has been brought up in a school of financiers who do not seem to know where to stop in their financial vagaries. The expenditures on Consolidated Fund Account amounted, in round figures, in 1910, to $79,000,000; in 1911, to $87,000,000; in 1912, to $98,000,000, and in 1916, after deducting interest charges caused by pensions and war necessities, to $107,000,000. I have already stated, in the course of another debate, that the Minister of Finance should, during the war, reduce the ordinary expenditures of this country by 50 per cent. If he cannot or will not do that, I beseech him to come back to the figure of our times of prosperity of 1911 or 1912 when we were not exceeding $98,000,000 of ordinary expenditure. I am sorry that I have spoken at such length-

speechtext:
More sorry however for the vote that will be given by the superloyalists who say: "Hear, hear," by the " win-the-war " members, who exploit the sentiments of the people at the present juncture in order to make it easy for Mackenzie and Mann to raid the Canadian treasury.
It was stated a moment ago that the Minister of Finance might, at least, have referred the whole matter to the Exchequer Court. I will not enlarge on that subject, but the reason why the matter is not referred to Sir Walter Cassels is no doubt, because, during recess, a matter quite similar to the present one was referred to him by the Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Cochrane). Every one will remember the raid made on the public treasury by the Quebec and Saguenay Railway. The matter, fortunately, for Canada, went before Sir Walter Cassels, the senior judge of the Exchequer Court, and what happened there? Although a limit had been fixed by the present Government as to the amount that should be paid to the Quebec and Saguenay, the Lotbiniere and Megantic, and the Que-

bee and Montmorency railways, although the attorney appointed by the Government, was ready to let go, Sir Walter Gassels- and I have his judgment in my hand- refused to let go and did not accept the conclusions of the Government attorney. He took the law into his own hands and declared what was the value of the Quebec and Saguenay and of the Quebec and Montmorency railways, and, with one stroke of the pen, he saved millions of dollars for the country. That explains why the same people are coming again with implementing legislation to get, by other means, what they could not get before honest Sir Walter Cassels. Sir, let it 'be known that the people who are to-day raiding the Canadian treasury in this transaction are the very same people who are interested in the Quebec and Saguenay railway and who will, in a few days ask the Parliament of Canada to pay them whatever money they have invested in that losing concern. The very same people were also the pledgees, the bondholders, the financiers of the Quebec and Saguenay, and it is to them that the Minister of Finance will shortly ask this Parliament to hand over another J arge sum of money out of the public treasury.
I repeat, if we had a free press in this country the people would know of these damnable transactions and would rise in revolt against a Government which is raining them whilst playing on their noblest sentiments. Conscription ! Win the war! Union Government!-those are but a ruse to facilitate the conspiracy of the buccaneers and rovers who are anxious to once more lay their hands on the Canadian treasury.	.
On the motion of Mr. R. B. Bennett, the debate was adjourned.
